Equilibrium uniqueness and the balance of forces

pages.text: Agglomeration and Dispersion Forces Economic activity is intensely concentrated in space — in cities, and within cities in neighborhoods such as Manhattan or the Square Mile in London — and explaining this concentration is the central organizing question of spatial economics. Agglomeration forces make density productive and pleasant: knowledge spillovers, input sharing, labor-market matching, love of variety from increasing returns, and consumption or amenity externalities all raise productivity and utility where people and firms cluster. Dispersion forces push activity apart: the fixed supply of land and housing, the cost of commuting, congestion in amenities and transport, and the idiosyncratic heterogeneity of preferences that keeps workers willing to remain in less productive places. Quantitative spatial economics parameterizes both force families, most canonically as density elasticities of productivity and amenities, and shows that their balance determines whether a spatial equilibrium is unique, whether agglomeration is self-reinforcing, and how responsive the spatial distribution is to trade, transport, and policy shocks. This page develops the taxonomy, the canonical estimates, and the formal uniqueness conditions that recur across the corpus. The taxonomy of forces The microfoundations of agglomeration have been classified since Marshall as knowledge spillovers, thick labor markets, and backward-and-forward linkages; the modern survey convention, following Duranton and Puga, groups them into sharing, matching, and learning (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Quantitative models rarely model these mechanisms separately. Instead, the survey's menu of building blocks captures them through a small set of reduced-form devices: increasing returns and love of variety that make a location more attractive the larger its market, endogenous productivity that depends on surrounding economic activity, and endogenous amenities that respond to the density of residents (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). The dispersion side of the menu is equally spare: a fixed factor such as land in utility or production is a congestion force, commuting costs disperse workplaces from residences, congestion in transportation raises travel times with use, and idiosyncratic preferences make the supply of labor to each location upward-sloping rather than perfectly elastic (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). A compact formalization that unifies much of the menu is the local-spillover specification of Allen and Arkolakis, in which overall productivity and amenity in a location depend on its own population density: $$A(i) = \overline{A}(i)L(i)^{\alpha}, \qquad u(i) = \overline{u}(i)L(i)^{\beta},$$ where $\alpha$ is a productivity spillover and $\beta$ an amenity spillover, the latter often negative because it absorbs inelastic housing supply (allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography). For particular parameter values the framework is isomorphic to the Krugman monopolistic-competition model, the Helpman model with residential land, and Ricardian and Armington trade models with external economies; the same agglomeration-and-congestion building blocks appear in trade models and in models of a single city's internal structure (allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Production externalities The canonical intra-city specification makes a block's productivity an increasing, spatially decaying function of the travel-time-weighted density of workplace employment around it: $$A{j} = a{j}Y{j}^{\lambda}, \qquad Y{j} \equiv \sum{s=1}^{S} e^{-\delta\tau{js}}\left(\frac{H{Ms}}{K{s}}\right),$$ where $H{Ms}/K{s}$ is workplace employment density per unit of land, $\delta$ governs spatial decay with travel time, and $\lambda$ is the elasticity of productivity with respect to the externality (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Structural GMM estimation on the Berlin Wall natural experiment yields $\lambda \approx 0.07$ with decay $\delta \approx 0.36$, so production externalities fall to near zero within roughly ten minutes of travel time — a figure toward the high end of the 3–8% range estimated across cities (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The within-city estimate holds travel times constant; a doubling of total city population typically combines densification with an expansion of built-up area that raises average travel times and attenuates the externality at rate $\delta$ (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Evidence from other settings is broadly consistent. For Bogotá's bus rapid transit expansion, Tsivanidis estimates a productivity spillover of $\mu{A} \approx 0.25$, larger than Berlin's but identified off a transport shock in a developing city with substantial reallocation (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). For Chinese cities, Wu and You estimate a city-size elasticity of wages and productivity of roughly 0.1 using historical city size as an instrument, embedded in a production function with skill-specific externalities of about $\varphi{H} \approx 0.08$ for high-skill and $\varphi{L} \approx 0.02$ for low-skill labor (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Across all of these settings, a doubling of density raises productivity and wages by on the order of 3–10 percent, with the exact number depending on spatial scale and on whether travel times or land area are held fixed. Cross-paper pattern (2026-07): Within-city density elasticities are consistent in sign and magnitude across very different settings — $\lambda \approx 0.07$ in Berlin, $\mu{A} \approx 0.25$ in Bogotá, $\varphi \approx 0.1$ for Chinese cities — and all are highly localized, decaying to near zero within minutes of travel time (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure; wu-you-2025-urbanization). Comparison is nonetheless hazardous: the estimates differ in whether they hold travel times fixed, in the density measure used, and in the identifying shock (severed externalities, expanded transit access, or a level regression on city size). Residential and amenity externalities Amenities are themselves endogenous to density. Ahlfeldt and coauthors model residential amenities symmetrically to production: $B{i} = b{i}\Omega{i}^{\eta}$ with $\Omega{i} \equiv \sum{r=1}^{S} e^{-\rho\tau{ir}}(H{Rr}/K{r})$, estimating an elasticity of amenities with respect to residence density of $\eta \approx 0.15$ and a decay rate $\rho \approx 0.76$, again near zero within about ten minutes of travel time (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). This underpins the "consumer city" view that consumption externalities are an agglomeration force comparable to production externalities (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The same logic operates at the level of skill composition: in Bogotá, Tsivanidis finds that residential amenities depend on the college share of a neighborhood's residents, so a transit improvement that attracts high-skilled workers raises amenities and pulls in further high-skilled residents — a residential-externality channel that acts as a force for skill segregation (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Cross-city evidence points the same way: Diamond shows that the rising geographic sorting of US college graduates into high-wage, high-rent cities was partly fueled by endogenous amenity growth within higher-skill cities, widening inequality beyond the direct effect of the wage premium (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Because amenities and productivity are correlated, the central identification problem is separating residential externalities from shared locational fundamentals — high land prices and dense residence could simply reflect an attractive natural site (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Dispersion forces: land, commuting, congestion, taste Four dispersion forces recur. The first is the immobile factor: land used residentially or commercially is a congestion force because concentration bids up land prices and reduces real wages — the force behind the Helpman uniqueness condition $\sigma(1-\alpha) > 1$, where a higher land share $(1-\alpha)$ strengthens dispersion (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography). The second is commuting, which disperses workplaces from residences and, by letting workers access high-productivity employment without living there, relieves the land-price congestion of central locations (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). Commuting flows follow a gravity equation with a travel-time semi-elasticity of roughly $\nu \approx 0.07$ per minute in Berlin, and a distance elasticity of about $-4.4$ versus roughly $-1.3$ for goods trade across US counties — moving people is costlier than moving goods (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). The third is congestion, modeled either as increasing travel times with use or as a negative density elasticity of amenities, as in $a{t}(r) = \bar{a}(r)\bar{L}{t}(r)^{-\lambda}$ in the dynamic models of Desmet and coauthors (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). The fourth is taste dispersion: when workers draw idiosyncratic preferences from a Fréchet distribution, the supply of labor to each location is upward-sloping in real income, and the elasticity is governed by the dispersion parameter $\varepsilon$ (or $\Omega$ dynamically) — so greater preference heterogeneity is itself a dispersion force (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). The degree of heterogeneity is quantitatively decisive for counterfactuals: as the Fréchet shape parameter moves from 3 to 5, the implied average treatment effects on population and land rents vary by around 50–70% (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). Equilibrium uniqueness and the balance of forces The central analytical result is that the sign of the net elasticity of welfare with respect to local population determines uniqueness and stability. In the Allen–Arkolakis framework the relevant object is $$\gamma{1} \equiv 1 - \alpha(\sigma-1) - \beta\sigma > 0,$$ together with $\gamma{2}/\gamma{1} \in [-1,1]$ for uniqueness: $\gamma{1}$ is (up to a constant) the partial elasticity of welfare with respect to population, so $\gamma{1} > 0$ means a marginal migrant reduces incumbent welfare — dispersion dominates — giving local stability, while $\gamma{1} \le 0$ means agglomeration can concentrate the economy into a "black hole" (allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography). In the empirically relevant range, uniqueness holds when $\alpha + \beta \le 0$; when $\alpha + \beta > 0$ the equilibrium is stable but need not be unique — the one-dimensional circle exhibits a continuum of equilibria each concentrating activity around a different point (allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography). The same logic appears with different notation in every framework the survey considers: the Helpman model requires $\sigma(1-\alpha) > 1$; the internal-city model has a unique equilibrium when productivity and amenities are exogenous and potential multiplicity when agglomeration is added, handled by conditioning on observed data and selecting the counterfactual equilibrium closest to the initial one (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). In the dynamic model of Desmet, Nagy and Rossi-Hansberg the balance is struck between static agglomeration $\alpha/\theta$, returns to innovation $\gamma{1}/\xi$, and the three dispersion forces of amenity congestion $\lambda$, land congestion $1-\mu$, and taste dispersion $\Omega$: $$\frac{\alpha}{\theta} + \frac{\gamma{1}}{\xi} \le \lambda + 1 - \mu + \Omega.$$ When this holds, a unique equilibrium — and with an additional term, a unique balanced-growth path with a non-degenerate spatial distribution — exists; otherwise the economy may cycle or concentrate into a measure-zero region (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). Cross-paper pattern (2026-07): The substantive content of the uniqueness condition is identical across the Armington, Eaton–Kortum, Helpman, internal-city, and dynamic frameworks: the spatial equilibrium is unique and stable if and only if dispersion forces — land, commuting, congestion, and taste heterogeneity — dominate agglomeration forces (allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). Only the notation changes; the economics is the same balance of centripetal and centrifugal forces. Identifying forces empirically Because cross-sectional correlations between density and productivity are consistent with strong agglomeration forces or with shared natural advantages, the gold standard is a natural experiment that exogenously shifts the surrounding concentration of economic activity. The Berlin Wall is the canonical within-city example: its division severed all local economic interactions between East and West Berlin — in the model, prohibitive commuting costs and infinite decay of production and residential externalities across the Wall — while leaving physical fundamentals unchanged, and reunification reversed the shock (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). The structural estimate exploits the model's recursive structure: given observed floor prices, employment, land area, and travel times, the equilibrium conditions can be inverted to recover unique values of the unobserved fundamentals even when the model has multiple equilibria, and the agglomeration parameters are then identified from moment conditions requiring that changes in structural residuals be uncorrelated with the distance-grid-cell variation in the shock (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Equally important, models with exogenous productivity and amenities are quantitatively unable to account for the data: simulating division while holding productivity and amenities at their 1936 values predicts a floor-price treatment effect of about $-0.41$ log points against the actual $-0.80$ for the closest blocks to the pre-war central business district, and the reunification counterfactual predicts close to zero against the actual $+0.40$ (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Only with the estimated externalities does the model reproduce the observed reallocations. Other natural experiments converge on the same conclusion: million-dollar-plant location decisions confirm that local employment responses are larger where commuting markets are more open (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting); the Bogotá transit expansion identifies productivity and amenity spillovers from a shock that shifts the supply of labor and residents differentially across tracts (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure); and the Tennessee Valley Authority and the Richmond revitalization program provide place-based evidence of substantial, localized spillovers (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Current assessment (2026-07): Natural experiments remain the gold standard for identifying agglomeration and dispersion forces; cross-sectional density-wage regressions deliver reduced-form coefficients that are not structurally interpretable and need not be invariant to policy. Confidence is highest for the within-city externalities identified off the Berlin Wall and the Bogotá transit shock, and the recursive-inversion argument of Ahlfeldt et al. is why identification survives the presence of multiple equilibria (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Dynamic agglomeration: innovation and diffusion The static balance has a dynamic counterpart: density raises the incentive to innovate because a larger local market lets the fixed cost of innovation be shared among more consumers, and this scale effect turns spatial concentration into a growth engine. In the spatial development model of Desmet and Rossi-Hansberg, firms invest in innovation by bidding for land, and because future returns are capitalized into land rents, the dynamic problem collapses into a sequence of static ones — but innovation incentives are stronger where market size is larger, so density, innovation, and productivity growth are positively linked (desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development). This channel helps explain the postwar rise in the spatial concentration of US services and the mid-1990s take-off of service productivity growth (desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The dynamic dispersion force is spatial technology diffusion: innovations diffuse to neighbors at a rate declining with distance, so no location keeps a permanent advantage. In Desmet, Nagy and Rossi-Hansberg's world-development model, local productivity evolves as the product of past innovation and a spatially diffused aggregate technology, and because dynamic agglomeration adds a third agglomeration term, the condition for a unique balanced-growth path is strictly stricter than the static uniqueness condition — without diffusion the economy would concentrate into a point in the long run (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). The interaction of agglomeration, innovation, and structural transformation is developed on its own page (spatial-innovation-and-structural-transformation). Scale dependence and open questions Agglomeration estimates depend on spatial scale. Within-city estimates from Berlin are somewhat higher than the across-city estimates surveyed by Rosenthal and Strange, but the two are reconciled by the rapid spatial decay of externalities and by the fact that a larger city combines higher density with a larger land area and longer average commutes (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). A structural elasticity estimated in one city need not generalize to another: the local employment elasticity is heterogeneous across locations depending on commuting openness, so a single reduced-form estimate applied out of sample can mislead (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting; redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). Whether agglomeration estimates are structural parameters or reduced-form features of a specific equilibrium remains open, as does the frontier the survey identifies: most models concern goods while much activity is in services, most are static while the important forces are dynamic, and the geography of firm and worker networks is underexplored (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The literature is only beginning to extend these estimates to developing cities, where the parameters — as the Bogotá and Chinese evidence suggests — may differ (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure; wu-you-2025-urbanization). pages.text: Data is a non-rival factor of production: the same dataset can be used by any number of firms simultaneously without depletion. This property fundamentally alters how data markets function in spatial equilibrium, creating a distinctive economic logic that standard quantitative spatial equilibrium (QSE) models — designed around rival factors such as labor and physical capital — do not capture. In a spatial economy, data produced in one region can be sold to firms in many regions at negligible marginal replication cost, decoupling data production from data consumption across geographic space. This non-rivalry introduces scale economies that arise from market size itself, not from the density of economic activity. Lin, Liu, and Zhou (2026) formalise these ideas by embedding a data intermediary sector that purchases raw data from consumers, processes it into workable data, and sells it to intermediate goods producers. Because the same workable data can be sold to multiple firms simultaneously, the equilibrium data price falls with the number of buyer firms — a pure scale economy that does not exist for rival inputs and that generates efficiency gains beyond those from traditional goods-market integration. The economic nature of data: non-rivalry and its implications Non-rival goods are defined by the property that one agent's use does not preclude simultaneous use by others, and the marginal cost of replication is effectively zero. Data fits this definition: a consumer's transaction history, once recorded, can be analysed by any number of firms without degrading the original record. This stands in sharp contrast to rival factors such as labor (a worker can be in only one location at a time) or physical capital (a machine can produce for one firm at a time). The economic implication is profound for pricing: marginal-cost pricing for a non-rival good recoups none of the fixed cost of production, so data markets must develop alternative pricing mechanisms. In the Lin-Liu-Zhou framework, a distinction is drawn between raw data, which is owned by consumers who incur a privacy cost from sharing it, and workable data, which is the cleaned, labelled, and processed form produced by a data intermediary (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market). This separation of ownership and processing stages follows Jones and Tonetti (2020), who first formalised data as a non-rival good in a macroeconomic setting, and allows the model to treat the pricing of raw data (determined by consumers' privacy trade-off) separately from the pricing of workable data (determined by the intermediary's cost structure and the non-rival nature of the product). A spatial model with a data sector Lin, Liu, and Zhou build a two-region economy (East and West) in which a representative consumer in each region chooses consumption $c{n,t}$ and data sharing $d{n,t}$ to maximise lifetime utility, subject to a privacy cost parameter $\kappa{n,t}$. The utility function takes the form: $$ u{n,t} = z_n \left( \frac{c{n,t}^{1-\theta}}{1-\theta} - (1 + h{n,t}\mathbb{I})\kappa{n,t} d{n,t}^2 \right) $$ where $h{n,t}\mathbb{I}$ captures the additional privacy cost when data can flow across regions, and $z_n$ is an amenity shifter that includes congestion effects and idiosyncratic location preferences. Consumers sell raw data to a data intermediary at price $p{b,t}^D$, so their budget constraint is $P{n,t}C{n,t} = w{n,t}L{n,t} + p{b,t}^D D{n,t}$, establishing the trade-off between privacy costs and data-sharing income. The data intermediary purchases raw data from both regions and processes it according to: $$ T_t = \chi \left(\sum_i D{i,t}\right)^\gamma \left(L_t^D\right)^{1-\gamma} $$ where $\gamma$ is the share of raw data in data production and $\chi$ is data-processing productivity. The resulting workable data $T_t$ is sold to intermediate goods firms, which use it as a productivity shifter: $$ A{i,t}(\omega) = A{i,t}^o(\omega) \cdot \varphi{i,t}(\omega)^\zeta $$ where $\varphi{i,t}(\omega)$ is the quantity of workable data used by firm $\omega$ and $\zeta$ is the elasticity of productivity with respect to data. This embeds the data sector into a canonical QSE architecture with interregional trade and migration (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). Market structure for non-rival data: intermediaries and pricing The data intermediary is the institutional mechanism that makes non-rivalry operational in spatial equilibrium. Because the same processed dataset can be sold to any number of firms — the only constraint is $\varphi{i,t}(\omega) \leq T_t$ — the intermediary's revenue is $p{s,t}^D \sum_i I{i,t}\varphi{i,t}$, where $I{i,t}$ is the mass of firms in region $i$. Under a zero-profit benchmark, the price of workable data is: $$ p{s,t}^D = \frac{p{b,t}^D D_t + w{w,t} L_t^D}{I{e,t}\varphi{e,t} + I{w,t}\varphi{w,t}} $$ This expression reveals the distinctive non-rival pricing logic: the numerator is the total cost of data production (raw data purchases plus labour), while the denominator sums data purchases across all firms. Since the same workable data serves many firms, the price per firm falls below the marginal cost of production — a pricing pattern impossible for rival goods. An equally important modeling choice is that cross-regional data flows incur no additional iceberg cost: the same workable dataset is sold to firms in both the East and West at the same price, with no additive transport or transaction cost. This assumption captures the technical reality that digital transmission costs are negligible relative to the value of data itself, and it embodies the institutional objective of a unified national data market in which regional data barriers are eliminated (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market). In segmented markets, by contrast, the intermediary cannot sell across regions, so the market is restricted to local firms only — equivalent to an infinite iceberg cost for data. As the number of firms increases, the denominator grows and the price falls further, creating the virtuous cycle that underpins the scale economy mechanism. Crucially, the price declines with the number of buyer firms even when the intermediary earns zero profit, because the fixed cost of producing the dataset is spread across more users. When the intermediary possesses market power, modelled as a price markup $\varpi$, the price rises to $p{s,t}^D = (1+\varpi)\frac{p{b,t}^D D_t + w{w,t} L_t^D}{\sum_i I{i,t}\varphi{i,t}}$, which reduces data adoption but does not eliminate the scale economy (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market). Cross-pattern observation: The non-rival data scale economy is a distinct mechanism from standard agglomeration economies. Standard agglomeration operates through the density of economic activity — thicker labour markets, knowledge spillovers, input sharing — whereas the data scale economy operates purely through the number of firms purchasing the same non-rival product. The two mechanisms can coexist and reinforce each other, but they are analytically separate. The scale economy mechanism In a unified data market, the interplay between data pricing and market size generates a positive feedback loop that has no analogue for rival factors. As data market integration lowers the workable data price, firms expand their data input, raising productivity. Higher productivity raises expected profits from entry, attracting more firms. Since the data price falls with the number of buyer firms, the new entrants further reduce the data price, deepening the incentive for data adoption. Lin, Liu, and Zhou trace the cycle as: data price falls → data input rises → productivity rises → expected profits rise → new firms enter → scale economy strengthens → data price falls further. In their quantitative exercise, this feedback loop contributes substantially to the headline result: a unified data market raises aggregate GDP by approximately 12.3% relative to a segmented market baseline. The decomposition shows that roughly half this gain comes from the intensive margin (productivity per firm rises ~1%) and half from the extensive margin (firm count rises ~5.6%). The scale economy channel dwarfs the resource allocation channel in magnitude, confirming that non-rivalry — not just comparative advantage in data processing — is the primary source of efficiency gain (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market). Data market segmentation and data types in China The theoretical mechanism acquires its policy salience from the depth of data market fragmentation in China. Between 2015 and 2023, 27 provinces launched data trading platforms, yet the total cumulative transaction volume of the top five platforms barely exceeded 20 billion yuan — a tiny fraction of the market's potential scale. More critically, the platforms operate under incompatible data standards, fragmented governance regimes, and local protectionist policies, creating "data islands" and "data chimneys" that prevent cross-regional data flows. Lin, Liu, and Zhou classify data markets along two dimensions — transaction cost (low vs. high) and market structure (competitive vs. monopolistic) — yielding four types. Low-transaction-cost competitive markets (financial data) suffer from homogeneous products and dispersed trading. Low-transaction-cost monopolistic markets (credit, social security, internet platform data) face institutional silos and low willingness to share across agencies. High-transaction-cost competitive markets (industrial, agricultural data) struggle with incompatible formats and weak standardisation. High-transaction-cost monopolistic markets (government administrative data) face the most severe barriers: complex ownership, privacy regulation, bureaucratic fragmentation, and stringent security approval requirements (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market). Comparative advantage and welfare effects of integration Because data production is less tied to physical geography than goods production, regions with comparative advantage in data production — low privacy costs, abundant data-processing labour, digital infrastructure endowments — can serve the entire national market. In the unified-market counterfactual, data production shifts from East to West, consistent with the "Eastern data–Western computing" (东数西算) strategy. Western data-sector employment more than doubles relative to the segmented baseline, while the East specialises further in goods production. This new spatial division of labour generates welfare gains for both regions: per-capita welfare rises approximately 6.5% in the East and 3.5% in the West. The efficiency gain from data integration is additional to the standard gains from goods-market integration — it is driven by the scale economy mechanism, not by allocative efficiency alone. Data integration also creates what Lin, Liu, and Zhou call a "multiplier effect": the same productivity, trade-barrier, or migration-cost reduction generates a larger GDP response under a unified data market than under segmented markets, because data's scale economy amplifies the initial impulse through the feedback loop described above (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market; liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). Current assessment (2026-07): The estimated welfare gains from data market integration are derived from a static or recursively dynamic QSE framework. Whether this understates or overstates the dynamic gains is an open question. On one hand, the model does not capture the innovation spillovers from cumulative data reuse ("learning from data"), which would amplify the gains. On the other, the "complete segmentation vs. full integration" counterfactual likely represents an upper bound, as real-world institutional barriers will be removed only partially. Robustness and boundary conditions Lin, Liu, and Zhou test the sensitivity of their results along four dimensions. First, a higher data input share ($\zeta$) amplifies the gains from integration, while a lower share attenuates them — a result with direct policy implications for deepening enterprise digitalisation. Second, when raw data from different regions are imperfect substitutes (CES with elasticity $\rho$), the aggregate welfare effect is largely unchanged but the regional distribution shifts: the East benefits more because the intermediary substitutes toward Eastern data. Third, higher consumer privacy costs reduce data supply, weaken the scale economy, and compress the gains. Fourth, introducing monopoly power in the data intermediary (markup $\varpi$ = 0.2 or 0.5) reduces data sharing, raises the workable data price, and narrows but does not eliminate the gains from integration. The robustness checks suggest that the central scale economy mechanism is resilient, but complementary policies — data standardisation, privacy protection through trusted computing and federated learning, and competition regulation — are necessary to realise the full potential of integration (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market). Current assessment (2026-07): Among the boundary conditions, the relative quantitative importance of privacy concerns versus monopoly power remains unsettled. Both channels reduce the gains from integration by comparable orders of magnitude in the calibration, but the policy responses they demand are very different — privacy-enhancing technology on one hand, antitrust enforcement on the other. Disentangling their effects in real-world data markets is a priority for future empirical work. Frontier: QSE policy translation for China The Lin-Liu-Zhou model provides a directly operational framework for analysing China's national unified data market strategy. Three policy implications stand out. First, because the scale economy depends on market size, fragmenting the data market along provincial lines is particularly costly for a non-rival good. Policy should prioritise the interoperability of data standards and trading platforms across provinces, alongside the institutional "soft connectivity" of mutual recognition and coordinated governance. Second, data market integration creates a "multiplier effect" for other reforms: it amplifies the growth impact of productivity improvements, trade liberalisation, and migration-barrier reductions. Data market reform should therefore be sequenced alongside hukou reform and trade integration, not treated as an independent initiative. Third, integration also amplifies negative shocks — data-security breaches cause more damage in an interconnected data environment — so investment in data security infrastructure (trusted computing, privacy-preserving computation, verifiable data流通) must accompany market-building, not follow it (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market; liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). Extending the static model to a fully dynamic QSE framework with capital accumulation and forward-looking migration, as surveyed by Zhao, Chen, and Fu (2022), would sharpen these policy conclusions — particularly for understanding the transition path and the speed of convergence to an integrated market equilibrium (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). pages.title: Economics of the Hukou System
headings: The hukou as a fiscal wedge
Skill heterogeneity in the hukou friction
Frontier: QSE policy translation for China
pages.excerpt: The hukou (household registration) system is China's institutional mechanism for controlling internal migration and determining access to local public services. Established in the 1950s, it assigns each citizen a registration status (agricultural or non-agricultural) in a…
pages.text: Economics of the Hukou System The hukou (household registration) system is China's institutional mechanism for controlling internal migration and determining access to local public services. Established in the 1950s, it assigns each citizen a registration status (agricultural or non-agricultural) in a specific location; changing one's hukou location or category requires government approval, which is difficult to obtain, especially in large cities. In economic terms, the hukou system functions as a fiscal wedge between migrants and natives: migrants without local hukou face higher prices for publicly-provided services such as education and healthcare, restricted access to social security, and limited employment rights. Unlike sunk moving costs, hukou costs are recurring flow costs that persist as long as the migrant lacks local hukou. In quantitative spatial models, these costs are parameterized as multiplicative disutility or fiscal wedges that reduce the effective wage migrants receive, creating a gap between the marginal product of labor and the private return to migration. The friction is not a single scalar: it is skill-differentiated (the probability of obtaining local hukou rises steeply with education), city-tier-differentiated, and dynamic, entering forward-looking migration decisions as a state variable that shapes the entire future migration stream. The system is the single most important spatial distortion in the Chinese economy and a central friction in every major QSE study of China. Institutional background (1950s–2020s) The hukou system was formally instituted in 1958 to control population mobility and maintain social stability. Before the economic reforms began in 1978, individuals were prohibited from living or working outside their hukou county. This prohibition was relaxed in the 1980s, but workers without local hukou still had to apply for a temporary residence permit, a difficult and risky process. A nationwide administrative reform in 2003 greatly streamlined the process for obtaining permits, and several coastal provinces eliminated the requirement altogether tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china. By 2000, the share of Chinese living outside their birth county had risen to 15%, up from only 3% in 1990; by 2010, this share had grown to 18% wu-you-2025-urbanization. Despite these relaxations, the system has not been abolished. Today, each Chinese city operates its own hukou policy under national guidelines, with city-specific quotas and point-based systems. The most desirable cities—Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen—maintain the most restrictive policies, while small and medium cities have largely liberalized their hukou requirements. The result is a highly differentiated system: hukou policy is not a single national barrier but a spectrum of city-specific restrictions that vary with a city's economic appeal, and within each city a two-track system that naturalizes skilled migrants far more readily than the low-skilled wu-you-2025-urbanization. The hukou as a fiscal wedge The economic essence of the hukou system is that it creates a fiscal wedge between migrants and natives. Migrants without local hukou face higher user fees for publicly-provided private goods—education, healthcare, and social benefits—while paying the same taxes as natives. This wedge enters the individual's location choice as a reduction in the effective real wage available outside one's hukou city. Wu and You (2025) estimate this wedge using a revealed-preference approach in the spirit of Rosen (1979) and Roback (1982): individuals' location choices reveal how they trade off local hukou status against income differences. The estimated average fiscal wedge was 50.7% of destination wage income in 2000, declining to 32.5% in 2005, 15.0% in 2010, and 15.0% in 2015. These magnitudes indicate that the costs of lacking local hukou were initially very high and declined quickly but remained substantial. Chen, Shi, and Tang (2019) provide corroborating evidence from housing markets, estimating the market valuation of urban hukou in Jinan—a tier-2 city—at approximately 90,000–126,000 RMB ($13,314–$18,639, or 1.5–2.1 times GDP per capita) in 2017 wu-you-2025-urbanization. Because the wedge is a resource transfer between natives and migrants rather than a deadweight loss, its welfare consequence depends on who gains and who loses, which is why the native-vs-migrant split of welfare effects is central to evaluating the system wu-you-2025-urbanization. Modeling hukou in QSE frameworks The hukou system enters QSE models through four distinct approaches, each capturing different features of the friction. Tombe-Zhu approach. Tombe and Zhu (2019) model migration costs as recurring flow costs (rather than sunk costs), motivated by the hukou system's ongoing nature: a migrant without local hukou faces higher costs every period. In their Eaton-Kortum framework with 30 provinces and two sectors (agriculture and non-agriculture), workers choose locations based on real wages, migration costs, land-ownership rebates, and idiosyncratic Fréchet-distributed preferences. Migration costs include both symmetric geographic costs (distance) and an additional loss of land income when leaving one's home region—a feature motivated by China's collective land ownership, where migrants forfeit access to collectively-owned land tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china. Wu-You approach. Wu and You (2025) develop a richer dynamic framework with 340 prefectures, two skill groups, and forward-looking migration decisions. The hukou system enters through two channels: (1) skill-specific hukou lottery probabilities (θ), capturing the chance that a migrant obtains local hukou, and (2) a fiscal wedge (λ), capturing the price discount that natives enjoy for publicly-provided private goods. The hukou-granting probability is estimated directly from census microdata: in tier-1 cities in 2010, only 3.3% of migrants with primary schooling received a local hukou, compared to 37.3% of college graduates, and the probability is monotonically increasing in educational attainment across all city tiers wu-you-2025-urbanization. The fiscal wedge is then estimated from a structural revealed-preference equation. This approach captures the fact that hukou status is a state variable in workers' dynamic optimization: obtaining local hukou changes a worker's entire future stream of migration options. Ma-Tang approach. Ma and Tang (2020) model migration barriers as origin-destination-specific disutility parameters (δ) in a Melitz-style framework with endogenous firm entry. They estimate these parameters using Simulated Method of Moments (SMM) on bilateral migration flow moments from 279 prefectures. The destination-specific barriers are identified from the difference between predicted and observed migration flows into each city, controlling for geographic costs. Their estimates reveal that Shanghai's barriers are 24% above the national average, followed by Guangzhou (13%) and Beijing (8%) ma-tang-2020-geography-trade. Liu-Wang-Chen approach. Liu, Wang, and Chen (2024) treat the hukou as a skill-differentiated iceberg cost on labor mobility, interpreted through the labor-compensation channel: migrating workers forgo a fraction of effective labor income. This treatment is embedded in a heterogeneous-aggregation framework with cross-skill productivity and public-service spillovers, where the friction's removal interacts with skill composition and with property-tax design liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation. Cross-pattern convergence: Despite using different modeling frameworks—Eaton-Kortum (Tombe-Zhu), dynamic discrete choice with fiscal wedges (Wu-You), Melitz with SMM (Ma-Tang), and heterogeneous iceberg costs (Liu-Wang-Chen)—all four approaches converge on the finding that hukou costs are large and economically significant, though their mapping to specific parameter values differs across methods. Skill heterogeneity in the hukou friction The hukou friction is not a uniform tax on mobility; it is a skill-selective device. The hukou-granting probabilities estimated by Wu and You (2025) rise steeply with education in every city tier: in tier-1 cities in 2010 the share of migrants receiving local hukou was 3.3% for primary school or less, 3.9% for junior high, 11.6% for senior high, and 37.3% for college graduates, and the same monotone pattern holds in tier-2 and tier-3 cities with higher overall probabilities. This skill selectivity is a deliberate design of the two-track system: cities grant hukou to high-human-capital migrants while keeping the low-skilled on temporary status, so the distributional bite of the friction falls hardest on the low-skilled in the largest cities wu-you-2025-urbanization. The skill dimension also changes the welfare economics of reform. Liu, Wang, and Chen (2024) show that, once cross-skill productivity and public-service spillovers are present, optimizing the spatial allocation of human capital raises social welfare, and the Pareto-efficient frontier is reached by redistributing from high-skill workers in high-wage cities toward low-skill workers in low-wage cities; a property tax financing local public services can implement much of this redistribution and partially substitute for the hukou's allocative role, reducing the required transfers from high-wage to low-wage cities (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation). Because hukou liberalization would disproportionately raise the low-skilled population of the largest cities (116% versus 50% for the high-skilled in Wu–You's counterfactual), the skill composition of the marginal migrant is itself a welfare-relevant outcome that skill-selective reform policies directly manipulate (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Cross-paper pattern: Across the corpus the hukou friction is not a single scalar — it is a skill-differentiated, city-tier-differentiated wedge whose distributional bite is largest for the low-skilled in the largest cities. Every major quantitative treatment reflects this, whether through skill-specific hukou-granting probabilities (wu-you-2025-urbanization), skill-differentiated iceberg costs (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation), or city-specific origin-destination barriers (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). Estimated magnitudes of hukou costs The estimated magnitude of hukou costs varies across frameworks but consistently points to very large barriers. Tombe and Zhu (2019) find that in 2000, the average cost of rural-to-urban migration within a province was equivalent to shrinking real income by a factor of nearly 3, while between-province moves were an order of magnitude more costly (a factor of ~25). By 2005, migration costs had declined to 82% of their 2000 level, with between-province costs falling to 61% of their initial level—a drop driven by the 2003 administrative reforms and province-specific hukou liberalizations. Wu and You (2025) translate the aggregate consequences into macro-level losses: the hukou system as a whole created a GDP loss of 13.6% and a welfare loss of 4.7% averaged over 2000–2020. The aggregate welfare loss is smaller than the GDP loss because rising housing prices in destination cities partially offset wage gains, and because the wedge is modeled as a resource transfer rather than an iceberg cost. In a robustness check varying key parameters, the 20-year-average GDP effect ranges from 8.6% to 19.1% and the welfare effect from 2.1% to 7.9%. Ma and Tang (2020) find that the additional barriers in the four largest cities (Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen) result in a 0.7% to 3.9% loss in national welfare, and Li, Ma, and Tang (2024) embed migration frictions of the hukou type alongside firm-level wedges, where the interaction between the two determines both aggregate welfare and spatial inequality (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). Hukou reform and its effects The hukou system has undergone significant but incomplete reform. The 2003 administrative reform that streamlined temporary residence permits reduced between-province migration costs by nearly 40% and was the single largest policy-driven reduction in measured migration costs tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china. Between 2000 and 2005, within-province rural-to-urban migrants increased by roughly 15% and between-province migrants by 82%, largely due to these cost reductions. The post-2014 period saw a new wave of reform: the central government pushed for hukou liberalization in small and medium cities (urban population under 3 million) while maintaining or tightening restrictions in the largest cities. Tier-1 cities introduced point-based systems that favor college graduates, skilled workers, and investors. The result is a "two-track" system: hukou has become nearly irrelevant for moving to small cities but remains a binding constraint for moving to Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen. The Wu-You estimates of the fiscal wedge confirm this: the wedge declined from 50.7% to 15.0% of destination wage between 2000 and 2015, reflecting substantial liberalization, but the remaining wedge is concentrated in the largest cities and is increasingly skill-selective (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Hukou vs. other migration barriers The hukou system differs from standard migration barriers in several economically important ways. First, hukou costs are policy-determined rather than geography-determined: while geographic distance and cultural differences affect migration everywhere, hukou costs are created and enforced by government regulation. Second, hukou costs are recurring flow costs, not one-time moving expenses: a migrant must pay the hukou premium every period, whereas typical migration barriers (information frictions, moving expenses, cultural adjustment) are largely sunk. Third, hukou interacts with land institutions: because rural land is collectively owned and lacks a rental market, migrants who leave their hukou location lose access to land-based income, which Tombe and Zhu (2019) estimate adds a factor of ~1.9 to the overall migration cost, and whose elimination through private land ownership and functioning land rental markets would raise welfare by nearly 12 percent. This institutional interaction means that hukou reform alone may be insufficient—land reform that severs the link between registration and land rights is a natural complement (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). The hukou–land nexus The hukou system is inseparable from China's land-quota system: both are instruments by which the central state rations the spatial allocation of factors. Zhao and Chen (2021) quantify the interaction in a quantitative spatial model of interregional land allocation. Since 2003, urban construction-land supply has been tilted toward central and western provinces—the eastern share fell from 65% in 2003 to about one-third by 2017—which narrowed regional gaps but raised eastern housing prices and distorted factor allocation. Their counterfactuals show that maximizing GDP requires allocating more land to the eastern provinces (raising GDP 5.3% and total welfare 4.6% but widening the regional per-capita income gap by 8.2%), while minimizing the income gap achieves the opposite at little GDP cost; the actual land allocation balances the two, raising GDP 2.3% and welfare 2.6% while cutting the gap by 0.7% (zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation). The key policy result is the complementarity of the two systems. Lowering migration costs into the eastern and southern coastal provinces raises welfare 35.5% and cuts the regional income gap 20.5% but widens house-price divergence 26.2% as migrants crowd into the developed coast; combining this with east-leaning land allocation yields welfare gains of 47.1%, a gap reduction of 13.5%, and a much smaller house-price divergence of 16.4% — the joint "land + hukou reform" guides both population and land toward the east and achieves efficiency, equity, and housing-price objectives simultaneously, whereas either reform alone founders on one of the objectives (zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation). This is why the policy literature treats the hukou and land-quota systems as a single reform package rather than separable distortions, and why hukou reform alone is judged insufficient for regional equalization (wu-you-2025-urbanization; tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Hukou in dynamic QSE The hukou wedge is not a static parameter; in forward-looking models it is a state variable whose persistence shapes the entire transition path. Wu and You (2025) model hukou as a Markov process: each period a migrant draws a lottery for the destination hukou, and winning changes the value of every future migration option, so the wedge's removal has dynamic as well as static effects (wu-you-2025-urbanization). The dynamic QSE survey of Zhao, Chen, and Fu (2022) frames migration frictions as a dynamic choice problem in which workers form expectations over future utility; their Chinese application shows that introducing population migration dramatically slows the economy's convergence — real GDP and capital half-lives lengthen far beyond the classic neoclassical benchmark — and that the wedge's persistence, by slowing the reallocation of population toward high-productivity locations, delays regional convergence and the "new demographic dividend" from improved labor allocation (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). The persistence of the hukou wedge also feeds into the dynamic interaction between migration and capital accumulation. Kleinman, Liu, and Redding (2023) show that forward-looking capital and migration dynamics interact systematically: convergence is slow when the gaps of capital and labor from steady state are positively correlated, and the average half-life of income convergence across US states is around 20 years. In the Chinese context, the recurring-flow nature of the hukou cost means the wedge operates period after period, so its removal accelerates not only the migration margin but also the capital-accumulation margin that responds to the anticipated population distribution (kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The implication for reform sequencing is that gradual, anticipated hukou liberalization has different welfare and convergence consequences than a one-off removal, because forward-looking workers and firms re-optimize along the transition path (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). Frontier: QSE policy translation for China The evolution of hukou policy in the 2020s raises new questions for QSE modeling. Most Chinese cities have now relaxed hukou restrictions entirely, leaving only the very largest cities—Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and a few others—with binding constraints. The key policy question is therefore not whether to abolish the system but how to manage the transition in the remaining restricted cities. Partial reform creates complex dynamics that QSE models are only beginning to capture. For example, liberalizing hukou for college graduates only (as Beijing and Shanghai currently do) changes the skill composition of migration, with implications for local public finances, housing markets, and aggregate productivity. The hukou–land evidence of Zhao and Chen (2021) implies that residual barriers should be relaxed in tandem with land allocation and fiscal transfers toward the receiving regions, so that the distributional losses to incumbent natives are compensated by complementary supply-side policies rather than by continued restriction. The digitalization of public services—e-health consultations, online education platforms, and digital social security portability—may reduce the hukou wedge by enabling migrants to access services remotely without changing their registration status (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market; liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). To the extent that these digital substitutes lower the fiscal wedge, they reduce both the distortionary effect of the hukou system and the welfare gain from fully abolishing it. Dynamic treatments further suggest that the timing of reform matters: because the wedge is a persistent state variable, announcing and sequencing liberalization affects the transition path, and skill-differentiated reform (property tax, transfers, settlement-point reform) can redistribute toward the low-skilled who bear the largest residual burden (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation). Current assessment (2026-07): Post-2020 reforms have substantially reduced measured hukou costs, but the remaining barriers in the largest cities continue to generate economically significant distortions. The QSE literature provides robust evidence that eliminating these residual barriers would raise aggregate welfare substantially, though the distributional consequences require complementary policies — most importantly joint land-allocation reform and fiscal transfers (zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation), skill-aware redistribution (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation), and dynamic sequencing of reform (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). pages.title: Gravity in Spatial Economics
headings: Gravity in Goods Trade: Structural Foundations
Methodological Diversity and the Gravity Slope
pages.excerpt: The gravity equation in spatial economics states that bilateral flows — whether of goods, migrants, or daily commuters — between two locations are proportional to the product of their economic masses (typically population, employment, or total expenditure) and inversely…
pages.text: Gravity in Spatial Economics The gravity equation in spatial economics states that bilateral flows — whether of goods, migrants, or daily commuters — between two locations are proportional to the product of their economic masses (typically population, employment, or total expenditure) and inversely proportional to some measure of distance or friction between them. In quantitative spatial models, gravity is not an empirical approximation but a structural relationship derived from underlying assumptions about preferences (CES or Fréchet), technology (constant-returns Armington, Ricardian Eaton-Kortum, or monopolistic competition with firm heterogeneity), and the distribution of idiosyncratic shocks. The elasticity parameter that governs the slope of the gravity relationship — whether the trade elasticity for goods or the commuting or migration elasticity for people — is the single most important structural input to quantitative spatial equilibrium (QSE) models, because it governs the sensitivity of all equilibrium outcomes to changes in frictions and appears as a sufficient statistic in welfare formulae. The same gravity form unifies goods trade, commuting, and migration, and the elasticity estimates that discipline it now come from a common toolkit spanning international trade and urban economics. Gravity in Goods Trade: Structural Foundations The gravity equation for goods trade arises from three distinct microfoundations, each yielding the same reduced-form relationship but giving different structural interpretations to the key elasticity parameter. Under the Armington assumption — goods differentiated by location of origin with perfect competition — allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography derives the gravity equation from CES preferences: $$ X(i,j) = \left(\frac{T(i,j)w(i)}{A(i)P(j)}\right)^{1-\sigma} w(j)L(j), $$ where $X(i,j)$ is the value of trade from $i$ to $j$, $T(i,j)$ is the iceberg trade cost, $\sigma$ is the elasticity of substitution between varieties, $w(i)/A(i)$ is the marginal cost of production, and $P(j)$ is the CES price index capturing multilateral resistance. The trade elasticity here is $\sigma-1$. Under the Eaton-Kortum Ricardian framework, productivity for each good is drawn from a country-specific Fréchet distribution $F_i(z) = e^{-T_i z^{-\theta}}$, and the trade elasticity is $\theta$ — the dispersion of productivity draws rather than the substitutability of varieties. Solving for the probability that location $i$ is the lowest-cost supplier to $n$ delivers the structural gravity equation $$ \pi{ni} = \frac{T_i (c_i d{ni})^{-\theta}}{\Phi_n}, \qquad \Phi_n = \sum{k} T_k (c_k d{nk})^{-\theta}, $$ where $d{ni}$ is an iceberg barrier, $c_i$ is the input cost, and the price parameter $\Phi_n$ — equivalently the price index $p_n = \gamma\Phi_n^{-1/\theta}$ — is the multilateral resistance term summarizing the technology, costs, and barriers of all potential suppliers (eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade). tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china employs this framework for China's internal trade, with the gravity equation providing the identifying variation. Under monopolistic competition with firm heterogeneity (Melitz), the gravity relationship includes additional terms reflecting firm selection into exporting. ma-tang-2020-geography-trade develops a Melitz-based QSE variant for Chinese cities, in which the aggregate gravity elasticity combines both the intensive margin (existing exporters ship more) and the extensive margin (new firms enter export markets). The extensive margin amplifies the aggregate trade response to cost changes, and this amplification varies with the dispersion of firm productivities. Cross-pattern (2026-07): Despite their different microfoundations, the Armington, Eaton-Kortum, and Melitz frameworks all produce the same gravity functional form for aggregate trade flows, and the same welfare formula in terms of the domestic trade share (Arkolakis, Costinot, and Rodriguez-Clare 2012). The frameworks diverge only in predictions about margins the aggregate gravity equation does not capture — such as the distribution of trade across firms or the response of variety to trade liberalization. This convergence is a central theme across the QSE literature (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The Trade Elasticity Parameter The trade elasticity — the parameter governing the slope of the goods-trade gravity equation — is the central structural parameter in QSE models because it scales the welfare gains from trade and the sensitivity of all equilibrium outcomes to trade-cost changes. In the Armington model, the trade elasticity is $\sigma-1$, estimated from price and expenditure data. The quantitative illustration in redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial sets the elasticity of substitution to $\sigma = 5$, implying a trade elasticity of 4 in line with cross-country price-based estimates, while allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography uses $\sigma = 9$ (trade elasticity of 8), calibrated to Eaton and Kortum (2002). In the Eaton-Kortum framework, the trade elasticity $\theta$ is estimated from the cross-sectional relationship between trade flows and trade costs; Eaton and Kortum's central method-of-moments estimate is $\theta = 8.28$, with alternative estimates of 3.60 from wage data and 12.86 from price data, and typical values used in applications range from 4 to 8 (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). At the sectoral level, the tripartite estimator of caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta — which cancels iceberg costs and fixed effects by forming ratios of trade flows across country triplets — yields sectoral elasticities ranging from 0.37 to 51.08 and an aggregate elasticity around 4.5, and rejects a common elasticity across sectors. The trade elasticity determines the sufficient-statistics formula for welfare gains from trade. In any QSE model satisfying the gravity structure, the welfare gain from moving from autarky to the observed trade equilibrium is $\hat{W} = \pi{nn}^{-1/(\sigma-1)}$ in the Armington case or $\hat{W} = \pi{nn}^{-1/\theta}$ in the Eaton-Kortum case, where $\pi{nn}$ is the domestic trade share (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). This parameter is also the key determinant of the spatial responsiveness of populations and wages to changes in trade costs: a higher trade elasticity means locations adjust more to a given reduction in trade frictions. Gravity in Commuting The gravity structure extends naturally to commuting flows when workers have idiosyncratic preferences for residence-workplace pairs drawn from a Fréchet distribution. monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting derives the conditional commuting probability: $$ \lambda{ni n}^{R} = \frac{B{ni}(w_i / \kappa{ni})^{\epsilon}}{\sum{s \in N} B{ns}(w_s / \kappa{ns})^{\epsilon}}, $$ where $\lambda{ni n}^{R}$ is the probability that a resident of location $n$ commutes to workplace $i$, $B{ni}$ captures average amenities of the commute pair, $\kappa{ni}$ is the iceberg commuting cost, and $\epsilon$ is the Fréchet shape parameter — the commuting elasticity. This equation exhibits exactly the same gravity form as goods trade: the bilateral flow depends on the attractiveness of the destination (wage $w_i$) and the bilateral friction ($\kappa{ni}$), relative to a multilateral resistance term capturing all alternative workplaces. A key empirical finding is that the commuting distance elasticity is substantially higher than the trade distance elasticity. monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting estimates the composite commuting distance coefficient at $-4.43$, compared to $-1.29$ for goods trade, consistent with the intuition that moving people is more costly than moving goods across geographic space. The commuting elasticity $\epsilon$ is estimated at approximately 3.30, smaller than typical trade elasticities, implying that commuting flows are relatively insensitive to economic incentives. In Berlin, ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density estimates the commuting semi-elasticity with respect to travel time at approximately 0.07 per minute, again implying a steep decay of commuting probabilities with distance. Within-city commuting gravity also emerges from Fréchet-distributed match productivities in tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure: the probability that a type-$g$ worker residing in $i$ works in $j$ is $w{jg}^{\theta_g}/d{ija}^{\theta_g}$ relative to a commuter-market-access term, with the aggregate commuting elasticity estimated at roughly $\theta = 3.4$ and high-skilled workers substantially less elastic ($\theta_H = 2.44 < \theta_L = 4$). These estimates carry direct welfare consequences: Monte, Redding, and Rossi-Hansberg find that the median reduction in commuting costs over 1990–2010 (about 12 percent) raises welfare by 3.3 percent, and Tsivanidis finds that a value-of-travel-time-saved calculation captures only about 52 percent of the total welfare gain from transit. Cross-pattern (2026-07): The three flow domains have very different gravity slopes. Goods-trade distance elasticities are around $-1.3$; commuting distance elasticities are around $-4.4$; and the Berlin travel-time semi-elasticity is about 0.07 per minute. The consistently steeper gradients for people than for goods imply that policies affecting the movement of workers — transit investment, housing supply, commuting infrastructure — have larger local incidence than policies affecting goods trade. Gravity in Migration The same Fréchet-based gravity structure governs migration flows, with a crucial difference: migration involves permanent relocation rather than daily commuting, and therefore depends on expected future utility rather than just current wages. In static QSE models, the gravity equation for migration has the same form as for commuting, with migration costs playing the role of commuting costs (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china applies the Eaton-Kortum gravity framework to estimate migration costs in China, finding that the average cost of rural-to-urban migration within a province in 2000 was equivalent to shrinking real income by a factor of nearly three, with between-province moves an order of magnitude more costly. These enormous frictions explain why, despite large income differentials, only 4.2 percent of Chinese workers migrated across provinces in 2000. The gravity equation for migration provides the identifying variation for these cost estimates. Migration gravity also connects to welfare sufficient statistics when labor is mobile. redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare shows that with Fréchet preference heterogeneity across locations, the common change in expected utility between autarky and trade depends on changes in both the domestic trade share and population: $$ \frac{\bar U^T}{\bar U^A} = \left( \frac{1}{\pi{nn}^T} \right)^{\alpha/\theta} \left( \frac{L_n^A}{L_n^T} \right)^{1/\varepsilon + (1-\alpha)}, $$ so that the gravity-based home-share formula must be augmented by a population term once workers can relocate. In dynamic settings, migration gravity inherits a forward-looking component: kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial show that the gravity structure for migration flows is preserved but now depends on expected continuation values rather than current utility alone, and their dynamic exact-hat algebra solves for transition paths using only observed migration shares and structural parameters. Bilateral vs. Multilateral Resistance A distinctive feature of structural gravity in QSE models — distinguishing it from reduced-form gravity regressions — is the presence of multilateral resistance terms. In the goods trade gravity equation, the denominator $\Phi_n$ (or the CES price index $P(j)$) captures the fact that location $n$ imports from all potential suppliers, not just $i$. A change in trade costs between locations $i$ and $n$ affects not only their bilateral trade but also trade between all other pairs through general-equilibrium adjustments in the price index (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography). The same logic applies to commuting and migration gravity: the denominator $\sum_s B{ns}(w_s/\kappa{ns})^{\epsilon}$ captures the attractiveness of all alternative workplaces. In city models, the multilateral-resistance object is the commuter market access (CMA) term — the sum over workplaces of wages discounted by commuting costs and by the employment-side CMA — which tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure shows is the sufficient statistic through which transit improvements raise incomes and reshape the city, and which monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting uses to account for the spillover of local labor demand shocks across commuting links. A transport improvement that reduces commuting costs to one employment center also reduces the relative attractiveness of all other centers, potentially drawing commuters away from them. This interdependence is what makes reduced-form estimation of gravity relationships potentially misleading for policy: the treatment effect of a transport improvement depends on the broader network structure, not just on the improved link. Cross-pattern (2026-07): The multilateral resistance structure provides an explanation for the "distance puzzle" — the observation that the estimated distance coefficient in gravity regressions has not declined over time despite declining transport costs. In structural gravity, the distance coefficient reflects both the direct effect of bilateral distance and the general-equilibrium effect of changing remoteness, and these two forces can move in opposite directions as transport networks expand (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Empirical Gravity: Estimation and Identification Structural gravity estimation in QSE models typically proceeds in two steps. First, the gravity equation is estimated using origin-destination fixed effects to absorb multilateral resistance, yielding consistent estimates of the trade elasticity from the coefficient on bilateral trade costs. Eaton and Kortum (2002) pioneered this two-step strategy, estimating the competitiveness of 19 OECD countries from bilateral trade and geography and recovering the trade elasticity from price data. allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography implements a sophisticated variant that combines geographic information system (GIS) data on transportation networks with the fast-marching method to construct mode-specific trade costs, then uses a discrete-choice framework to estimate the relative costs of road, rail, water, and air transport; the estimated geographic trade costs predict 65 percent of the variation in observed bilateral trade flows from the Commodity Flow Survey. At the sectoral level, caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta form a triple-ratio estimator that cancels unobserved iceberg costs and fixed effects, identifying sectoral trade elasticities from tariff asymmetries alone. Second, the estimated trade costs and trade elasticity are used within the structural model to recover unobserved fundamentals (productivities, amenities) and to compute counterfactuals. tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china applies this approach to China's internal trade, using inter-regional input-output tables for 2002 and 2007 and the Head-Ries approach to back out trade costs from trade shares and the trade elasticity. They find that internal trade costs fell by 10–15 percent over this period, driven by policy reforms that reduced local market protections and by infrastructure investments. A recurring challenge is the endogeneity of trade costs: transportation networks are not randomly assigned but are typically built where trade volumes are already large. allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography mitigates this by estimating travel cost parameters from mode-specific trade shares, which controls for the overall level of bilateral trade through what amounts to an origin-destination fixed effect, though endogeneity concerns remain for the relative mode-specific shares. Current assessment (2026-07): The identification of the trade elasticity from cross-sectional gravity faces an inherent challenge: observed trade flows are jointly determined by trade costs and the trade elasticity. A given pattern of trade can be rationalized with high trade costs and a high elasticity or low trade costs and a low elasticity. Estimating the trade elasticity separately requires additional variation — either from time-series changes in trade costs (as in Tombe-Zhu's use of panel data) or from micro-level price data — and the same challenge applies to the commuting and migration elasticities estimated from cross-sectional flows. Methodological Diversity and the Gravity Slope The fact that the same gravity equation arises from different microfoundations means that the trade elasticity has different structural interpretations across models. In the Armington model, it is the elasticity of substitution between varieties; in the Eaton-Kortum model, it is the dispersion of productivity draws; in the Melitz model, it combines both the intensive and extensive margins of trade. These different interpretations matter for counterfactual predictions along margins beyond aggregate trade flows — such as the response of the measure of varieties or the distribution of firm sizes to trade liberalization (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). ma-tang-2020-geography-trade demonstrates that the Melitz-based QSE model generates different welfare predictions from Eaton-Kortum for the same aggregate trade elasticity, because the extensive margin of firm entry amplifies the welfare effects of trade cost reductions in locations with more favorable productivity distributions. This divergence is largest for counterfactuals involving large changes in trade costs, where selection effects are strongest. The ACR equivalence among the three families also breaks when factors are mobile: redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare shows that with heterogeneous-worker labor mobility, constant-returns and increasing-returns models calibrated to the same initial equilibrium have different counterfactual predictions for trade-cost reductions, because population reallocation changes the measure of goods produced in the increasing-returns case. Open Questions Several frontiers remain in gravity analysis. In dynamic settings with forward-looking migration, the gravity structure becomes time-dependent, with current migration flows depending on expectations of future wages and amenities as well as current frictions (kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial). The extension of gravity to non-rival data flows, as explored by lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market, raises new questions about the appropriate structural form when the good being traded is non-rival and can be replicated at zero marginal cost. The estimation of gravity in the presence of firm heterogeneity and selection bias — where only firms that export appear in the trade data — remains a methodologically active area, with implications for the interpretation of estimated trade elasticities. The sectoral elasticity estimates of caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta, which span two orders of magnitude across sectors, raise the question of when a single aggregate elasticity is an acceptable simplification in gravity-based counterfactuals. And within cities, the separate estimation of commuting elasticities by skill group (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure) shows that the gravity slope itself is heterogeneous across workers, so that aggregate elasticities may mask substantial distributional differences in how locations and workers respond to transport improvements.
