pages.text: Internal City Structure and Density The internal structure of a city — where people live, where they work, how much floor space costs, and how land is divided between commercial and residential use across a city's many heterogeneous blocks — is itself an object of spatial equilibrium. Quantitative urban models treat a city not as a point but as a collection of discrete locations connected by a commuting network, in which workers choose residence-workplace pairs under idiosyncratic taste shocks, firms hire labor supplied through that network, and a land market allocates floor space between competing uses. The canonical model, operationalized on Berlin by Ahlfeldt, Redding, Sturm and Wolf and extended to a developing city by Tsivanidis, delivers a gravity equation for commuting flows, measures of commuter market access, and endogenous productivity and amenity externalities from surrounding density, balanced against commuting costs and inelastic land supply to shape the city's employment and residence gradients. Density — the concentration of employment and residents per unit of built land — is the central endogenous variable, and its equilibrium pattern, together with the dispersion of land prices, is the model's empirical signature. This page develops the architecture, the key parameters, and the natural experiments that identify them. From monocentric to quantitative city models The classical theory of urban structure is the monocentric city of Alonso, Muth and Mills, in which all production occurs at a central business district and workers trade off commuting costs against cheaper land, generating a land-price gradient that declines with distance from the center (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The monocentric benchmark imposes symmetry and a single exogenous center, abstracting from the locational fundamentals and polycentric patterns of real cities. Fujita and Ogawa and Lucas and Rossi-Hansberg generalized it to non-monocentric equilibrium in continuous, symmetric space; but symmetry still made distance from the center the summary statistic, and most data are reported for discrete units such as blocks or census tracts (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The quantitative urban model completes the break. It keeps the agglomeration forces of the non-monocentric tradition — production externalities from surrounding workplace density and residential externalities from surrounding residence density — but allows an arbitrary number of heterogeneous blocks differing in productivity, amenities, density of development, and access to the transport network, and makes the model tractable by adding idiosyncratic commuting shocks that generate a gravity equation for commuting flows (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). The toolkit is portable to continuous space: Allen and Arkolakis model the spatial economy on any surface with arbitrary geography, show the price index is a sufficient statistic for geographic location, and estimate that removing the Interstate Highway System would reduce US welfare by 1.1–1.4 percent (allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography). The quantitative urban model architecture The model's building blocks are the residence-workplace choice, production with commuting-linked labor supply, and a land market. Workers have preferences over a final good, residential floor space, residential amenities, the disutility of commuting, and an idiosyncratic taste shock for each residence-workplace pair. The shock is drawn from a Fréchet distribution, so the probability that a worker resides in block $i$ and works in block $j$ takes the gravity form $$\pi{ij} = \frac{T{i}E{j}\left(d{ij}Q{i}^{1-\beta}\right)^{-\varepsilon}(B{i}w{j})^{\varepsilon}}{\sum{r=1}^{S}\sum{s=1}^{S}T{r}E{s}\left(d{rs}Q{r}^{1-\beta}\right)^{-\varepsilon}(B{r}w{s})^{\varepsilon}},$$ where the iceberg commuting cost $d{ij} = e^{\kappa\tau{ij}}$ rises with travel time, $\varepsilon$ controls the dispersion of idiosyncratic utility, and the scale parameters $T{i}$ and $E{j}$ capture average utility from residing in $i$ and working in $j$ (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Firms produce a single final good under constant returns, taking the supply of workers who commute to each block as given, and the land market allocates each block's floor space between commercial and residential use through a no-arbitrage condition, the observed floor price being the maximum of the commercial and residential prices (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). A decisive property of this architecture is its recursive invertibility. Given the parameters and observed data on floor prices, workplace and residence employment, land area, and travel times, the equilibrium conditions can be solved for unique values of the unobserved location fundamentals — productivity, amenities, and density of development — even when the model has multiple equilibria, because the observed data are held fixed as an equilibrium and the fundamentals are solved as structural residuals (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Tsivanidis extends the architecture to a developing city with multiple worker groups, transit modes, car ownership, and an endogenous supply of migrants (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Commuting gravity and commuter market access The model's empirical workhorse is its gravity prediction for commuting flows: a semi-log relationship between log commuting probability and travel time, with residence and workplace fixed effects absorbing all other origin and destination characteristics. Estimating this on micro data for Berlin's 12 districts in 2008 yields a semi-elasticity of commuting flows with respect to travel time of $\nu = \varepsilon\kappa \approx 0.07$ per minute — each additional minute reduces commuter flows by about 7 percent — and the specification explains 83–91 percent of the variation in bilateral commuting, robust across OLS, Poisson, and Gamma estimators (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). The same gravity structure characterizes commuting across US counties, where the distance elasticity of about $-4.4$ is more than three times the goods-trade elasticity of about $-1.3$ (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). Commuting gravity is the foundation of commuter market access — the two directional measures through which a transport shock propagates. A resident's access to jobs (residence commuter market access, RCMA) is the travel-time-discounted sum of workplace opportunities reachable from a residence; a firm's access to workers (workplace commuter market access, FCMA) is the analogous sum of residents reachable from a workplace, both constructed in the Berlin model from the transformed wages that solve commuting market clearing (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). In Bogotá, Tsivanidis shows that the value of TransMilenio is precisely that it raises RCMA for some neighborhoods and FCMA for others, and identifies productivity and amenity spillovers by regressing model-inferred outcomes on these plausibly exogenous changes in market access (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). The log-linear relationship is validated empirically: adjusted productivity and amenities recovered from the gravity model correlate with observable block characteristics such as green areas, water, and war-time destruction (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Cross-paper pattern (2026-07): Commuting flows are highly distance-sensitive and follow gravity across very different settings — Berlin districts (semi-elasticity $\nu \approx 0.07$ per minute), US counties (distance elasticity $-4.4$, far above the $-1.3$ for goods trade), and Bogotá tracts (commute elasticities $\theta{H}=2.4$, $\theta{L}=4$, differing by skill) (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting; tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). The consistent finding is that moving people is substantially costlier than moving goods, and that more educated workers' commute choices are less sensitive to travel time. Density, externalities, and the internal spatial equilibrium The internal spatial equilibrium balances agglomeration against dispersion. Agglomeration operates through density externalities with exponential spatial decay: productivity in block $j$ depends on the travel-time-weighted sum of workplace employment density around it, $A{j} = a{j}Y{j}^{\lambda}$ with $Y{j} = \sum{s} e^{-\delta\tau{js}}(H{Ms}/K{s})$, and amenities in block $i$ depend symmetrically on residence density, $B{i} = b{i}\Omega{i}^{\eta}$ with $\Omega{i} = \sum{r} e^{-\rho\tau{ir}}(H{Rr}/K{r})$ (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Structural estimates from Berlin give a productivity elasticity of about $\lambda \approx 0.07$ and an amenity elasticity of about $\eta \approx 0.15$, both decaying to near zero within roughly ten minutes of travel time; Tsivanidis' estimates for Bogotá are larger on the production side ($\mu{A} \approx 0.25$) and add an amenity externality that depends on the college share of residents (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Against these stand commuting costs — which, because workers self-select into bilateral commutes, equalize average utility conditional on a commute across all pairs even when some commutes are very long — and an inelastic supply of land, which converts density into higher floor prices (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). The interaction of these forces generates the city's gradients. Production externalities concentrate employment where productivity is high; commuting costs make residents trade off cheaper land against access to employment; and localized residential externalities make residence density itself an amenity. The equilibrium is reflected in the dispersion of land prices across blocks, which the model reproduces and which serves as an over-identification check: the implied ratio of floor space to land area is strongly and approximately log-linearly related to separate data on the density of development, with a coefficient close to one (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Land-price dispersion also connects internal structure to the system of cities, whose size distribution and commuting-technology efficiency jointly shape the spatial allocation of population (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The Berlin Wall natural experiment The quantitative urban model was built to be identified off one of the cleanest natural experiments in urban economics: the division of Berlin after the Second World War and its reunification after the fall of the Iron Curtain. Division severed all local economic interactions between East and West Berlin — in the model, infinite commuting costs and infinite rates of decay of production and residential externalities across the Wall — while leaving the physical characteristics of West Berlin blocks unchanged, and reunification reversed the severing (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). The reduced-form evidence is striking. In difference-in-difference specifications with 500-meter distance-grid cells from the pre-war central business district, West Berlin blocks closest to the pre-war CBD lost roughly 55 percent of their floor-space value between 1936 and 1986 (coefficient $-0.800$ on the first grid cell), then gained roughly 49 percent between 1986 and 2006 (coefficient $+0.398$), robust to controls for transport access, parks, water, war destruction, and land use, and with no evidence of pre-trends (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). The treatment effect is driven by proximity to the pre-war concentration of economic activity in East Berlin, not by proximity to the Wall itself: there is little effect along more remote sections of the Wall (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). The experiment separates externalities from fundamentals. A model with exogenous productivity and amenities, holding fundamentals fixed, predicts floor-price treatment effects far smaller than those observed — about $-0.41$ against the actual $-0.80$ for division, and close to zero against the actual $+0.40$ for reunification — whereas the model with the structurally estimated externalities reproduces the observed effects almost exactly (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The estimated model also answers counterfactuals no experiment provides: removing the automobile from Berlin's 2006 transport network — reverting to travel times based solely on public transport — would reduce city employment by about 14 percent and output by about 12 percent, cut average floor prices by about 20 percent, and make locations less specialized in workplace versus residence activity (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Current assessment (2026-07): The Berlin Wall design is the gold standard for separating within-city externalities from locational fundamentals, because division exogenously severed density linkages while holding physical geography fixed, and because the recursive inversion of the model identifies fundamentals without taking a stand on the strength of externalities (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Cross-sectional regressions of outcomes on density cannot achieve this separation; they remain vulnerable to the fundamental-confound the natural experiment eliminates. Transit, density, and urban reallocation in a developing city Tsivanidis carries the internal-structure toolkit to a developing city, building a quantitative urban model of Bogotá with multiple worker groups, car ownership, and transit modes to evaluate the city's bus rapid transit system, TransMilenio. The model is identified off the transit expansion, which shifts commuting costs and therefore commuter market access differentially across tracts. The first-order welfare gain from travel-time savings — the value-of-travel-time-savings (VTTS) measure standard in transit appraisal — is 1.25 percent, but the full general-equilibrium gain is 2.39 percent, so the VTTS captures only about 52 percent of the total; Proposition 2 shows via the envelope theorem that the VTTS is exactly the first-order welfare impact only when the equilibrium is efficient, with the gap due roughly three-quarters to amenity and productivity externalities and one-quarter to approximation error (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Equilibrium reallocation effects, in short, matter for valuing urban infrastructure, not just time savings. The distributional results are sobering. Because the amenity externality runs through the college share of residents, the reallocation raises welfare inequality between high- and low-skilled workers by 0.59 percent, though the test of whether high-skilled gain more than low-skilled has a p-value of only 0.14 (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). With an upward-sloping supply of migrants into the city, the aggregate welfare gain falls to 0.69 percent as population rises 11 percent and bids up floor-space values, while GDP rises 17.5 percent (6.5 percent per capita); TransMilenio accounts for between 3 and 17 percent of Bogotá's GDP growth over 2000–2016 and up to 40 percent of its population growth (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Land-value capture can finance a substantial share of the system's costs, and allowing for congestion raises the estimated welfare gain modestly as commuters substitute from cars to the dedicated lanes (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Current assessment (2026-07): The Bogotá distributional result — welfare inequality rising by 0.59% — should be treated with caution: the p-value of 0.14 on the high-versus-low-skilled difference falls well short of conventional significance, and the estimates are specific to one city, one transit system, and one model structure (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). The robust and portable finding is the VTTS accounting: first-order time-savings measures capture roughly half of general-equilibrium welfare gains, so cost-benefit analysis of urban transit that ignores reallocation and externalities is materially incomplete. Density, innovation, and city size Internal structure is not only static allocation; density also shapes growth and city size. The spatial development model of Desmet and Rossi-Hansberg shows that a scale effect in innovation links density to growth: firms in denser locations face larger markets, innovate more, and push up local productivity, and because future returns to innovation are capitalized in land rents, the postwar concentration of US services helped trigger the mid-1990s take-off of service productivity growth and the associated rise in the level and dispersion of land rents (desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development). The dispersion of land prices is thus simultaneously an outcome of the internal spatial equilibrium and a marker of the dynamic concentration of innovative activity. City-size optimality bridges internal structure to the system of cities. Wu and You calibrate a system-of-cities model with urban agglomeration externalities and land-based congestion to Chinese data and find that most large Chinese cities have surpassed their locally optimal sizes while remaining smaller than their nationally optimal sizes, because the most productive sites should receive more people even at the cost of exceeding their local optima — a local-versus-national tension: relaxing migration restrictions raises aggregate welfare but lowers the welfare of incumbents in the most desirable cities (wu-you-2025-urbanization). The welfare effects of density at the city level also depend on the extensive margin of firm entry: Ma and Tang show that inflows of migrants raise welfare in Chinese destination cities — real income up 4.7 percent and welfare up 4.0 percent over 2000–2005 — because more residents support more firms and varieties, and that this result reverses if firm entry is shut down, in which case migration depresses wages and raises congestion disutility (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). Open questions The frontier of the internal-structure literature is defined as much by what the models leave out as by what they capture. Housing supply is typically treated as an exogenous density of development rather than a fully endogenous response of construction to prices, and the models abstract from congestion in transportation — travel times are fixed inputs rather than outcomes of commuting volumes — although the Bogotá extension begins to close this gap (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). The potential for multiple equilibria is handled by an equilibrium-selection rule rather than resolved, which matters for the external validity of counterfactuals (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Finally, the parameters — commuting semi-elasticities, externality elasticities, and their decay rates — are estimated city by city, and how far they generalize across income levels, transport technologies, and land-use regulations remains open, with Berlin and Bogotá already differing by a factor of three on the production externality (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). pages.text: The local employment elasticity measures the percentage change in local employment by workplace in response to a one-percent change in local labor demand, typically proxied by a productivity shock. This parameter is central to evaluating the employment effects of local tax incentives, infrastructure investments, and place-based policies. In a closed-economy framework without spatial linkages, this elasticity is a single constant determined by local factor supply conditions. However, once commuting and migration linkages between locations are recognized, the local employment elasticity becomes an endogenous variable that varies systematically across locations depending on their degree of commuting openness — the extent to which residents can work in nearby employment centers without relocating. The key mechanism is that commuting allows employment and residence to decouple: a location receiving many inward commuters can expand employment substantially without a commensurate increase in residents, and therefore without experiencing the full force of local land-price congestion. This openness logic conditions local employment responses not only across US counties but also within a single city, across skill groups, and — with migration access substituting for commuting — across Chinese cities, where it is channeled through the hukou and land-supply systems. The Conventional Approach: Single-Elasticity Local Labor Markets A large empirical literature has estimated the effects of local labor demand shocks using variation from sectoral composition (Bartik shocks), productivity, international trade, natural resource abundance, and business cycle fluctuations (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). The standard approach defines local labor markets as commuting zones (CZs) — spatial aggregates designed to minimize commuting flows across boundaries — and treats these zones as independent observations in reduced-form regressions, typically assuming the local employment elasticity is a single parameter that applies across treated locations, with little attention to linkages between spatial units in goods and factor markets (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). A central limitation is that no choice of boundaries for local labor markets can completely eliminate commuting spillovers. For a typical US county in 2006–2010, around 27 percent of residents work outside the county and 20 percent of workers live outside it; at the ninety-fifth percentile, these figures rise to 59 and 43 percent (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). Even at the CZ level, commuting beyond boundaries remains substantial — the median CZ has around 7 percent of residents working outside, rising above 20 percent at the ninety-fifth percentile. The share of residents working locally also fell from a median of 91 percent in 1960 to 69 percent in 2000, reflecting transport expansion and the growing spatial separation of workplace and residence (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). Counties therefore differ substantially in how shocks spill across boundaries, and a single-elasticity approach risks substantial bias. A Quantitative Spatial Framework with Commuting and Migration Monte, Redding, and Rossi-Hansberg (2018) develop a quantitative general equilibrium model with spatial linkages in both goods markets (trade) and factor markets (commuting and migration), building on the broader class of quantitative spatial models surveyed in Redding and Rossi-Hansberg (2017). An arbitrary number of locations differ in productivity, amenities, and geographical relationship to one another. Workers have Cobb-Douglas preferences over final goods consumption and residential land, and draw idiosyncratic amenity shocks from a Fréchet distribution for each residence-workplace pair, which makes them heterogeneous in where they live and work when faced with the same prices and wages, giving rise to upward-sloping supply functions for residents and workers at each location. Commuting costs enter utility as an iceberg disutility parameter $\kappa{ni} \in [1, \infty)$, while goods trade is subject to iceberg trade costs $d{ni}$. The resulting probability that a worker resides in location $n$ and works in location $i$ follows a gravity equation. A key expression is the conditional commuting probability — the probability that a worker commutes to workplace $i$ given residence $n$: $$ \lambda{ni n}^{R} = \frac{B{ni} (w_i / \kappa{ni})^{\epsilon}}{\sum{s \in N} B{ns} (w_s / \kappa{ns})^{\epsilon}}, $$ which implies a commuting gravity equation with an elasticity of commuting flows with respect to commuting costs of $-\epsilon$. The estimated commuting distance elasticity ($-4.43$) is substantially larger than the trade distance elasticity ($-1.29$), consistent with the intuition that moving people is considerably more costly than moving goods across geographic space (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). The Fréchet shape parameter $\epsilon$, estimated at 3.30, determines the dispersion of idiosyncratic amenities and therefore the elasticity of labor supply to each workplace. The model can be inverted to recover unique values of the unobserved location fundamentals — productivity and amenities — that exactly rationalize the observed data on wages, employment, commuting flows, and land area as an equilibrium of the model (allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). This invertibility, which holds when dispersion forces dominate agglomeration forces, allows counterfactual analysis of changes in commuting costs, trade costs, or local productivity without observing all structural fundamentals. Population reallocation through migration and commuting is the labour-mobility mechanism that equalises expected utility across locations and turns access to high-wage locations into a welfare-relevant object (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). Heterogeneous Local Employment Elasticities Using the quantified model, Monte, Redding, and Rossi-Hansberg (2018) compute 3,111 counterfactual exercises in which each US county receives a five percent productivity shock holding all else constant. The general equilibrium elasticities of local employment range from approximately 0.5 to 2.5 across counties, with a mean of around 1.52, while the elasticity of residents (employment by residence) ranges only from about 0.2 to 1.2. Since employment and residents can differ only through commuting, this contrast itself indicates that commuting links are the primary source of the heterogeneity. Across the full distribution of US counties, the local employment elasticity ranges from roughly 0.5 to 2.5, and this substantial heterogeneity is robust to the introduction of variable land supply elasticities, spatially correlated shocks reproducing the industrial composition of the US economy, and aggregation to commuting zones rather than counties (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). The key determinant of this heterogeneity is the openness of the local labor market to commuting, measured by the residence own commuting share $\lambda{ii i}^{R}$ — the fraction of residents who work in the same county where they live. This single variable alone explains 89 percent of the cross-county variation in local employment elasticities, far exceeding the explanatory power of standard empirical controls such as county employment, wages, and land area, which together achieve an $R^2$ of only about 0.5 (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). Counties with more open commuting markets (lower own commuting shares) exhibit higher employment elasticities because they can draw additional workers from surrounding areas without requiring large increases in the local resident population and therefore without bidding up land prices as severely. The heterogeneity is not an artifact of the specific model structure: heterogeneous local employment elasticities are a generic prediction of the entire class of models consistent with a gravity equation for commuting flows, and the finding is robust to alternative measures of commuting openness — the workplace own commuting share, their average, and their minimum. Within-City Evidence: Berlin and Bogotá The openness-to-commuting logic is not confined to counties. Ahlfeldt, Redding, Sturm, and Wolf (2015) show the same mechanism operating inside a single city using the Berlin Wall as a natural experiment. In their quantitative model of internal city structure, workers draw idiosyncratic utility shocks for each residence–workplace pair from a Fréchet distribution, yielding a gravity equation for commuting flows with a semi-elasticity of about 0.07 per minute of travel time. Berlin's division corresponds to prohibitive commuting costs across the East–West boundary, severing access to the pre-war central business district in East Berlin; reunification removes them. Both reduced-form and structural results show that West Berlin blocks closest to the pre-war CBD lost the most in floor prices, workplace employment, and residence employment after division and recovered the most after reunification — driven by the change in commuting access, not proximity to the Wall itself. Structurally, the production-externality elasticity (productivity with respect to workplace-employment density) is approximately 0.07, and both production and residential externalities decay essentially to zero within about ten minutes of travel time (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Tsivanidis (2026) pushes the same logic to the neighbourhood scale and across skill groups in Bogotá. Estimating the commuting elasticity separately by skill using the variation in travel times induced by TransMilenio, he finds that high-skilled workers have a lower commuting elasticity than low-skilled workers ($\theta_H = 2.44$ versus $\theta_L = 4$), so high-skilled commutes are less sensitive to travel time and hence more costly to sustain — a given reduction in commute costs is therefore more valuable to them. The aggregate sufficient-statistic approach that uses a single elasticity $\theta = 3.401$ delivers an average welfare gain of about 2.4 percent, but it cannot reveal who wins and loses: with skill-differentiated commuting elasticities and imperfect substitutability between skill groups, welfare inequality rises by 0.59 percent, the high-skilled gaining more because they are concentrated in the city's north and connected to high-skill-intensive industries in the centre (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). The openness-to-commuting logic that drives heterogeneity across US counties also operates within a single city and across skill groups — the same mechanism at different spatial scales, from metropolitan areas to city blocks (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting; ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Quasi-Experimental Evidence from Million Dollar Plants To provide independent empirical evidence for the role of commuting, Monte, Redding, and Rossi-Hansberg (2018) exploit quasi-experimental variation from competitions for large manufacturing plants (Million Dollar Plants, or MDPs), following the design of Greenstone, Hornbeck, and Moretti (2010). Firms publicly report the winning county and one or two runner-up counties that survived a lengthy selection process but narrowly lost; the identifying assumption is that runner-up counties provide a valid counterfactual for the winner, conditional on observables. An event-study analysis of 82 MDP announcements from 1972 to 2003 shows no statistically significant differences in employment between winner and runner-up counties in the ten years before the announcement, then a gradual rise to approximately 4 percent higher employment in winner counties by ten years after (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). This timing supports the identifying assumption and is consistent with direct plant operations plus indirect multiplier effects on suppliers and ancillary services. The central prediction — that employment responses should be larger in more open commuting markets — is tested by interacting the treatment effect with the residence own commuting share. The estimated interaction coefficient is negative and statistically significant: a county completely closed to commuting ($\lambda{ii i}^{R} = 1$) experiences virtually no employment increase from the MDP, while a fully open county would see an increase of approximately 25 percent (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). The standardized interaction coefficient is close in absolute magnitude to the standardized main effect, underscoring the economic relevance of commuting openness, and the results are robust across alternative commuting measures, industry-year fixed effects, and census-region-year or state-year fixed effects. An event-study specification for the interaction confirms the absence of pre-trends. Current assessment (2026-07): The MDP runner-up design provides some of the cleanest quasi-experimental evidence for commuting-driven heterogeneity, as comparing winners and runners-up within the same plant competition holds constant both the scale and timing of the labor demand shock. The MDP sample is, however, limited to 82 cases, and the external validity of these large-plant shocks for smaller or more diffuse labor demand shifts remains open. Housing Supply and Commuting as Alternative Adjustment Channels An important implication of the framework is that commuting and housing supply elasticity provide alternative channels through which locations can accommodate increases in labor demand. When the model is extended to incorporate the Saiz (2010) estimates of developed land supply elasticities — which range from 0.76 to 3.09 across US metropolitan areas — the heterogeneity in local employment elasticities remains largely unchanged; the variable land supply elasticity primarily affects the resident elasticity, shifting its distribution rightward and increasing its dispersion, while the employment elasticity distribution is affected much less (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). The pattern is intuitive: commuting lets workers access high-productivity employment locations with inelastic housing supplies without residing there and paying high land prices. Consequently, improvements in commuting technologies provide an alternative policy lever to relaxing housing supply constraints — a possibility informally discussed in the housing supply literature but for which Monte, Redding, and Rossi-Hansberg (2018) provide the first quantitative empirical evidence. Commuting Cost Reductions and Welfare The model also provides a platform for evaluating the aggregate welfare implications of changes in commuting costs. Using observed commuting flows between US counties from 1990 and 2010, Monte, Redding, and Rossi-Hansberg (2018) apply a Head-Ries (2001) adjustment to back out the implied changes in the ease of commuting. Between these two decades, the median implied reduction in commuting costs was 12 percent, with a twenty-fifth percentile reduction of 4 percent and a seventy-fifth percentile reduction of 21 percent. Counterfactual simulations using these empirically grounded changes show substantial welfare effects: reducing commuting costs by the median 1990–2010 decline increases welfare by approximately 3.3 percent — comparable to the gains from opening the US economy to international trade in canonical trade models — and by 6.9 percent at the seventy-fifth percentile (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). The gains arise because commuting lets workers work in high-productivity locations while living in high-amenity ones, concentrating employment in net commuter-importing locations (such as Manhattan) and residents in net commuter-exporting locations (such as parts of New Jersey). The spatial pattern of employment changes is strongly predicted by the initial employment-to-residents ratio, a variable difficult to proxy with land area, size, or housing-supply elasticities. Chinese City-Size Application The elasticity logic is also load-bearing for the Chinese debate over whether governments should restrain urbanisation, where the relevant openness margin is migration access rather than commuting. Wu and You (2025) build a quantitative spatial model with agglomeration and congestion forces, calibrate it to 340 Chinese prefectural cities between 2000 and 2020, and reach a nuanced diagnosis: from the national perspective most of the largest Chinese cities are too small, but from the local perspective they are already too large. Because equilibrium city sizes deviate from both local and national optima, the hukou system's internal migration restrictions — modelled as a fiscal wedge between migrants and natives — trade off correcting for city-size deviations against the welfare cost of distorting mobility. Averaged over 2000–2020, the hukou policy imposes a GDP loss of 13.6 percent and a welfare loss of 4.7 percent, and restricting any single city's size through further migration barriers is generally welfare-reducing even though some cities are locally oversized (wu-you-2025-urbanization). The policy lever that most directly determines how employment and city-size responses translate into welfare is the price elasticity of urban land supply: increasing it has the largest effect on aggregate welfare, but the scarcity of developable land in the most productive sites is the fundamental constraint behind the trade-off between promoting and restraining urbanisation (wu-you-2025-urbanization). This Chinese application mirrors the MRRH result from the opposite direction. Whereas in the United States the local employment response operates through the commuting margin, in China the adjustment margin runs through migration and the firm-entry margin, since a larger city population supports more firms and varieties, and the resulting love-of-variety gains are a crucial part of the local impacts of migration (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). The same structural logic that makes commuting openness the summary statistic for US employment elasticities therefore reappears in China as migration and land-supply policy, tying the concept to the wider hukou and land-quota debate (wu-you-2025-urbanization; monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). Current assessment (2026-07): In China the employment-elasticity logic is channelled through hukou and land-supply policy rather than through commuting alone, and the relevant "openness" margin is migration access. The Wu–You finding that large cities are locally oversized but nationally undersized is the empirical backbone of the land-supply and migration-policy debate, and it shows that whether restraining city size raises or lowers welfare depends on which margin — migration, land supply, or commuting — is the binding constraint. Empirical Signatures and Implications for Research The framework yields several testable predictions distinguishing it from a closed-economy approach. First, commuting openness should correlate positively with the employment response to a labor demand shock, with the residence own commuting share accounting for the great majority of the cross-sectional variation. Second, the correlation with the resident response should be substantially weaker, since commuting lets employment adjust without commensurate changes in residents. Third, the commuting distance elasticity should exceed the trade distance elasticity — confirmed by $-4.43$ for commuting versus $-1.29$ for trade (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). Fourth, standard empirical controls — employment, wages, land area, neighbor characteristics — are substantially less successful than commuting openness in explaining heterogeneity in treatment effects. This finding suggests that reduced-form studies of local labor demand shocks should routinely include measures of commuting openness in their specifications, as these variables can capture in a parsimonious way the otherwise unmodeled spatial spillovers through factor markets (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The within-city and Chinese evidence extends these signatures to finer spatial scales and to migration access (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure; wu-you-2025-urbanization). Current assessment (2026-07): The broader lesson for the local labor markets literature is that the spatial structure of commuting networks conditions the local impact of demand shocks in ways that standard empirical proxies — county size, density, industrial composition — do not capture. Researchers evaluating place-based policies or estimating local multipliers should either incorporate commuting openness directly or recognize that their estimated treatment effects are weighted averages over locations with potentially very different underlying elasticities. The quantitative spatial framework provides a template for analyzing these interactions in any spatial context where bilateral commuting flow data are available. Open Questions Three open questions connect the concept to the wider corpus. First, skill heterogeneity: the Bogotá finding that high-skilled commuters have a lower commuting elasticity implies that aggregate elasticities conceal who bears the incidence of transport and place-based policies, and the analogous skill margin in Chinese migration — hukou holders versus migrants — conditions the distributional effects of urban policy (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure; wu-you-2025-urbanization). Second, endogenous commuting networks: the commuting openness that determines local employment elasticities is itself a product of transport infrastructure and urban form, so policy changes that alter the network also alter the very elasticities used to evaluate them (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Third, the interaction of commuting openness with migration policy: the US evidence operates with free internal migration, whereas in China, where migration access is the binding margin, the elasticity logic must be re-expressed in terms of who can move and where land can be built (wu-you-2025-urbanization; ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). pages.title: Multi-Sector Trade and Input–Output Linkages
headings: Input–Output Linkages and the Input-Bundle Channel
I-O Linkages in Spatial and Regional Applications
pages.excerpt: Multi-sector quantitative trade models extend the single-sector Eaton-Kortum framework to economies with many sectors, sector-specific trade elasticities, and input-output (I-O) linkages: each sector produces a continuum of goods using labor and composite intermediate inputs…
pages.text: Multi-Sector Trade and Input–Output Linkages Multi-sector quantitative trade models extend the single-sector Eaton-Kortum framework to economies with many sectors, sector-specific trade elasticities, and input-output (I-O) linkages: each sector produces a continuum of goods using labor and composite intermediate inputs drawn from all sectors. Because a sector's input-bundle cost depends on the price indices of its input-supplying sectors, a trade-cost or tariff change propagates through the production network — an amplification channel absent from single-sector models. Caliendo and Parro's (2015) study of NAFTA is the canonical implementation, delivering a multi-sector gravity equation, a tripartite estimator for sectoral trade elasticities that is robust to any gravity microfoundation, and exact-hat-algebra welfare counterfactuals in which traded intermediates and I-O linkages roughly double the measured welfare effects of tariff changes. Chinese applications in this corpus — Tombe and Zhu's internal-trade analysis and Liu, Zhang, and Cai's network-infrastructure study — use exactly this machinery on interregional input-output tables. This page develops the model components, the estimation strategy, the amplification result, and the extensions that carry I-O structure into dynamic and non-rival-factor settings. From One Sector to Many The starting point is the single-sector Ricardian framework, in which a country's productivity for each good is a Fréchet draw with a common dispersion parameter $\theta$, and trade shares take the structural gravity form $\pi{ni} = T_i(c_i d{ni})^{-\theta}/\Phi_n$ (eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade). The multi-sector extension allows productivity dispersion to differ across sectors: productivity in sector $j$ of country $n$ is drawn from $F_n^j(z) = e^{-\lambda_n^j z^{-\theta^j}}$, where $\lambda_n^j$ governs absolute advantage and the sector-specific $\theta^j$ governs comparative advantage. Each sector produces a continuum of intermediate goods, some tradable and some not; non-tradable sectors are the limiting case in which trade costs are infinite. The sectoral price index is $P_n^j = A^j \Phi_n^{j^{-1/\theta^j}}$, where the sector-specific price parameter $\Phi_n^j = \sum_i \lambda_i^j (c_i^j \kappa{ni}^j)^{-\theta^j}$ is the multi-sector analogue of the Eaton-Kortum price parameter. Trade shares in each sector are the multi-sector gravity equation $$ \pi{ni}^j = \frac{\lambda_i^j \left[ c_i^j \kappa{ni}^j \right]^{-\theta^j}}{\sum{h} \lambda_h^j \left[ c_h^j \kappa{nh}^j \right]^{-\theta^j}}, $$ where $\kappa{ni}^j$ combines iceberg costs and ad-valorem tariffs. The survey of redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial situates this multi-sector structure inside the broader quantitative spatial toolkit, emphasizing that input-output linkages provide an additional mechanism through which local shocks spread across the economy. Because sectors differ in $\theta^j$, the same aggregate trade pattern can hide very different sectoral responses to a common tariff change — the fact that motivates sectoral heterogeneity in the first place. Input–Output Linkages and the Input-Bundle Channel The distinctive structural feature of the multi-sector model is that production uses intermediate goods from all sectors. The cost of the unit input bundle in sector $j$ of country $n$ is $$ c_n^j = \Upsilon_n^j \, w_n^{\gamma_n^j} \prod{k=1}^{J} \left( P_n^k \right)^{\gamma_n^{k,j}}, $$ where $\gamma_n^j$ is the value-added share, $\gamma_n^{k,j}$ is the share of materials from sector $k$, and $\Upsilon_n^j$ is a constant. The dependence of $c_n^j$ on the price indices of all sectors is the key difference from a one-sector or a no-linkages model: a change in policy that affects the price in any single sector affects all sectors indirectly through the input bundle. In the NAFTA application, caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta document that the input-bundle channel is quantitatively central — most goods traded are intermediates (over 80 percent of Mexico's imports from NAFTA partners in 1993), and I-O tables show strong cross-sector and tradable-nontradable interdependence. The same Cobb-Douglas input-bundle structure is used by tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china for China's two-sector (agriculture, non-agriculture) internal trade model, with intermediate shares calibrated to China's interregional I-O tables, and by liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure, who embed a network-infrastructure term in the effective trade cost of a Caliendo-Parro-style model. The input-bundle channel is also what makes tariffs in one sector affect the cost competitiveness of exporters in another, so that a tariff cut on electrical machinery improves the position of downstream assemblers even if their own tariffs are unchanged. Exact-Hat Algebra with Intermediate Goods A central methodological contribution of caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta is to solve the model in relative changes from a base year, following the exact-hat algebra of Dekle, Eaton, and Kortum. The counterfactual equilibrium is characterized by the relative change in input-bundle costs $\hat c_n^j = \hat w_n^{\gamma_n^j} \prod_k (\hat P_n^k)^{\gamma_n^{k,j}}$, the relative change in sectoral price indices $\hat P_n^j = \left[ \sum_i \pi{ni}^j (\hat \kappa{ni}^j \hat c_i^j)^{-\theta^j} \right]^{-1/\theta^j}$, the relative change in trade shares $\hat \pi{ni}^j = \left( \hat c_i^j \hat \kappa{ni}^j / \hat P_n^j \right)^{-\theta^j}$, and market-clearing conditions for expenditure and trade balance. This system requires only two tariff structures, base-year trade shares, value-added shares, I-O shares, and the sectoral elasticities $\theta^j$; it avoids estimating fundamental productivities and iceberg costs entirely, which is the point of the relative-change formulation. The same technique underlies the counterfactual exercises of tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china for China and of the dynamic spatial model of kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial, who generalize exact-hat algebra to accommodate forward-looking capital accumulation. Within the multi-sector model, the change in real wages can be decomposed into a final-goods term (changes in domestic expenditure shares weighted by $\alpha_n^j/\theta^j$), an intermediate-goods term (the same weighted by $(1-\gamma_n^j)/\gamma_n^j$), and a sectoral-linkages term capturing relative price changes across input-supplying sectors. This decomposition is what allows the welfare effects of a tariff change to be attributed to distinct economic channels rather than treated as a black box. Sectoral Trade-Elasticity Estimation The sectoral dispersion parameters $\theta^j$ are the only structural parameters the multi-sector model requires, and caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta propose a method to estimate them that is consistent with any trade model delivering a multiplicative gravity equation. The estimator forms a ratio of trade flows across a triplet of countries $(n, i, h)$, taking the cross-product of flows in one direction over the cross-product in the other: $$ \frac{X{ni}^j X{ih}^j X{hn}^j}{X{nh}^j X{hi}^j X{in}^j} = \left( \frac{\kappa{ni}^j}{\kappa{in}^j} \frac{\kappa{ih}^j}{\kappa{hi}^j} \frac{\kappa{hn}^j}{\kappa{nh}^j} \right)^{-\theta^j}. $$ All price terms, technology parameters, and country fixed effects cancel, leaving a relationship between observable trade flows and observable tariff asymmetries that identifies $\theta^j$ without assuming symmetric iceberg costs. Using 1993 data across 20 tradable sectors, the estimates range from 0.37 (other transport equipment) to 51.08 (petroleum), and an F-test rejects a common elasticity across sectors — echoing the fact that eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade's aggregate estimate of $\theta = 8.28$ is a single value that sectoral heterogeneity masks. The estimated aggregate elasticity (around 4.5) is in line with the values used elsewhere in the corpus. Because the estimator relies only on the multiplicative structure of gravity, the same method applies under Armington, Eaton-Kortum, or Melitz microfoundations. Current assessment (2026-07): The Caliendo-Parro tripartite estimator produces a wide and statistically heterogeneous range of sectoral elasticities, and the rejection of a common elasticity is robust. But the sectoral estimates are not all stable to sample trimming: several sectors (basic metals, machinery, autos) change sign when small-trade observations are dropped. Welfare conclusions that lean heavily on the elasticity of one or two sectors should therefore be read with caution. The Amplification Result The headline quantitative finding of caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta is that intermediate goods and I-O linkages amplify the measured welfare effects of tariff changes. For NAFTA, the benchmark model implies welfare effects that are on average about 71 percent lower in a one-sector model, about 62 percent lower in a multi-sector model without materials, and about 50 percent lower in a multi-sector model without sectoral linkages; trade effects are correspondingly reduced by about 50, 26, and 18 percent. The mechanisms are distinct. The materials channel operates because a tariff reduction lowers the price of imported intermediates, which feeds into the input bundles of all sectors that use them. The sectoral-linkage channel operates because sectors purchase materials from many other sectors, so a price decline in one sector propagates to the competitiveness of downstream producers. In the NAFTA numbers, Mexico's welfare rises by 1.31 percent, the United States by 0.08 percent, and Canada falls by 0.06 percent; the gains are concentrated in sectors that were highly protected (textiles), highly substitutable (petroleum), or deeply embedded in cross-border production chains (electrical machinery, autos). The same pattern recurs in tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china's China application: the gains from internal trade cost reductions are roughly three to four times larger with intermediates than without, and the authors attribute the bulk of the difference between their full model and a simple back-of-the-envelope calculation to intermediate inputs in production. Cross-pattern (2026-07): Across the two most influential applications — Caliendo-Parro for NAFTA and Tombe-Zhu for China — intermediate goods and I-O linkages consistently raise the measured effects of trade-cost and tariff changes by large factors. The one-sector or no-materials model does not merely scale down the answer; it removes a mechanism (cost transmission through the production network) that is first-order for sectoral reallocation and for the distribution of gains across countries. I-O Linkages in Spatial and Regional Applications The multi-sector I-O machinery has been carried directly into regional and infrastructure applications in this corpus. tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china calibrate a two-sector model with intermediate input shares from China's interregional I-O tables, and their counterfactuals show that internal trade cost reductions raise aggregate labor productivity and welfare by over 11 percent, with intermediates accounting for most of the gap between the full model and a no-intermediates version. liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure build a Caliendo-Parro-style model with tradable and non-tradable sectors and I-O linkages to evaluate China's network infrastructure, using the real-wage decomposition to split welfare gains into a trade-share channel and an I-O linkage channel. At the national level the I-O channel accounts for roughly 53 percent of the welfare gain and the trade-share channel roughly 47 percent, but the split is strongly regional: the I-O channel dominates in the east (about 59 percent), where industrial linkages are denser, while the trade-share channel dominates in the west (about 64 percent), where infrastructure primarily reduces the cost of importing goods. These applications show that the amplification result is not confined to international tariff policy; it is equally central for evaluating internal trade frictions and domestic infrastructure investment. Extensions: Dynamics and Non-Rival Factors Two extensions push the multi-sector I-O structure beyond its static, goods-only domain. The first adds dynamics. kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial develop a dynamic spatial general equilibrium model with forward-looking capital accumulation and migration, but their baseline is a single-sector Armington economy without I-O linkages; they explicitly note that multiple sectors and input-output linkages can be incorporated, and they generalize dynamic exact-hat algebra to the intertemporal setting. The interaction of I-O structure with gradual capital and labor dynamics — how a sectoral tariff shock propagates over time as capital accumulates and workers relocate — remains largely unexplored. The second extension introduces non-rival factors. lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market incorporate a data sector as a non-rival intermediate factor in a multi-sector quantitative spatial model of China, showing that market integration for data operates through scale economies and resource-reallocation effects rather than through the conventional trade-cost channel. Because data can be replicated at zero marginal cost, the gravity and welfare logic of the I-O model must be re-derived when the intermediate good itself is non-rival — a frontier that connects the I-O machinery to the wiki's treatment of data as a non-rival factor. Current assessment (2026-07): Multi-sector models with I-O linkages remain almost entirely static, and dynamic spatial models with forward-looking investment have so far been built without I-O structure. Combining the two — sectoral production networks with gradual capital accumulation and migration — is an open frontier, and the non-rival-data extension of Lin, Liu, and Zhou (2026) is an early step toward one direction of it. Tensions, Limitations, and Open Questions The strengths of the multi-sector I-O framework come with identifiable limitations. The model is static, holds fundamental total factor productivity and aggregate trade deficits fixed, and treats capital implicitly through the intermediate-input share; it therefore measures the pure effect of trade-cost and tariff changes conditional on a stable production structure. Welfare results are sensitive to the sectoral elasticities, and the range of estimated $\theta^j$ values is wide enough that results for sectors with poorly identified elasticities (those flagged in the robustness analysis) should be treated cautiously. The framework also abstracts from firm heterogeneity, so the extensive margin of firm entry and exit — which the Melitz-based spatial model of ma-tang-2020-geography-trade shows can be decisive in a spatial setting — is absent. And because the standard implementation holds populations fixed, it sets aside the factor-mobility channel that redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare shows is first-order for welfare in single-sector quantitative spatial models: with mobile labor, the domestic-trade-share sufficient statistic must be augmented by population changes, a margin the I-O framework does not endogenize. redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial note that richer specifications with multiple sectors, non-traded goods, and factor mobility are feasible within the same toolkit, but each addition raises the data and computational burden. Open questions include the role of non-traded inputs in propagating shocks, sectoral dynamics of structural transformation, and the endogeneity of technology to market size along the lines of spatial growth models.
