pages.title: Carbon Policy and Spatial Leakage
headings: The policy setting: from energy dual-control to carbon dual-control
The trade channel: constraint-cost versus output-reduction effects
Instrument comparison and the deadweight-loss wedge
Policy translation: carbon control in the Chinese spatial equilibrium
pages.excerpt: Carbon-policy spatial leakage is the mechanism by which a carbon-control constraint imposed on one set of regions shifts emissions and economic activity to other, less-constrained regions, weakening the policy's environmental effectiveness and redistributing its economic costs.…
pages.text: Carbon-policy spatial leakage is the mechanism by which a carbon-control constraint imposed on one set of regions shifts emissions and economic activity to other, less-constrained regions, weakening the policy's environmental effectiveness and redistributing its economic costs. In a quantitative spatial general-equilibrium framework, a regional carbon constraint raises local unit production costs (or forces output contraction), and this shock travels to every other region through two endogenous channels rather than fixed input-output shares: trade linkages (intermediate-goods prices and total-demand shocks) and labor migration (workers relocate toward higher-productivity, less-constrained regions). Luo and Luo's quantitative spatial model of China's carbon-control transition is the anchor study: leakage averages about 49.7 percent of a controlling region's abatement, non-controlling regions' GDP gains offset about 38 percent of its GDP loss, and command-style instruments produce welfare losses two to three times those of carbon-pricing tools because they melt the carbon revenue into deadweight loss. The policy setting: from energy dual-control to carbon dual-control The mechanism is studied against China's institutional transition from energy dual-control to carbon dual-control. From the Eleventh through the Thirteenth Five-Year Plans, China built targets on energy intensity, carbon intensity, and total energy consumption; the Thirteenth Plan's energy dual-control encountered divergent regional compliance, and the 20th Party Congress and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee shifted the regime to carbon dual-control, with a 2024 State Council timetable moving from carbon budgets to rigid total caps (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). The transition matters for the mechanism because energy control is a blunter instrument than carbon control: it hits renewable and fossil energy alike and suppresses the renewable substitution that carbon control rewards. The analytical premise is that regions are not isolated islands: a constraint in one region changes production costs and competitiveness everywhere, so a target decomposed region by region cannot be evaluated region by region (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). This is the same general-equilibrium logic that motivates unified-national-market analysis (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions) and the dynamic spatial framework's carbon application (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). The model architecture The model builds on the Eaton-Kortum trade structure with Fréchet-distributed productivity, adding energy as a produced input in a multi-level nested CES technology: labor, energy, and intermediates at the top; fossil and renewable energy in the middle; and coal, oil, and gas within fossil energy (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). A carbon or energy constraint enters as a policy wedge on each energy type's actual cost — proportional to its carbon coefficient under carbon control, its coal-equivalent coefficient under energy control — so the constraint's shadow price is endogenous. Households have heterogeneous location preferences and migrate subject to hukou-related frictions, modeled as differential access to local public services, and the economy is solved in exact-hat changes following standard quantitative spatial practice (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). The economy has N−1 domestic regions plus a foreign region; domestic workers migrate across regions but not across the border. Two parameter choices connect the model to the corpus: migration elasticity $\kappa = 1.5$ and trade elasticity $\theta = 4$, estimated for China by tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china. Renewable energy is supplied regionally with an elasticity of 0.6 in the baseline, while fossil energy is priced internationally. Under pure command control the deadweight-loss rate is set to unity, so the carbon revenue disappears from the economic circuit rather than being rebated — the modelling choice that generates the central instrument-comparison result. The trade channel: constraint-cost versus output-reduction effects A carbon constraint acts on a region's unit production cost through two opposing forces. The constraint-cost effect raises the price of fossil energy and pushes unit costs up; but the higher energy cost makes the pre-existing output scale unprofitable, output contracts, and reduced factor demand pushes factor prices down — the output-reduction effect — pulling unit costs back (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). In most regions the constraint-cost effect dominates and unit costs rise; in a few — Shandong, Hubei, and Sichuan in the simulations — the output-reduction effect wins, and which effect wins depends on factor-supply elasticities and, for labor, on the migration response. These local unit-cost changes transmit to other regions through intermediate-goods prices and total demand. Rising controlling-region unit costs make its intermediate goods more expensive for importers, pushing their unit costs up (trade attenuation); falling unit costs give importers a relative competitiveness advantage (trade compensation). Independently, the controlling region's output contraction lowers the total demand its trading partners face, transmitting a deflationary impulse through the trade network (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). On average the intermediate-price effect dominates — carbon control in any region raises non-controlling regions' unit costs — and the transmission's strength is governed by the internal trade costs and elasticities that tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china estimates for China's interprovincial economy. The migration channel: GDP–welfare separation The second transmission channel runs through population. Carbon control lowers income in the constrained region, widening the gap between expected income there and elsewhere, and households migrate out — both the share of local residents staying and the share of outsiders moving in fall under any region's carbon control (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). This migration response produces a striking GDP–welfare separation. Because people move toward higher-productivity, less-constrained regions, aggregate efficiency can rise: non-controlling regions' GDP gains offset, on average, about 38 percent of the controlling region's GDP loss, and for a few regions the spillover is large enough that national GDP rises even as the controlling region loses output. But welfare falls everywhere: residents leave not because expected income elsewhere improved, but because the constraint reduced local income — a forced relocation in which migrants pay migration costs and arrive with lower welfare. Migration costs of the kind tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china estimates for China are precisely what make this forced mobility welfare-reducing, and the result argues for coupling carbon policy with hukou-reform and labor-market measures that lower relocation costs. Carbon leakage and abatement effectiveness Carbon leakage is the flip side of the transmission channels: the emissions the constrained region avoids reappear elsewhere. Luo and Luo decompose leakage into a domestic component — emissions increases in non-controlling Chinese regions — and a foreign component, both measured relative to the controlling region's initial emissions (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). Averaged across regions, a single region's 1 percent carbon control generates leakage equal to about 49.71 percent of its abatement, meaning the effective reduction is roughly halved; in Qinghai and Ningxia leakage fully offsets the local reduction. Leakage operates through both margins above — output reallocation that changes fossil-energy use elsewhere, and factor-price changes that alter the fossil-to-renewable mix in non-controlling regions. A systematic feature is that foreign leakage exceeds domestic leakage. Because domestic workers can migrate to non-controlling regions, their increased labor supply lowers the relative cost of labor there and pushes firms to substitute labor for fossil energy, dampening domestic leakage; with the border closed, no such substitution occurs abroad, so the foreign component is larger (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). At the national level, all four instruments leak more than 20 percent of the domestic reduction abroad — actual abatement is only about 80 percent of the target — directly limiting China's mitigation contribution and trade competitiveness, echoing the cross-regional cost-shifting logic documented for investment and trade distortions by zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions. Current assessment (2026-07): This mechanism currently rests on a single paper (Luo–Luo 2025), and its magnitudes are point estimates with data caveats — the raw markdown is an OCR-degraded MinerU-VLM conversion in which some figure values are not legible, and the 49.71 percent and 38 percent figures are averages across many heterogeneous regional simulations. The qualitative transmission structure (trade cost pass-through plus forced migration) is robust to the parameter ranges reported, but the leakage numbers await independent replication. Instrument comparison and the deadweight-loss wedge The four instruments differ not in how much carbon they remove — each is calibrated to a national 1 percent reduction — but in what happens to the carbon revenue. Under a carbon market or carbon tax, the compliance cost becomes revenue that stays inside the economic circuit; under command control, the carbon revenue "melts," producing deadweight loss that disappears from the system and is amplified through the input-output multiplier (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). The counterfactual table is stark: the carbon market and carbon tax both cost 0.042 percent of GDP and 0.046 percent of welfare; command carbon control costs 0.045 percent of GDP but 0.114 percent of welfare; command energy control costs 0.046 percent of GDP and 0.116 percent of welfare. Command instruments thus deliver roughly two to three times the welfare loss of carbon-pricing instruments at nearly the same GDP cost — the gap is the melted revenue, plus the weakened substitution away from fossil energy that energy control fails to reward. The instruments also differ in incidence. Carbon-market revenue is transferred toward regions with low marginal abatement costs, which are disproportionately the regions with lighter industry and lower energy dependence; this cross-regional revenue transfer tends to widen regional gaps, and the simulated Gini increase is slightly larger under the carbon market (0.024) than under the carbon tax (0.023) and well below the command-control values (0.032) (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). This is the spatial-efficiency-versus-spatial-equity tension in its fiscal form, analogous to the regional-gap effects of fiscal-expenditure equalization studied by zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization and to the incentive-compatibility problems zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions identifies when national-market reform redistributes resources across localities. Policy translation: carbon control in the Chinese spatial equilibrium The policy translation from this mechanism is threefold. First, the dual-control transition itself is a mechanism change: moving from energy control to carbon control shifts the wedge from the coal-equivalent coefficient to the carbon coefficient, which rewards renewable energy and removes the energy-control deadweight loss — a move from the command-energy column of the instrument table toward the market columns (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). Second, why spatial general equilibrium rather than exogenous input-output shares: the Lucas-critique argument for quantitative spatial models generally (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial) applies with special force, because a carbon constraint changes the structural parameters — energy shares, factor prices, trade flows — that fixed-coefficient approaches treat as given. Third, market-based instruments with revenue redistribution: the paper recommends expanding the national carbon market, using some carbon revenue as a reverse-adjustment fund for regional coordination, and pairing carbon policy with hukou and unified-market reforms that lower migration costs (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). The equity–efficiency tension connects the mechanism to the wider corpus. Smoother population mobility reduces the GDP and welfare losses from carbon control and roughly stabilizes leakage, while deeper trade linkages amplify the shock; higher renewable-supply elasticity and renewable-fossil substitution lower the losses — the paper's "事缓则圆" (steady-as-she-goes) logic that a gradual, elastic transition dominates a sharp one (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). This is the environmental-policy instance of the corpus-wide finding that market-based instruments dominate command instruments in the Chinese spatial economy (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions), and the policy domain the dynamic spatial framework singles out for carbon compensation and trading (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). Cross-paper pattern: Across luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission, zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions, and zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization, the strongest environmental-policy conclusion in the corpus is that market-based instruments with explicit revenue handling dominate command-and-control instruments — command tools melt the scarcity rent into deadweight loss while pricing tools keep it circulating. This is the environmental mirror of the unified-national-market finding that replacing administrative allocation with market allocation raises efficiency. headings: Theoretical Framework: Spatial Development with Transport Costs
The Transport Sector in General Equilibrium
Dynamic Growth, Technology Diffusion, and Infrastructure
Labour Mobility and the Welfare Margin
pages.excerpt: Lead The endogenous infrastructure mechanism describes the bidirectional interaction between transport infrastructure investment and the spatial evolution of economic activity over the course of development. In this mechanism, the location, timing, and quantity of infrastructure…
pages.text: Endogenous Infrastructure and Spatial Development Lead The endogenous infrastructure mechanism describes the bidirectional interaction between transport infrastructure investment and the spatial evolution of economic activity over the course of development. In this mechanism, the location, timing, and quantity of infrastructure investment respond to the spatial concentration of production and the demand for interregional trade; in turn, reduced trade costs reshape the geography of comparative advantage, market access, and agglomeration, feeding back into further infrastructure demand. Crucially, infrastructure is both a cause and a consequence of spatial development: employment in the transport sector and investment in fixed infrastructure absorb labor and capital that could otherwise be used in production, generating a dynamic trade-off between the short-run costs and long-run growth benefits of infrastructure spending. The mechanism now connects to a broader dynamic spatial growth literature in which connectivity improvements interact with technology diffusion and labour mobility, and in which the welfare gains from infrastructure depend on the population reallocation that lower trade costs set in motion. Understanding this two-way interaction is of first-order importance for evaluating infrastructure policy in both historical and modern contexts. Theoretical Framework: Spatial Development with Transport Costs The canonical framework for the interaction between transport costs and spatial development builds on the model of desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development, which features a continuum of locations, two sectors (manufacturing and services), and endogenous innovation with spatial diffusion of technology. trew-2014-spatial-takeoff applies this framework to the first industrial revolution in England, calibrating the model with Shaw-Taylor parish-level occupational data for c. 1710 and showing that the initial spatial concentration of manufacturing productivity in the North of England was critical to whether and when an industrial takeoff occurred. trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure extends the 2014 model to incorporate a third sector -- transport and distribution -- alongside endogenous infrastructure investment, so that trade costs are no longer an exogenous iceberg parameter but instead emerge from the interaction of transport labor, fixed infrastructure stock, and the volume of goods traded across space. The general equilibrium structure follows the standard quantitative spatial equilibrium approach surveyed in redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial, in which goods and factor markets clear across a continuum of locations, labor is perfectly mobile, and land is the fixed local factor. What distinguishes the endogenous-infrastructure extension is the explicit modeling of the transport sector as a user of labor and capital whose marginal product varies across space and over time. These dynamic growth foundations -- innovation responding to market size and technology diffusing across space -- are shared with the global model of desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development, which operates at a $1^{\circ} \times 1^{\circ}$ resolution for the whole world. The Transport Sector in General Equilibrium Transport costs at a location are determined by two components: a physical cost that depends on the stock of fixed infrastructure (roads, canals, railway tracks) and a toll charged by landowner-carriers who hire transport labor to facilitate the wholesaling and distribution of goods. trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure models the transport sector's production as a constant-elasticity-of-substitution function of infrastructure stock and transport labor, where these two inputs are substitutes. The physical transport cost declines exponentially in the infrastructure stock, capturing the idea that better roads and railways reduce the "melt" of goods in transit. The toll, in turn, is set by landowners to cover the wages of transport labor, and the equilibrium toll rises with the volume of trade passing through a location but falls with better infrastructure and higher transport productivity. A key general equilibrium constraint is that transport labor is drawn from the same labor pool as agricultural and manufacturing labor. Faster growth in output and trade increases the demand for transport services, which pulls labor out of production and can delay the point at which manufacturing firms reach the scale required to cover the fixed costs of innovation. In the baseline calibration for England and Wales, the transport sector absorbs about 8 percent of the labor force initially, and the substitutability between transport labor and infrastructure stock determines how much of this labor infrastructure improvements release back into production -- the central trade-off of the mechanism. Two Channels of Interaction The endogenous interaction between infrastructure and spatial development operates through two distinct channels. The first is the productivity channel: growth in industrial concentration generates demand for interregional trade, creating local incentives for infrastructure improvement, which lowers trade costs, further reinforcing agglomeration and innovation through scale effects. In England and Wales, the rise of industrial hotspots in the North and the specialization of the South in agriculture meant that a greater quantity of output was traded over greater average distances, generating local demand for turnpikes, canals, and railways (trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure). This channel parallels the static findings of allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography, who estimate that the U.S. interstate highway system increased welfare by 1.1 to 1.4 percent through reductions in trade costs. The second is the labor reallocation channel: transport employment growth reduces the labor available for production, potentially delaying innovation take-off, whereas infrastructure that reduces the labor required to provide transport services releases labor back into production and can accelerate innovation. The net effect on the timing of take-off depends on which channel dominates. The same two-way logic operates in the commuting version of the framework: monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting show that local labor markets are integrated through commuting as well as goods trade costs, so transport improvements that reduce commuting costs reallocate workers across residences and workplaces before any innovation response occurs. Current assessment (2026-07): The tension between the productivity-driven demand for infrastructure and the labor reallocation cost is a robust feature of the model, but the quantitative magnitude of each channel depends on the substitutability between transport labor and infrastructure stock -- a parameter for which direct empirical estimates remain scarce. Historical Application: England and Wales, 1710--1881 The most detailed quantitative application is the calibration of trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure to the Industrial Revolution in England and Wales. Using occupational data from the Shaw-Taylor and Wrigley project at three dates (1710, 1817, and 1881), mapped into a one-dimensional north-south interval, the model captures the aggregate structural transformation across primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors simultaneously with the spatial evolution of economic activity. A striking finding is that the growth of tertiary (transport and distribution) employment occurs relatively uniformly across all locations, in contrast to the spatial concentration of agricultural specialization in the South and the manufacturing hotspot in the North. The model explains this as an equilibrium response to the increased output and trade volumes generated by the other two sectors: every location needs more transport services as more goods are produced and traded. This is consistent with the historical conjecture of Shaw-Taylor and Wrigley (2014) that most tertiary employment growth in the nineteenth century was required simply to move increased output longer average distances. Infrastructure development proceeds endogenously through a Nash equilibrium among "counties" deciding whether to invest in infrastructure improvements, coordinated by a stylized parliamentary mechanism. The model replicates the acceleration of infrastructure supply around 1850 and the spatial pattern of improvements concentrated around the northern industrial hotspot. The location of takeoff is robust across exercises: the initially high manufacturing productivity of the North of England, together with its cheap energy, makes it the cradle of the Industrial Revolution in all counterfactuals, echoing the conclusion of trew-2014-spatial-takeoff that the initial spatial concentration of productivity was decisive. Counterfactual Policy Experiments The endogenous infrastructure framework permits counterfactual analysis of alternative infrastructure policies. Two central findings emerge from trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure's counterfactual exercises. First, exogenously higher transport costs can, paradoxically, bring forward the date of industrial take-off by increasing agglomeration forces: activity concentrates more densely, increasing firm scale and making it more likely that firms can amortize the fixed costs of innovation. This mirrors Proposition 3 of desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development, which establishes that higher transport costs can raise aggregate productivity in a stagnant sector. Second, early infrastructure investment accelerates industrial take-off only when it is spatially targeted. In the baseline with endogenous infrastructure, takeoff occurs in 1782.7; bringing the model's endogenously generated infrastructure improvements forward by 50 years advances takeoff to 1777.6 (roughly 5 years earlier), and bringing them forward by 100 years advances takeoff by over 13 years. However, if the same total infrastructure investment is distributed uniformly across all locations rather than concentrated where demand is greatest, the effect on take-off is reversed: uniform early investment actually delays take-off by over 4 years. Spatially targeted improvements release labor from transport where it matters most, while leaving trade costs high elsewhere -- preserving the agglomeration benefits of costly trade -- whereas uniform improvements lower trade costs everywhere, weakening agglomeration forces without a sufficiently compensating release of transport labor. Current assessment (2026-07): The finding that uniform infrastructure spending has muted or even negative effects on the timing of industrial take-off is robust within the model's structure, but has not been directly tested empirically. The result highlights the importance of spatial targeting in infrastructure policy, though it also raises the challenge of identifying ex ante which locations will become industrial hotspots. Dynamic Growth, Technology Diffusion, and Infrastructure The historical transport mechanism sits inside a broader dynamic spatial growth literature in which connectivity, technology diffusion, and migration jointly determine long-run development. desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development provide the canonical global version: a world economy at $1^{\circ} \times 1^{\circ}$ resolution in which firms invest in local technology, the return to which depends on the market size reachable given transport costs, and technology diffuses spatially. Transport costs delimit the market that justifies innovation -- lower trade costs expand it and raise the incentive to innovate, but also weaken the spatial concentration that agglomeration rewards. The stakes are large: raising trade costs by 40 percent reduces world real GDP by 30.1 percent and welfare by 34.2 percent, an order of magnitude larger than static one-sector trade models would predict. Connectivity improvements and migration liberalization are also substitutes: the gains from fully liberalizing migration rise from 125.8 percent to 156.9 percent of real income when trade costs are 40 percent higher. Cross-pattern observation: Across this corpus, the welfare effect of connectivity improvements depends on the spatial pattern of the improvement and on the mobility margin that responds -- labour reallocation in desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development and redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare, transport-labour release in trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure, and the narrowing of the digital divide in liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure. No single mechanism governs the return to infrastructure; the identity of the responding margin is what determines it. Labour Mobility and the Welfare Margin A second new foundation is the labour-mobility welfare margin emphasized by redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare. In a quantitative spatial model with trade costs, heterogeneous worker preferences, and a rich geography of locations, a change in transport costs -- exactly what an infrastructure improvement is -- triggers population reallocation toward locations whose market access improves most. The welfare gain from the improvement is a sufficient-statistic function of the changes in domestic trade shares and the changes in population, with the population term absent from the conventional immobile-labor calculation. In the model's transport-improvement exercise, the road/railroad raises common expected utility by around 9 percent, but a policy analyst who falsely assumed labor immobility and used only domestic trade shares would measure the treated locations' gain as a welfare increase of about 22 percent -- a substantial overstatement, because true expected utility is equalized across locations once population reallocation and land-price adjustment are accounted for. The reallocation effects are large relative to the welfare effect, echoing the Fogel (1964) observation that the huge population movements induced by new transport technology need not imply welfare gains of the same magnitude. This is the welfare-relevant counterpart of the two channels in trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure: the labour released (or attracted) by infrastructure is not a friction to be minimized but a margin through which gains are transmitted. The same logic underlies the commuting-based counterfactuals of monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting and the general equilibrium treatment surveyed by redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial. Modern Extension: Digital Infrastructure The logic of endogenous infrastructure extends beyond physical transport to digital networks. liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure develop a quantitative spatial equilibrium model in which broadband and mobile base stations reduce the information and search costs that function as trade costs in the modern economy. Their estimates indicate that China's network infrastructure construction between 2012 and 2019 generated approximately 3.26 percent welfare gains, with the narrowing of the digital divide across regions serving as a key mechanism (the precise figure is partially illegible in the OCR-garbled raw text, but the magnitude is consistent across the paper's summary and tables). The parallel to the historical transport mechanism is instructive. Just as turnpikes and canals lowered the cost of moving goods in eighteenth-century England, network infrastructure lowers the cost of moving information in twenty-first-century China. In both cases, the productivity-enhancing effect is concentrated in regions where economic activity is already growing, while the narrowing of infrastructure gaps between regions serves as a convergence mechanism. Both studies also find that aggregate welfare effects depend on the spatial pattern of improvements, not merely their total magnitude. Current assessment (2026-07): The parallel between transport and digital infrastructure is compelling at the theoretical level, but direct empirical evidence on the degree of similarity in the underlying mechanisms -- particularly the labor reallocation channel for digital networks -- remains limited. Empirical Signatures The endogenous infrastructure mechanism implies three empirical signatures that distinguish it from models with exogenous trade costs. First, the transport employment share rises during periods of rapid spatial transformation, reflecting the growing demand for interregional trade as production becomes more spatially concentrated -- evident in the rising tertiary employment share in the England and Wales data (trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure) and, by analogy, in the growth of the information and communications technology sector in China (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). Second, infrastructure investment is concentrated in regions with growing industrial output. In the England and Wales model, improvements cluster around the northern industrial hotspot, declining where output is stagnant -- consistent with the historical record of local financing for turnpikes, canals, and railways in precisely the regions where industrial demand emerged. Third, trade costs decline fastest in regions experiencing both output growth and infrastructure investment, generating a negative correlation between the rate of trade-cost decline and initial income or productivity levels. allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography find that geographic location explains at least 20 percent of the spatial variation in U.S. incomes, but in a static framework without endogenous infrastructure. The endogenous mechanism suggests this share could evolve over the course of development, and the dynamic global model of desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development shows how the density-income correlation itself reverses as connectivity, diffusion, and migration play out over centuries. Open Questions Three open questions delimit the mechanism's current reach. First, embedding endogenous infrastructure in a dynamic quantitative spatial model with capital accumulation -- of the kind developed by kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial -- would let infrastructure investment compete with private capital for savings, a margin the current Trew framework (in which infrastructure companies maximize one-period dividends) abstracts from. Second, identification of the substitution parameter between transport labor and infrastructure stock remains unresolved, and it is the single parameter that determines whether the productivity or the labor-reallocation channel dominates (trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure). Third, whether the historical transport mechanism generalizes to digital networks is open: the digital case studied by liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure lowers search and information costs rather than physical transport costs, and the welfare margin that responds is the digital divide rather than transport labor, so the two mechanisms may diverge in precisely the ways the cross-pattern callout above highlights. pages.excerpt: Firm-Level Frictions and Spatial Misallocation Firm-level frictions — output wedges that distort firm revenue and labor wedges that distort payroll costs — generate dispersion in the marginal products of capital and labor across firms within the same location, lowering aggregate…
pages.text: Firm-Level Frictions and Spatial Misallocation Firm-level frictions — output wedges that distort firm revenue and labor wedges that distort payroll costs — generate dispersion in the marginal products of capital and labor across firms within the same location, lowering aggregate productivity relative to the efficient allocation. When these frictions vary systematically across space, they create a distinct channel of spatial misallocation: resources concentrate in locations with more distorted firm distributions rather than in locations with higher fundamental productivity. Migration interacts with this mechanism in a countervailing way: workers can move away from heavily distorted regions, partially offsetting the aggregate welfare loss from frictions, but because migrants disproportionately move to already-productive, less-distorted regions, migration amplifies spatial inequality even as it alleviates aggregate misallocation. A complementary, state-driven channel operates across regions rather than within prefectures: cross-regional investment distortions and product-market segmentation push capital to flow against unit returns, generating spatial misallocation of comparable magnitude to within-prefecture wedges. This mechanism connects the micro-level misallocation literature of Hsieh and Klenow (2009) to the quantitative spatial equilibrium (QSE) framework: firm-level distortions are not merely a national phenomenon but have a spatial distribution that itself shapes regional inequality and migration patterns. The Hsieh-Klenow Framework for Measuring Micro-Frictions The canonical approach to measuring firm-level frictions, developed by Hsieh and Klenow (2009), infers the presence and magnitude of distortions from observed dispersion in firms' revenue and input choices. In a frictionless efficient allocation, the marginal revenue products of capital and labor should be equalized across firms within an industry. In practice, they are not: in China and India, the dispersion of marginal products is substantially larger than in the United States, implying large total factor productivity (TFP) losses from misallocation. Li, Ma, and Tang (2024) build directly on this framework, classifying frictions into two types. Output frictions (revenue wedges), denoted $\tau_y$, act as a tax on firm revenue: a firm receives only a fraction $1 - \tau_y$ of its revenue. Labor frictions (payroll wedges), denoted $\tau\ell$, affect the cost of hiring: a firm must pay $(1 + \tau\ell)$ times the local wage to hire one unit of labor. Both can be negative (subsidies). Under standard assumptions — CES demand, monopolistic competition, and Cobb-Douglas production — these wedges can be recovered from firm-level data on sales, payroll, and intermediate input costs using the pricing equations of the model (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). The same dispersion logic operates at the sectoral-regional level in tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china, who find reductions in internal trade and migration frictions accounted for about 28 percent of China's labor-productivity growth between 2000 and 2005 — evidence that the wedge and spatial-reallocation approaches measure the same underlying misallocation. Extending Micro-Frictions to a Multi-Region Spatial Model Li, Ma, and Tang (2024) embed the Hsieh-Klenow wedge approach into a multi-region general equilibrium framework with heterogeneous firms, endogenous entry, internal trade, and migration — extending the Melitz-based spatial model of ma-tang-2020-geography-trade within the broader quantitative spatial equilibrium paradigm surveyed by redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial. In each of 237 prefectures, firms draw productivity $a$ and the two wedges $(\tau_y, \tau\ell)$ from a location-specific joint distribution $G_j(a, \tau_y, \tau\ell)$. The firm's pricing decision incorporates both wedges: $$ p{ij}(k) = \frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon-1} \frac{t{ij} c_j(k)}{A_j a(k) (1 - \tau_y(k))}, $$ where the unit cost $c_j(k)$ itself depends on the labor wedge through $(1 + \tau\ell(k))^{\beta_j} \bar{c}j$. The output wedge drives a wedge between the firm's marginal cost and its revenue; the labor wedge distorts the firm's input mix. Crucially, because firms draw their wedges from location-specific distributions, the aggregate consequences of within-prefecture frictions spill across space through trade linkages and migration flows. A firm in a high-friction prefecture charges higher prices, sells less, and employs fewer workers, affecting the local wage, price index, and ultimately the migration decisions of workers across all prefectures. The model also features endogenous firm entry: infinitely many potential entrants pay a fixed cost $f_e$ to draw from the joint distribution, and free entry equates expected profits to entry costs in each location. Frictions therefore affect aggregate welfare through both the intensive margin (distorted firm decisions) and the extensive margin (the number of varieties). Estimation Strategy: Simulated Method of Moments with Selection A key empirical challenge is that only surviving firms are observed in the data — those whose draw of productivity and wedges allows them to operate profitably above the revenue threshold of the Annual Surveys of Industrial Firms (ASIF). Estimation without accounting for this selection yields biased results (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). Li, Ma, and Tang overcome this through a Simulated Method of Moments (SMM) procedure that uses the sampling scheme to approximate sample selection without solving the full general equilibrium. They assume marginal distributions: $\log(1 - \tau_y) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma{y,j})$, $\log(1 + \tau\ell) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma{\ell,j})$, and productivity $a$ follows a Type-I Pareto with shape $\theta_j$, with dependence captured by a Gaussian copula. Six parameters per prefecture — two standard deviations, one Pareto shape, and three correlations — are estimated by matching 17 moments from the revenue and estimated-wedge distributions across 237 prefectures for the period 1998–2007. The Gaussian copula is central to this design: it lets the correlation between productivity and each wedge vary freely across prefectures while keeping the marginal distributions tractable, which is what allows the estimation to recover the productivity-correlation signature that ultimately drives the welfare results. Key Empirical Findings on the Spatial Distribution of Frictions Two distinct patterns emerge. First, while both output and labor frictions are prevalent in all prefectures, labor frictions are substantially more dispersed: the average standard deviation of output frictions across prefectures is 0.11, while that of labor frictions is an order of magnitude larger at 1.18. This indicates that input markets are far more distorted than output markets in China. Second, frictions are systematically less dispersed and less correlated with productivity in richer prefectures. On the Southern and Eastern Coasts — China's richest regions — the median dispersion of output frictions is 0.086 and 0.084, respectively, compared with 0.108 for inland and poorer regions. The correlation between output frictions and productivity is close to zero in coastal regions (median −0.020 and −0.068) but substantially positive in poorer regions (0.242 and 0.239). Regression analysis shows that prefectures with higher per-capita GDP enjoy significantly lower dispersion and productivity correlations, controlling for population, industry composition, and transport connectivity; a reduced-form decomposition attributes approximately 13% of the observed spatial variation in per-capita GDP to the friction-distribution parameters (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). Cross-pattern observation: The finding that labor-friction dispersion dominates output-friction dispersion by an order of magnitude mirrors similar patterns documented for other developing economies using the Hsieh-Klenow methodology, where payroll distortions arising from labor market regulations, state-sector wage premiums, and informal-sector dualism typically account for the bulk of measured misallocation. Aggregate Welfare Implications of Reducing Misallocation Counterfactually reducing the standard deviation of both output and labor frictions by 0.01 in all prefectures increases aggregate welfare by 3.19%, implying a semi-elasticity of −3.19. The welfare gain operates through three channels. First, as labor frictions converge toward zero, the marginal product of labor becomes more equalized across firms within each prefecture. Second, reduced dispersion in output frictions better aligns market share with firm-level productivity. Third, at the extensive margin, higher expected profits encourage firm entry, lowering the price index through a greater variety of available goods. The semi-elasticity of welfare to labor-friction dispersion (−1.97) exceeds that of output-friction dispersion (−1.20), consistent with the much larger estimated dispersion of labor wedges (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). Reducing frictions also decreases spatial inequality. The Gini coefficient of real wages declines by 0.30 percentage points when the dispersion parameters are reduced by 0.01. Poorer prefectures benefit disproportionately because they face higher initial dispersion; the uniform reduction therefore has a larger absolute impact on them, encouraging firm entry and attracting population inflows that narrow the welfare gap with richer prefectures. The distributional consequence is echoed from a city-size perspective in wu-you-2025-urbanization, who model hukou as a fiscal wedge transferring resources between migrants and natives: fully removing it would raise national GDP by 13.6% over 2000–2020 but impose welfare losses of 10–17% on tier-1 natives — a spatial channel distinct from firm-level wedges. The Interaction Between Migration and Misallocation To isolate the interaction, Li, Ma, and Tang compare friction-dispersion reductions in the baseline model (with migration) against a counterfactual with migration shut down. Without internal migration, the same 0.01 reduction in friction dispersion yields a larger welfare gain of 3.37% (compared with 3.19% with migration). Migration alleviates the aggregate impact of micro-frictions: people leave heavily distorted regions, reducing economic activity where frictions are most damaging. When migration is impossible, workers cannot escape distorted prefectures, so reducing within-prefecture frictions has a larger aggregate effect. However, the distributional implications run in the opposite direction. Spatial inequality becomes less responsive to firm-level frictions when migration is shut down. Lowering dispersion reduces the Gini coefficient by 0.30 percentage points with migration but only 0.25 without it. The mechanism is that migration itself is a source of spatial inequality: workers move from high-distortion (poor) to low-distortion (rich) regions, amplifying the real-wage gap. When friction dispersion falls, this migration channel is weakened because poor regions become more attractive, reversing some of the inequality created by selective migration. Current wiki assessment (2026-07): The finding that migration worsens spatial inequality even as it alleviates aggregate misallocation is robust across multiple model specifications reported in Li, Ma, and Tang (2024), including alternative congestion elasticities, migration elasticities, and elasticities of substitution. The qualitative pattern — that factor mobility acts as a substitute for place-based productivity policy at the aggregate level but a complement at the distributional level — has since been corroborated in dynamic frameworks such as kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial, which shows that capital-labor interaction dynamics can amplify spatial divergence during transitions. Cross-Regional Capital-Market Distortions Firm-level wedges within prefectures are not the only margin of spatial misallocation: Zhao, Wang, Dai, and Chen (2025) identify a parallel, cross-regional channel operating through capital markets. Using the near-universe of firm registration records, they document that Chinese capital flows run against unit capital returns — the highest-return southeast coast is a net capital exporter, while lower-return central and western regions absorb a disproportionate share of investment. The direct cause is cross-regional investment distortion: local governments offering tax incentives, cheap land, and subsidies to attract external capital drive a wedge between the effective return facing investors and the observed unit return. A second, interacting cause is product-market segmentation: mirroring tariff-jumping in international trade, firms facing high internal trade barriers build plants directly in protected local markets, so capital follows market protection rather than high returns (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). In a quantitative spatial general-equilibrium model that gives cross-regional investment decisions explicit micro-foundations, the two factors contribute roughly equal shares to the improvement in capital allocation: 45.5% to investment distortions, 44.3% to trade barriers, and 10.2% to their interaction; because they reinforce each other, ignoring the interaction understates the gains from domestic trade opening by about 20%. The reversal also cannot be undone by reforming a single market — lowering either distortion alone weakens but does not overturn the negative returns-flow correlation, and only simultaneous liberalization makes returns and flows positively correlated. Because local-government utility rises with investment-attraction tax cuts only up to a point but falls monotonically with trade openness, market integration faces genuine implementation resistance (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). Current wiki assessment (2026-07): The state's own instruments — capital tax incentives and local trade protection — are quantitatively comparable to within-prefecture wedges as sources of spatial misallocation. The Zhao–Wang–Dai–Chen decomposition (45.5%/44.3%/10.2%) and the Li–Ma–Tang wedge results are two faces of the same phenomenon: distortions are spatially organized, whether engineered by firm-level market structure inside a prefecture or by local-government incentives across prefectures. Any account of China's misallocation that ignores either margin is incomplete. Policy Contrast: Migration Liberalization vs. Misallocation Reduction Both migration liberalization and reductions in within-prefecture misallocation improve aggregate welfare — but their implications for spatial inequality are diametrically opposed. Li, Ma, and Tang simulate a reduction in migration barriers sufficient to achieve the same 3.19% welfare gain as the 0.01 reduction in friction dispersion. Migration liberalization increases the total number of migrants by 3.0% and worsens spatial inequality: the Gini coefficient of real wages rises by 0.002. Migrants flow toward the richer, less-distorted prefectures, and the resulting population concentration amplifies productivity advantages through agglomeration. In contrast, reducing friction dispersion reduces spatial inequality (Gini declines by 0.001 for the same welfare gain), because the productivity gap between poor and rich regions shrinks when firm-level distortions are alleviated. This policy contrast has a stark graphical representation: migration liberalization shifts population toward initially richer prefectures, while dispersion reduction shifts population toward initially poorer ones (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation, Figure 7). Migration and place-based productivity policies are therefore substitutes for aggregate welfare but opposing forces for spatial equity. The cross-regional capital-market channel reinforces the contrast: market integration raises efficiency but compresses underdeveloped regions' resources, widening per-capita gaps unless labor moves with the capital (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). Current wiki assessment (2026-07): This policy contrast is among the most policy-relevant results in the Chinese QSE literature. It implies that the standard policy prescription of "liberalize migration + compensate losers" may need refinement: because migration liberalization and misallocation reduction have opposing spatial-inequality effects, the compensatory transfers required to achieve spatial equity are potentially large, and the identity of winners and losers differs across the two policy levers. Empirical Signatures Four empirical signatures distinguish the firm-level-frictions-and-migration mechanism from alternative explanations of spatial inequality. First, the standard deviation of both output and labor wedges is negatively correlated with per-capita GDP across prefectures — richer places have less dispersed distortions. Second, the correlation between wedges and productivity is lower (closer to zero) in richer prefectures, so the most productive firms in poor regions face the highest distortions. Third, migration flows disproportionately originate from high-friction-dispersion prefectures and flow toward low-friction-dispersion prefectures, a pattern consistent with workers voting with their feet against distorted local economies (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). Fourth, capital flows run against unit returns: at both the regional and city level, net capital inflows are negatively correlated with unit capital returns, with the high-return southeast coast in net outflow — a signature of cross-regional investment distortions rather than of frictionless capital allocation (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). Together, the labor-flow and capital-flow signatures imply that both factors of production are systematically misallocated away from where their marginal products are highest. Frontier: QSE Policy Translation for China The firm-level frictions framework carries direct implications for China's ongoing policy agenda. First, the finding that state-sector size correlates positively with measured distortions (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation) connects to SOE reform: deeper reform of state-owned enterprises — long identified as a source of output and labor wedges through soft budget constraints and non-market wage setting — would reduce friction dispersion while raising aggregate welfare and reducing spatial inequality. Second, the complementarity between hukou reform and financial-market development emerges naturally: migration liberalization alone increases spatial inequality, but paired with policies that reduce firm-level frictions in lagging regions (credit-market deepening, regulatory reform) it achieves aggregate gains without the distributional cost. Third, the cross-regional capital-market channel adds a unified-national-market dimension: reducing investment-distortion and trade-barrier distortions requires aligning local-government incentives — for example, shifting the consumption tax from the production point to the consumption point so that market integration raises rather than lowers local fiscal returns (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). Fourth, the static Li-Ma-Tang framework assumes a given capital stock; extending it to dynamic capital accumulation, following kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial and zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china, would reveal how the spatial pattern of distortions slows capital accumulation in precisely the regions that need it most. A full dynamic QSE analysis with endogenous firm-level wedges, cross-regional capital, and local-government incentives remains an open frontier. pages.excerpt: Lead The spatial innovation mechanism describes how the geographic concentration of economic activity endogenously drives technological progress and sectoral reallocation in a growing economy. Firms in each location invest in innovation — buying a probability of drawing a…
pages.text: Spatial Innovation and Structural Transformation Lead The spatial innovation mechanism describes how the geographic concentration of economic activity endogenously drives technological progress and sectoral reallocation in a growing economy. Firms in each location invest in innovation — buying a probability of drawing a productivity improvement from a known distribution — while technology diffuses spatially with distance decay between periods. The key proposition is that competition for the fixed local factor (land) and the one-period spatial diffusion of technology make the dynamic innovation problem reduce to a sequence of static decisions, rendering an otherwise intractable spatial growth model solvable. As the economy grows, non-homothetic preferences shift consumption from goods to services, while the spatial concentration of manufacturing (and later services) determines which locations innovate. Technology diffusion plays a dual role: it is the channel through which agglomeration feeds back into innovation, and it is the dispersion force through which lagging regions catch up, offsetting the inherent urban bias of structural change. Transport costs enter because lower trade costs generate static gains but can reduce the density of agglomerations and slow the dynamic rate of innovation. Theoretical Framework: A Spatial Endogenous Growth Model desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development develop a model with a continuum of locations on the unit interval, two sectors (manufacturing and services), and two factors (labor and land). Firms in each location choose how much to invest in innovation, with the cost of buying a probability $\phi$ of innovating given by $\psi(\phi) = w(\ell,t)\big(\psi_1 + \psi_2 / (1-\phi)\big)$. Conditional on innovating, firms draw a technology multiplier $z_i$ from a Pareto distribution with shape parameter $a$, so the expected technology after innovation is $E[Z_i^+] = (\phi/(a-1) + 1) Z_i^-$. Technology diffuses across space between periods with exponential decay: $Z_i^-(\ell,t) = \max_r e^{-\delta \ell-r } Z_i^+(r, t-1)$. The spatial concentration of production creates a scale effect in innovation: the optimal innovation probability is increasing in local employment, consistent with evidence that a doubling of employment density raises patents per capita by roughly 20 percent (Carlino, Chatterjee, and Hunt, 2007). Land as a fixed local factor provides the congestion force that prevents complete agglomeration, while trade costs and spatial technology diffusion set the strength of the agglomeration forces. The same architecture scales to the whole world: desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development solve the model on a $1^\circ \times 1^\circ$ grid of about 65,000 cells, embedding the innovation decision in a technology-accumulation equation in which the parameter $1-\gamma_2$ governs the degree of spatial diffusion. trew-2014-spatial-takeoff and trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure extend the framework to two final goods with an agricultural subsistence requirement and, in the latter, an endogenous transport sector whose infrastructure stock determines trade costs. The Static-Innovation Proposition The central analytical result of desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development is Proposition 1: a firm's optimal dynamic innovation decisions maximize only current-period profits. The reasoning has three parts. First, because labor is perfectly mobile and technology diffuses at the end of each period with exponential decay, the advantage a firm gains from innovating today dissipates by tomorrow — competing firms in neighboring locations have access to the same technology. Second, the land market ensures that expected profits are zero in equilibrium (firms bid for land until they break even), so the only benefit of innovation is the increase in the land rent the firm can offer in the current period. Third, because innovation draws are spatially correlated and the diffusion process is continuous, a firm's own decisions do not affect the technology it wakes up with tomorrow, since neighboring innovations will have diffused to it regardless. The same reduction holds in the global model of desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development, where the location decision is likewise static despite migration frictions, which is what allows the world economy to be simulated on a fine grid. The contrast with other dynamic spatial approaches is instructive. kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial model forward-looking capital accumulation by geographically immobile landlords — a genuinely dynamic problem requiring transition-path solutions rather than static choices. zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china survey this trade-off: the static-innovation simplification avoids the "curse of dimensionality" that plagues models combining forward-looking migration and investment, while the landlord-investor approach preserves richer dynamics at the cost of greater computational complexity. The two are complementary — the static-innovation framework for long-run growth over centuries, the forward-looking framework for medium-run convergence over decades. Structural Transformation Through Non-Homothetic Preferences The transformation from manufacturing to services is driven by the interaction of differential innovation rates across sectors and non-homothetic preferences. The model uses CES preferences with an elasticity of substitution below one (calibrated to 0.4, consistent with Stockman and Tesar, 1995). When manufacturing productivity grows faster than service productivity — as it does initially, because manufacturing firms have higher initial productivity and thus larger scale, making innovation more profitable — the relative price of manufactured goods falls. With an elasticity of substitution below one, this price decline shifts employment toward the sector whose relative price is rising, namely services. This mechanism is the spatial analog of the structural transformation literature, with two crucial differences. First, the reallocation toward services is not exogenous but endogenously accelerates service-sector innovation, because the growing scale of service-producing locations makes it profitable for service firms to invest in innovation. Second, the Baumol effect — the fear that low productivity growth in services leads to long-run stagnation — fails to materialize because structural transformation itself makes the service sector concentrated enough for innovation to take off. Other specifications deliver the same income channel: eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change adopt the Price-Independent Generalized Linear (PIGL) class of indirect utility functions, in which the agricultural expenditure share declines with real income and asymptotes to a positive floor, while trew-2014-spatial-takeoff and trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure use Stone–Geary preferences with a subsistence agricultural requirement, so that productivity gains in agriculture release labor into manufacturing and power early industrialization. Technology Diffusion as a Spatial Convergence Force In the baseline framework, diffusion is an assumption: exponential spatial decay transmits innovations to neighbors, which is what makes the innovation decision static. The expansion of this corpus turns diffusion into a first-order determinant of regional convergence by making its strength a structural object. eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change model technology adoption explicitly: adoption costs depend on a region's lagged own productivity and a distance-weighted aggregate of other regions' productivity, giving a law of motion for sectoral productivity in which lagging regions catch up at a rate governed by a catch-up parameter per sector — $K{rt} = \mu_A A{rt-1}^{1-\lambda_A} \mathcal{F}{rAt}^{\lambda_A}$ in agriculture and an analogous expression in manufacturing. When the catch-up parameters are positive, less productive regions grow faster — a "benefit of backwardness" producing spatial convergence; when they are zero, productivity growth is spatially uniform and the productivity distribution is stationary. The estimated parameters are large: $\lambda_A = 0.73$ and $\lambda_M = 0.28$, implying that backward regions experienced faster productivity growth in both sectors. This is the model counterpart of the data's rural wage premium — wages in the initially most agricultural US regions grew 1.5 to 2 percentage points per year faster than in urban areas, and agricultural TFP growth alone would have raised rural wages by nearly 2% annually. A counterfactual that shuts down catch-up entirely reverses the spatial predictions of structural change — wage growth becomes urban-biased and rural industrialization collapses — establishing diffusion as the force that allowed rural America to benefit from, rather than be left behind by, the first structural transformation (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change). Cross-paper pattern: Diffusion functions as the dispersion/convergence force that offsets agglomeration and the urban bias of structural change across the whole corpus. In desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development, the degree of spatial diffusion $1-\gamma_2$ must be positive for a balanced growth path with a non-degenerate employment distribution to exist, and stronger diffusion lowers the incentive to concentrate, reducing innovation in the long run; in desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development, weaker spatial decay brings forward the services take-off and mitigates cross-location productivity differences; in trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure, the distribution of infrastructure determines how effectively lagging regions adopt technology. In every case, diffusion is the counterweight to agglomeration — a spatial convergence force. Spatial Concentration and the Take-Off of Services Innovation The timing of the productivity acceleration in services is endogenous. In the calibrated model of desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development, service productivity growth remains low from 1950 until the mid-1990s, then accelerates sharply. The acceleration coincides with three related spatial phenomena: the service sector becomes increasingly concentrated, with its spatial standard deviation approaching that of manufacturing by the 2000s; competition for land between the two clusters intensifies, driving up the dispersion of land rents; and the growing scale of service-producing firms makes innovation profitable in locations previously too small to amortize fixed innovation costs. Cross-pattern observation: The positive relationship between employment density and innovation in services, documented for the late twentieth century, mirrors the pattern found by Desmet and Rossi-Hansberg (2009) for manufacturing in the early twentieth century — the link between spatial concentration and productivity growth is a general feature of sectors undergoing rapid innovation. The collocation of manufacturing and service clusters is a distinctive prediction. Because goods are costly to transport, service-producing locations near manufacturing clusters have higher demand and thus larger scale, making them more likely to innovate; the service sector therefore clusters around the existing manufacturing belt rather than replacing it, and rising land costs eventually push manufacturing outward. The Chinese city-size evidence of wu-you-2025-urbanization — an inverted-U relationship between city size and welfare driven by agglomeration externalities versus congestion — is the same density-innovation logic operating on city size. Empirical Applications: From the Postwar US to the Industrial Revolution The calibrated model of desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development reproduces key features of the postwar US evolution: the declining manufacturing employment share, the timing and magnitude of the service productivity take-off in the mid-1990s, and the rise in the level and dispersion of land rents, with the standard deviation of log land values across US metropolitan areas rising from 0.87 in 1995 to 1.07 in 2005. The same mechanism, with a different sectoral pair, explains the first US structural transformation. eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change apply the framework to 495 US commuting zones from 1880 to 1920, during which the agricultural employment share fell from 50 to 25 percent while the most agricultural regions grew fastest in wages — the empirical counterpart of the catch-up estimates above. The historical takeoff literature pushes the mechanism back to the birth of industrialization: trew-2014-spatial-takeoff calibrates a two-sector model to England c. 1710 and reproduces the timing and location of the Industrial Revolution, with manufacturing takeoff at location 305 (Lancashire) around period 61, where the scale threshold for innovation is reached only because energy costs are low and manufacturing productivity is concentrated; flattening the productivity distribution makes takeoff immediate and everywhere, while retaining only the London peak produces no takeoff within 150 periods. trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure adds an endogenous transport sector, matching England and Wales over 1710–1881 and showing that the timing and spatial distribution of infrastructure development govern when takeoff occurs. Transport Costs, Agglomeration, and the Growth Trade-Off A counterintuitive result of the framework is that higher transport costs can generate dynamic gains that offset the standard static losses. desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development establish Proposition 3: for any level of transport costs such that aggregate productivity in an industry is stagnant, an increase in transport costs weakly increases aggregate productivity in that industry. Higher transport costs induce the lagging sector to locate more densely near the leading sector's cluster, increasing firm scale and making innovation profitable. In the model's comparative statics, lowering transport costs from $\kappa = 0.08$ to $\kappa = 0.07$ reduces the present discounted value of utility from 2.64 to 2.36, because weaker agglomeration delays the service take-off. The historical models strengthen this finding. trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure show that exogenously higher transport costs can bring forward the date of takeoff by increasing the agglomeration forces that help firms overcome fixed innovation costs, while early infrastructure investment accelerates takeoff only if focused on locations with local demand — a spatially uniform improvement has a severely muted effect. trew-2014-spatial-takeoff finds that inducing an industrial revolution in London would require reducing London energy prices by 56 percent, suggesting that transport infrastructure directed at the dominant population center is not a cost-effective way to induce takeoff. Current assessment (2026-07): Whether the static losses or dynamic gains from transport cost reductions dominate in practice remains an open empirical question. The framework implies that the net effect depends on the initial spatial distribution of activity and the strength of scale effects in innovation, and the historical evidence that lower transport costs weaken agglomeration and delay innovation reinforces the second-best logic. Direct empirical tests are scarce because transport costs and innovation outcomes are jointly determined. Connections to Dynamic QSE and Chinese Applications The spatial innovation mechanism grounds several extensions in the dynamic quantitative spatial equilibrium literature surveyed by zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china, including the forward-looking capital framework of kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial discussed above. For China, the density-innovation link is central to the city-size results of wu-you-2025-urbanization (an inverted-U between city size and welfare, with most large cities above their locally optimal size), and lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market extend the spatial innovation logic to data as a non-rival factor whose wider circulation amplifies the scale effects that drive innovation, providing a framework for understanding how a unified national data market could deepen the spatial division of labor in China's ongoing structural transformation. The US services-innovation concentration observed after 1995 may provide a template for innovation clusters in Chinese service sectors as the economy shifts from manufacturing-driven to service-driven growth.
