pages.text: The welfare effect of migration on destination-city residents is the central quantitative question in China's urbanization debate. When workers flow into a city, they simultaneously depress nominal wages through increased labor supply, bid up housing costs and crowd public services, but also expand local market size, induce entry of new firms, increase product variety, and lower the price of goods. The net local welfare effect is theoretically ambiguous and depends critically on the market structure of the goods-producing sector. Under an Eaton-Kortum framework with perfect competition and no firm entry margin — as in the quantitative analysis of Tombe and Zhu (2019) — migration inflows reduce local real wages because the downward wage pressure is not offset by an increase in varieties. Under a Melitz framework with monopolistic competition and endogenous firm entry — as in Ma and Tang (2020) — the inflow of workers induces firm entry, expands product variety, and lowers prices, yielding net local welfare gains for destination cities despite congestion. The sign question is only sharpened when the welfare of incumbents is disaggregated by skill and migration status, and when the magnitudes of China's barriers are placed against global free-migration benchmarks. This modeling contingency has direct policy implications: if migration benefits destination cities, restrictive hukou policies impose a double loss on both migrants and natives; if it harms destination-city incumbents, local welfare may justify maintaining restrictions even at the cost of national efficiency. The Four Channels of Local Welfare Impact Migration affects welfare in the receiving city through four distinct channels whose net balance determines whether inflows help or harm locals. The wage channel operates through standard labor-supply mechanics: an inflow of workers shifts the local labor supply curve outward, reducing the equilibrium nominal wage for a given labor demand curve. The magnitude of this effect depends on the elasticity of labor demand, which in turn depends on the production technology and the degree of openness to trade. The congestion channel captures the disutility and higher housing costs that accompany population density. In the Ma and Tang (2020) framework, congestion enters utility as an additive disutility term $C(L_j) = \rho (L_j / \bar{L})^\phi$, where $\phi$ governs how rapidly congestion disutility scales with city population. In the Tombe and Zhu (2019) framework, land functions as a fixed factor in production and housing, creating a similar congestion mechanism through rising land rents; in the dynamic system-of-cities framework of Wu and You (2025), congestion operates through an inelastic urban land supply whose elasticity falls as a city exhausts developable land. The variety channel is the key offsetting force: a larger market supports more firms and product varieties. Under a CES utility structure with love of variety, an expansion of the set of available goods $\Omega_j$ directly lowers the ideal price index and raises real income. The price channel operates through scale effects on production: a larger labor force reduces marginal production costs, which, under imperfect competition, partially passes through to lower prices. Cross-paper pattern: The four-channel decomposition is common across the QSE migration literature, but the weight assigned to each channel — particularly the variety channel — depends on modeling assumptions about market structure. Frameworks that suppress the variety channel (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china) find migration harmful locally; those that activate it (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade) find it beneficial. Modeling Approach A: Eaton-Kortum with No Firm Entry The Tombe and Zhu (2019) model assumes perfectly competitive goods markets with constant returns to scale, as in Eaton and Kortum (2002). In this structure, each location-sector produces a continuum of varieties under Fréchet-distributed productivity, and the equilibrium number of varieties in each location is fixed by the technological parameters — there is no endogenous firm entry or exit. Migration inflows affect local welfare through two channels: they depress nominal wages (wage channel) and increase the rental cost of land, which serves as a fixed factor in production and housing (congestion channel). There is no variety or price channel to offset these forces, because the set of available goods is technologically determined rather than market-size-dependent. The model's predictions are unambiguous: destination provinces that receive migrants experience declines in real income per worker. The aggregate gains from migration — roughly 4.8 percent higher labor productivity and 11.1 percent higher welfare nationally from the migration cost reductions of 2000–2005 — come entirely from the reallocation of workers from low-productivity agriculture to higher-productivity non-agriculture, not from any improvement in the productivity or variety of the destination economy. Within-province agriculture-to-non-agriculture reallocation accounts for 2.0 percent of the productivity gain, while between-province reallocation adds 2.8 percent (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). The coastal destination provinces — Shanghai, Tianjin, Beijing, and Guangdong — that experience the largest population inflows simultaneously see declining real incomes, a pattern that would rationalize restrictive hukou policies on local welfare grounds. The scope for further liberalization is large: lowering migration costs so that one-third of workers live outside their province of registration would raise real GDP per worker by 12.8 percent and welfare by 45.6 percent, the welfare gain inflated by the direct effect of removing recurring flow costs on migrants themselves (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Modeling Approach B: Melitz with Endogenous Firm Entry Ma and Tang (2020) build on the Melitz (2003) framework with heterogeneous firms, fixed entry costs, and endogenous firm entry and exit, estimated on 279 Chinese prefecture-level cities. The model also incorporates a detailed transportation network — road, rail, and waterway — estimated using Allen and Arkolakis's (2014) fast-marching method. In this structure, migration inflows generate two countervailing forces that are absent from the Eaton-Kortum framework. First, the inflow of workers increases local market size, raising expected profits for potential entrants and inducing more firms to enter. This expands the set of varieties available to local consumers and, because firms charge a constant markup over marginal cost, lowers the ideal price index proportionally to the elasticity of substitution $\varepsilon = 6$. Second, the inflow dampens nominal wages by expanding labor supply, which further reduces production costs and amplifies the price decline. These variety and price effects must be weighed against the congestion disutility that scales with population. The quantitative results confirm that the variety channel dominates. Between 2000 and 2005, the 40 Chinese cities that received net population inflows — primarily large coastal cities and provincial capitals — experienced an average 4.7 percent increase in real income and 4.0 percent increase in welfare. Congestion offsets roughly 15 percent of the real income gain when expressed in welfare terms. When the model shuts down the firm entry margin by fixing the number of firms at their 2000 levels, the local impacts of migration turn negative — 44 of the 55 receiving cities experience lower real wages — thereby replicating the Eaton-Kortum prediction within the same framework (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). This sharp reversal confirms that the extensive margin of firm entry is the decisive mechanism. Current assessment (2026-07): The empirical evidence supports the Melitz mechanism for Chinese cities. Ma and Tang (2020) find a positive and statistically significant relationship between city-level inflow rates and the growth rate of the number of firms using a model-based instrumental variables strategy. The IV estimates imply that a one-percentage-point increase in the inflow rate raises the growth rate of firms by approximately 1 percent, consistent with the structural mechanism. Quantitative Comparison of the Two Frameworks A direct comparison of the two frameworks within the same empirical context reveals that the modeling choice determines the sign of migration's local welfare effect but has relatively modest implications for aggregate welfare. In the Eaton-Kortum framework of Tombe and Zhu (2019), aggregate welfare rises by 11.1 percent from migration cost reductions, while in the Melitz framework of Ma and Tang (2020), the aggregate welfare gain from observed migration flows is 11.0 percent — very close in magnitude. The source of the gains, however, differs fundamentally. In the Eaton-Kortum model, the entire gain comes from labor reallocation across sectors and provinces; in the Melitz model, a substantial portion comes from the expansion of product variety in destination cities. The difference in local predictions has first-order implications for policy. If the Eaton-Kortum model is the correct description, then individual provinces have a local incentive to restrict in-migration, and national welfare must be traded off against local interests. If the Melitz model is correct, destination cities gain from migration, and restrictive hukou policies are unambiguously harmful — they reduce both national efficiency and local welfare. Ma and Tang (2020) provide a direct test by noting that when they shut down the entry margin, the local impacts turn negative, suggesting that the data (which show positive correlations between inflow rates and per-capita GDP growth) favor the Melitz mechanism. The welfare-accounting results of Wu and You (2025) complicate this clean contrast, however: even a framework that builds in agglomeration benefits finds that the incumbent natives of the largest cities lose from liberalization, because the local public-goods channel dominates — a point taken up in the next section. Natives, Migrants, and the Representative Resident: The Welfare Accounting Wu and You (2025) provide the disaggregated welfare accounting that the aggregate 11-percent numbers conceal, using a dynamic system-of-cities model with 340 prefectures, two skill groups, forward-looking migration, and a hukou policy represented as skill-specific lottery probabilities and a fiscal wedge. Under the counterfactual of removing all hukou restrictions from 2000 onward, they decompose welfare changes by skill, migration status, and city tier. In the tier-1 cities in 2010, low-skilled natives lose 17.0 percent and high-skilled natives lose 10.6 percent, while migrants gain between −0.2 percent (low-skill) and 5.4 percent (high-skill); tier-2 natives lose 6.3–4.0 percent and migrants gain 4.6–7.6 percent, and tier-3 natives lose only 2.3–2.1 percent while migrants gain 7.1–8.3 percent (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Migrants' welfare gains average 5.5 percent, above the national average of roughly 4.9 percent, because the direct removal of the fiscal wedge raises their real consumption. The decomposition of tier-1 natives' losses identifies the operative mechanism: holding the price of publicly-provided private goods constant nearly eliminates the loss (−6.9 percent for the low-skilled), implying that crowding in local education and health services — rival goods that migrants newly share — is the dominant distributional channel, with rising housing prices a secondary factor and land-rent shares and wages partially compensating natives (wu-you-2025-urbanization). The decline in the welfare of a "representative" resident who would evenly redistribute public goods and land rents between natives and migrants indicates that the tier-1 cities are locally oversized — a result that echoes the Ma and Tang (2020) finding that Shanghai's local welfare falls 8.3 percent when its additional barriers are removed (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade; tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Cross-paper pattern: Across the corpus the sign of migration's effect on incumbents is the contested fact — positive for the representative resident under Melitz (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade), negative for tier-1 natives under Wu–You's public-goods crowding channel (wu-you-2025-urbanization). The difference is partly market structure and partly whose welfare is being measured: the Melitz calculation averages over all residents including the new migrants, while the native-vs-migrant split isolates the incumbent losers. Skill Heterogeneity and the Hukou Friction The welfare effect of migration is not uniform across skill groups, because the hukou friction that constrains it is itself skill-differentiated. Liu, Wang, and Chen (2024) model the hukou system as an iceberg cost on labor mobility and embed it in a quantitative spatial general equilibrium with cross-skill productivity spillovers and public-service crowding; they find that optimizing the spatial allocation of human capital raises social welfare substantially, and that the efficient frontier is reached by redistributing from high-skill workers in high-wage cities toward low-skill workers in low-wage cities (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation). Because high-skilled migrants are more likely to be granted local hukou (37.3 percent of college graduates versus 3.3 percent of primary-school migrants in tier-1 cities in 2010), the distributional bite of the friction falls hardest on the low-skilled, whose entry into the largest cities is most restricted (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Wu and You (2025) likewise find that liberalizing hukou raises the low-skilled population of tier-1 cities by 116 percent against 50 percent for the high-skilled, so the skill mix of the marginal migrant is itself a welfare-relevant outcome. The hukou friction further suppresses the gains from reallocation: Liu, Wang, and Chen (2024) estimate that the settlement-threshold index reduces the welfare gains from optimizing human-capital allocation by roughly 2.4 percent, and design property-tax and transfer policies that can substitute for the hukou's allocative role (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation). Role of the Transportation Network in Shaping Local Impacts The geographic location of cities on China's transportation network substantially moderates the welfare effects of migration. Ma and Tang (2020) are the first to bring the comprehensive Chinese transportation network — roads, railways, and waterways digitized from high-resolution atlas data — into a structural migration model, using the fast-marching method of Allen and Arkolakis (2014). The estimated geographic costs matrix reveals large variation in trade costs conditional on physical distance: city pairs 1,000 km apart can have trade costs ranging from 1.15 to 1.37 depending on network connectivity. The transportation network creates a striking pattern in the distribution of migration's benefits. The top beneficiaries of internal migration are not the "superstar" cities themselves — Beijing, Shanghai, and Shenzhen — but their neighboring cities, which enjoy productivity spillovers through inter-city trade while being spared the surge in congestion disutility that accompanies rapid population growth in the primary destination (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). Tianjin (near Beijing), Suzhou and Hangzhou (near Shanghai), and Foshan (near Guangzhou) all rank among the top welfare gainers from the observed migration flows, despite receiving relatively modest net inflows themselves. Strategically positioned inland cities such as Wuhan (at the intersection of the Yangtze River and the Beijing-Guangzhou railway) and Nanjing also benefit disproportionately through improved market access. The frontier of this geography research is network expansion itself: quantitative spatial work on new internet infrastructure finds that narrowing the digital divide raises welfare through improved market access and lower transaction costs, a channel that interacts with migration by relaxing the information and service-access constraints that complement geographic barriers (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure; lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market). City-Specific Migration Barriers and Their Effects The largest Chinese cities maintain substantially higher migration barriers than the national average, which Ma and Tang (2020) estimate from the gap between model-implied and observed population inflows. Shanghai has migration barriers 24 percent higher than the national average, Guangzhou 13 percent higher, and Beijing 8 percent higher. These barriers reduce the national welfare by 0.7 to 3.9 percent, depending on the city. The barriers are identified from the fact that the observed population inflows into these cities are too small given their wage advantages, controlling for the estimated geographic and institutional migration costs. Removing these city-specific barriers produces divergent local and national welfare effects. For Beijing and Guangzhou, complete removal of the additional barriers raises local welfare by 9.7 percent and 18.6 percent respectively, as the increase in real income dominates the surge in congestion. For Shanghai, however, complete removal of barriers — which would bring an estimated 6 million additional migrants and push population toward 23 million versus roughly 17 million in 2005 — reduces local welfare by 8.3 percent because congestion costs overwhelm the real income gains (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). Shanghai is the exception that reveals the potential conflict between local and national welfare: the central government would prefer Shanghai to be substantially larger (population maximizing national welfare is roughly 22 million versus 17 million in 2005), but local residents would experience lower welfare at that population level. Wu and You (2025) generalize this tension across the urban hierarchy: 83 percent of tier-1 and 89 percent of tier-2 cities are locally oversized, yet relaxing any individual large city's hukou restrictions raises national welfare in 100 percent of tier-1 and 94 percent of tier-2 cases, because the friction introduced outweighs the gain from correcting city-size deviations (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Current assessment (2026-07): Shanghai's status as the exception where local and national welfare conflict has important political economy implications. It suggests that a uniform national hukou liberalization policy may be locally optimal in most but not all large cities, and that Shanghai-specific complementary policies — such as housing supply expansion or congestion pricing — may be needed to align local and national interests before full barrier removal (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Interaction with International Trade Liberalization Internal migration and international trade liberalization interact to amplify aggregate welfare gains. Ma and Tang (2020) simulate a 10-percent reduction in international trade barriers and find that migration amplifies the gains from trade by roughly 55 percent. The mechanism operates through local labor markets: trade liberalization increases labor demand in coastal cities, pushing up wages. Without migration, rising wages throttle firm growth and limit the expansion of export-oriented production. With migration, the inflow of workers from the interior dampens the coastal wage increase, enabling further firm expansion and larger gains from trade. Under migration, the aggregate real income increase from the trade liberalization is 12.7 percent, compared to 8.2 percent without migration. This amplification effect is specific to international trade. Internal trade liberalization and internal migration are substitutes rather than complements, because both serve to narrow spatial income differences — internal trade benefits smaller interior cities more than coastal ones, reducing the incentive to migrate (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). The amplification also depends on firm entry: when both migration and firm entry are shut down, the gains from trade liberalization fall to 5.5 percent, a magnitude comparable to the standard gains from trade in models without spatial labor mobility. The general-equilibrium logic that trade and factor mobility are interdependent welfare instruments is developed in the canonical QSE framework of Redding (2016) and surveyed in Redding and Rossi-Hansberg (2017): the welfare gains from goods-market integration depend on whether labor can move to exploit the newly created differences in real income, so migration and trade costs should be evaluated jointly (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Global Magnitudes as an Upper Bound The Chinese estimates can be read against a global upper bound. Desmet, Nagy, and Rossi-Hansberg (2018) develop a dynamic spatial growth model of the world economy at a 1°×1° resolution and quantify the gains from relaxing migration frictions. With current frictions only about 0.3 percent of people migrate across countries each year; under free mobility, 70.3 percent of the world's population changes country at impact. In present-discounted-value terms, fully liberalizing global migration raises welfare by 305.9 percent (amenity-adjusted real GDP) and real income by 125.8 percent (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). These numbers dwarf the Chinese estimates of welfare gains from hukou removal (roughly 4–11 percent in the static frameworks of Tombe–Zhu and Ma–Tang, and 4.7 percent on average in Wu–You's dynamic model) — a gap that reflects both the far larger dispersion of productivity and amenities across countries than across Chinese prefectures, and the fact that international borders are a far more severe migration barrier than China's internal hukou system. Current assessment (2026-07): The wide gap between the Chinese welfare estimates and the global free-migration upper bound is a calibration of relative frictions, not a forecast. It indicates that China's internal barriers, while the largest single spatial distortion in a national economy, are still an order of magnitude smaller than the institutional and cultural barriers that segment the world's labor market (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development; tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Frontier: QSE Policy Translation for China The contrasting welfare predictions of the Eaton-Kortum and Melitz frameworks have direct implications for hukou reform policy design. If the Ma-Tang (Melitz) framework correctly describes Chinese cities — and the empirical evidence on firm entry supports this — then the policy conclusion is unambiguous: further relaxation of migration restrictions benefits both national efficiency and local welfare in almost all destination cities. The one exception (Shanghai) suggests that complementary housing and infrastructure policies, rather than continued migration restrictions, are the appropriate response to congestion. The Ma-Tang framework has been extended by Li, Ma, and Tang (2024) to incorporate firm-level frictions (output and labor wedges), showing that migration alleviates the aggregate welfare impact of micro-level misallocation by allowing workers to move from heavily to lightly distorted regions. This interaction between migration and within-region distortions introduces a new policy consideration: reducing firm-level frictions (through SOE reform, financial development, or competition policy) and liberalizing migration are substitutes for raising aggregate welfare but have opposite effects on spatial inequality, with migration liberalization increasing it and friction reduction decreasing it. The welfare-accounting evidence of Wu and You (2025) sharpens the policy menu: conditional fiscal transfers tied to migrant inflows, greater supply of market-provided private goods (education, health), and a higher elasticity of urban land supply all mitigate the native losses from liberalization, with the land-supply elasticity the single most effective instrument (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Liu, Wang, and Chen (2024) add that property taxation financing local public services can substitute for the hukou's allocative role, shifting the required redistribution from high-wage to low-wage cities and toward low-skill workers (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation). Extensions incorporating dynamic migration with forward-looking firms, as in the dynamic QSE literature surveyed by Zhao, Chen, and Fu (2022), could further refine the welfare predictions by allowing firms and workers to anticipate future population inflows; dynamic models also reveal that migration and capital accumulation interact to slow convergence, so the persistence of the hukou wedge matters for the entire transition path, not just the steady state (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). The rapid expansion of digital infrastructure and the emergence of data as a non-rival production factor (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market) may also alter the local welfare calculus by reducing the fixed costs of firm entry and expanding the variety channel in smaller cities, and by enabling remote access to public services that lowers the fiscal wedge. These developments suggest that the welfare effects of migration in Chinese cities are not static but evolve with the technological, fiscal, and institutional environment. pages.text: Exact-Hat Algebra Exact-hat algebra (or simply "hat algebra") is a computational technique for undertaking counterfactual analysis in quantitative trade and spatial equilibrium models. Introduced by Dekle, Eaton, and Kortum (2008) and generalised across the quantitative spatial literature, it reformulates a model's equilibrium conditions in terms of "hatted" variables — the ratio of a counterfactual value to its initial value, such that $\hat{x} \equiv x'/x$ — and solves the counterfactual equilibrium as a fixed point in these proportional changes. Its defining property is that the levels of unobserved fundamentals (productivity, amenities) cancel out of the system, so a counterfactual can be computed using only observed initial-equilibrium data (trade shares, wages, populations, migration flows) and structural parameters. The technique underlies essentially every quantitative counterfactual in this wiki, from NAFTA welfare to Chinese internal-trade and migration liberalisation, and is the computational complement to model-inversion-and-fundamentals-recovery, which recovers fundamentals, and sufficient-statistics-in-spatial-models, which bypasses them. This page develops the canonical single-sector derivation, the multi-sector, mobile-factor, and dynamic extensions, and the limits of what the method can establish. The problem exact-hat algebra solves Counterfactual analysis in a model with many locations and sectors requires solving for a new general equilibrium after changing some exogenous variable — a tariff, a transport cost, a migration cost. In a naively parameterised Eaton–Kortum model, doing so appears to require knowing the levels of all unobserved fundamentals: the productivity states $T_i$ (or $\lambda_i^j$ in a sectoral version), amenities, and bilateral iceberg trade costs $d{ni}$, none of which are directly observed (eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Because these fundamentals enter the trade-share and price equations multiplicatively alongside the very variables being changed, a researcher who cannot observe them cannot in general solve the counterfactual levels equilibrium. The hat-algebra insight is that the counterfactual question itself is usually a question about changes: what happens to wages, prices, trade shares, and welfare when trade costs change from $d{ni}$ to $d{ni}'$, holding fundamentals fixed. When the equilibrium conditions are rewritten in proportional changes, every term containing the unobserved level of a fundamental divides out (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta; redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). The same property holds in internal-trade and migration applications, where the unobserved objects include provincial productivities and migration frictions rather than international ones (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). This is what makes hat algebra "exact": it is not a linearisation or a first-order approximation around a point, but an exact restatement of the model's equilibrium in a different variable system (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Hatted variables and the cancellation of fundamentals Formally, define the relative change of any variable as $\hat{x} = x'/x$, where $x'$ denotes the counterfactual value. In the multi-sector Eaton–Kortum structure of Caliendo and Parro, the equilibrium conditions in relative changes take a strikingly compact form (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta). The change in the cost of an input bundle is $$ \hat{c}n^j = \hat{w}n^{\gamma_n^j} \prod{k=1}^J \hat{P}n^{k^{\gamma_n^{k,j}}}, $$ the price index changes as $$ \hat{P}n^j = \left[ \sum{i=1}^N \pi{ni}^j \left(\hat{\kappa}{ni}^j \hat{c}i^j\right)^{-\theta^j} \right]^{-1/\theta^j}, $$ and bilateral trade shares change as $$ \hat{\pi}{ni}^j = \left[ \frac{\hat{c}i^j \hat{\kappa}{ni}^j}{\hat{P}n^j} \right]^{-\theta^j}. $$ Notice what these equations do not contain: the fundamental productivity parameters $\lambda_i^j$ and the levels of the iceberg costs $d{ni}^j$ have cancelled out of the system, because both numerator and denominator of the trade-share expression scale with them. What enters instead are the initial trade shares $\pi{ni}^j$ — observable data — together with the structural parameters $\theta^j$ and the assumed change in trade costs $\hat{\kappa}{ni}^j$ (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta; redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). The same cancellation recurs in the continuous-space and internal-economy variants of the model, so the technique transfers without modification from international to sub-national settings (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). The empirical signature of the method is thus that counterfactual predictions are invariant to the level of fundamentals but remain fully sensitive to the elasticities — a change in the Fréchet dispersion parameter $\theta$ rescales every counterfactual. The home-trade-share welfare formula The cleanest consequence of hat algebra is a closed-form welfare formula. In a single-sector Eaton–Kortum economy with a single factor, the real-welfare change from any trade-cost change equals the change in the domestic trade share raised to the power $-1/\theta$ (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade): $$ \hat{W}n = \hat{\pi}{nn}^{-1/\theta}. $$ The derivation follows directly from the price-index equation: the price index can be written solely in terms of the domestic trade share, $P_n^{-\theta} \propto A_n w_n^{-\theta}/\pi{nn}$, so taking ratios eliminates $A_n$ and $w_n$ terms that do not change. In a multi-sector setting the single formula generalises to a weighted sum across sectors, with each sector's domestic-share change weighted by its consumption share divided by its own elasticity (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta). This "home-trade-share ladder" is also where the choice of aggregation bites. Tombe and Zhu's internal-trade accounting uses the sectoral version of the same formula to relate the change in provincial labour productivity to the change in the provincial domestic trade share, $$ \hat{y}n^j = \hat{A}n^j \left(\hat{\pi}{nn}^j\right)^{-1/\theta}, $$ holding the productivity residual $\hat{A}n^j$ as the model's account of the unexplained component (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). When Caliendo and Parro compare a one-sector model against their 40-sector benchmark for the same NAFTA tariff change, the one-sector specification delivers welfare effects on average 71% smaller, because averaging sectoral elasticities into a single $\theta$ discards the covariance between sectoral trade-share changes and sectoral $\alpha^j/\theta^j$ weights that drives the gains (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta). Desmet, Nagy, and Rossi-Hansberg's dynamic global model similarly leans on domestic-trade and population responses to quantify the welfare consequences of migration liberalisation at the world scale (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). Current assessment (2026-07): The home-trade-share formula is the single most-used sufficient statistic in this corpus — nearly every quantitative welfare number on the wiki is, at root, a function of observed or counterfactual domestic trade shares. Its magnitude is governed entirely by the trade elasticity $\theta$ and by how finely the sectoral decomposition is taken; see trade-elasticity-estimation for why that parameter is so contentious. Counterfactuals as a fixed point: NAFTA in hats For a multi-country, multi-sector model the hat system does not collapse to a single formula; it must be solved numerically as a fixed point. Caliendo and Parro's procedure for the NAFTA counterfactual is the canonical implementation (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta). Given the change in tariffs — encoded as $\hat{\kappa}{ni}^j = (1+\tau{ni}^{j'})/(1+\tau{ni}^j)$ — the algorithm guesses a vector of counterfactual wage changes $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$; solves the input-cost and price-index equations for all sectors and countries; recovers counterfactual trade shares from the hat trade-share equation; solves for counterfactual expenditures; and iterates on wages until the trade-balance condition holds in every country. Only data on initial trade shares, value added, input–output coefficients, and the estimated sectoral elasticities are required — no estimates of fundamental productivity or of iceberg trade-cost levels (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Applied to the change in NAFTA tariffs between 1993 and 2005, this procedure yields Mexico's welfare rising by 1.31%, the United States by 0.08%, and Canada falling by 0.06%, with real wages rising in all three countries (1.72%, 0.11%, and 0.32%, respectively). Decomposing welfare into terms-of-trade and volume-of-trade components shows the gains are overwhelmingly a volume-of-trade phenomenon: trade creation within the bloc contributes 1.80% to Mexican welfare while trade diversion with the rest of the world subtracts 0.08% (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta). The counterfactual is driven throughout by the paper's estimated sectoral elasticities, which range from 0.37 to 51.08 across sectors, with an F-test rejecting a common elasticity (F(17, 7294) = 7.52); see trade-elasticity-estimation. The same fixed-point logic, with a different initial equilibrium and different cost shocks, underlies the internal-liberalisation counterfactuals in Tombe and Zhu, where reductions in Chinese internal trade costs raise aggregate real GDP per worker by 11.2% and welfare by 11.4%, versus 4.0% and 2.9% for external trade-cost reductions of comparable size (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Multi-sector and input–output extensions The power of the hat system is that it extends to arbitrarily rich production structures. When production uses intermediate inputs from all sectors, the input-cost equation couples every sector's price change to every other sector's, and the welfare formula acquires additional terms for final goods, intermediate goods, and sectoral linkages (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta). These linkages materially amplify the effect of a given trade-cost change: in the NAFTA application, removing intermediate goods from the model lowers welfare effects by 62% on average, and removing input–output connections lowers them by 50% — against a benchmark where Mexico's gain is 1.31%, a model without materials yields only 0.50% and one without sectoral interrelations 0.66% (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta). The same amplification appears in the internal-trade context. Tombe and Zhu show that the 11.2% real-GDP gain from Chinese internal trade-cost reductions collapses to roughly 3.0% when intermediate inputs are removed from the production structure, even though the trade-share responses are nearly identical — the extra gain comes from cheaper materials propagating through the input–output table, not from larger reallocations of trade (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Their decomposition of 2000–05 labour-productivity growth attributes 4.9% to internal trade, 0.5% to external trade, and 10.8% to migration, against a 40.9% productivity residual. This intermediate-input amplification is a general feature of the quantitative trade class, emphasised in the survey treatment as one of the reasons single-sector and no-materials models systematically understate the gains from liberalisation (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). Factor mobility and migration in hat form When labour is mobile across locations, hatted population becomes an endogenous outcome rather than a fixed datum, and the hat system must be augmented with a migration equation. Redding's model with heterogeneous worker preferences writes the counterfactual system for wage changes, trade-share changes, and population-share changes — $\hat{w}i$, $\hat{\pi}{ni}$, $\hat{\lambda}n$ — using only initial wages, trade shares, and population shares, plus the assumed change in trade costs (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). The welfare consequence is that the common change in expected utility depends on changes in both domestic trade shares and population reallocations: $$ \hat{\bar{U}} = \left[ \sum{n \in N} \frac{L_n}{\bar{L}} \left( \hat{\pi}{nn}^{-\alpha/\theta} \, \hat{L}n^{-(1-\alpha)} \right)^{\epsilon} \right]^{1/\epsilon}. $$ The domestic-trade-share term captures the change in goods-market access; the population term captures the price of the immobile factor, land, which is bid up in locations that expand. A researcher who ignores the population margin and computes welfare from the domestic trade share alone obtains an "incorrect immobile welfare" measure that is substantially wrong and spuriously heterogeneous across locations even though true expected utility moves together (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). The models in which population is immobile are the special case $\hat{L}n = 1$, where the formula collapses back to the domestic-trade-share sufficient statistic $\hat{\pi}{nn}^{-\alpha/\theta}$ — the canonical $\hat{\pi}{nn}^{-1/\theta}$ when goods are the only expenditure item (eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade; caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta). The same mobile-labour hat structure, with migration shares $m{ni}^{jk}$ replacing trade shares as the observable sufficient objects, drives the Chinese internal-migration counterfactuals of Tombe and Zhu, whose aggregate welfare change is a weighted sum over region-sector cells of real-income and own-stay migration-share changes (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Across the corpus, hat algebra makes the reallocation margin — population, varieties, sectors — the central quantitative question. The static home-share formula is the floor; the interesting action in every welfare number comes from how much of the change is channelled through a margin the single-formula version omits. This pattern is visible in Redding's population term, in Caliendo–Parro's sectoral linkages, and in Tombe–Zhu's intermediate-input amplification (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare; caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta; tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Dynamic exact-hat Hat algebra generalises to dynamic environments in which agents are forward-looking. Kleinman, Liu, and Redding extend the dynamic exact-hat methodology — developed for migration-only models by Caliendo, Dvorkin, and Parro — to incorporate forward-looking capital accumulation, where workers make migration decisions and immobile landlords choose consumption and investment in local buildings and structures (kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial). Their Proposition 2 shows that, given an initial observed allocation (population shares, capital stocks, trade and migration share matrices) and any convergent sequence of future changes in fundamentals, the economy's transition path can be solved in time differences $\dot{x}{t+1} = x{t+1}/x_t$ without observing the level of fundamentals. The linearised version of the model then yields a closed-form transition path governed by an impact matrix and a transition matrix that depend only on observed shares and structural parameters; the speed of convergence is characterised by the eigenvalues of the transition matrix, with an average half-life of around 20 years and a maximum of around 80 years across U.S. states (kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial). The dynamic spatial growth model of Desmet, Nagy, and Rossi-Hansberg provides a complementary dynamic analogue in which hat-type counterfactuals are computed along a transition to a balanced-growth path. Because the innovation decision reduces to a static problem, their migration-liberalisation experiments can be solved by reallocating the world's population across $1^\circ \times 1^\circ$ cells under alternative migration-friction scenarios: fully liberalising migration would move 70.3% of the world's population across countries at impact and raise welfare roughly threefold in present-value terms (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). Both dynamic treatments share the static method's defining feature — counterfactuals computed from observed initial conditions without observing fundamentals — while adding a time dimension (kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial; desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). Scope, limits, and relation to the wider toolkit What exact-hat algebra can and cannot do follows directly from what it is. Within the model, the method is exact: it delivers the precise general-equilibrium response to a specified change in trade or migration costs, conditional on the model's structure and parameter values (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). It cannot, however, validate the model. Because the levels of fundamentals are never observed, a hat-algebra counterfactual is silent on whether the underlying gravity structure, the Fréchet distribution, and the constant-elasticity assumptions are correct; it inherits those assumptions wholesale. It also requires a consistent initial equilibrium — the observed data must themselves satisfy the model's equilibrium conditions — and it is only as reliable as the parameters it is fed, so welfare statements hinge on the quality of the trade elasticities and the correct transcription of the policy change into hat costs (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta; kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial). Methodologically, hat algebra is one member of a three-part toolkit. model-inversion-and-fundamentals-recovery runs the equilibrium mapping backwards to recover the unobserved fundamentals that rationalise observed data; exact-hat algebra runs the model forwards in changes and thereby sidesteps fundamentals altogether; and sufficient-statistics-in-spatial-models compresses the welfare answer into a small set of observable statistics (domestic trade shares, populations, elasticities) that the hat system itself delivers (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). All three are facets of the same modelling technology, and applied papers typically use inversion for calibration, hat algebra for the counterfactual, and a sufficient-statistic formula for the headline welfare number (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Current assessment (2026-07): Exact-hat algebra validates counterfactuals only conditional on the model, never the model itself. The open methodological frontier is therefore less about the algebra — which is standard — than about the credibility of the initial equilibrium, the parameters, and the assumed cost shocks that feed it. Its computational limits at very large numbers of locations, and its extension to models with firm entry, capital, or non-CES structure, remain active research areas (kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial; desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). Inversion as Input to Parameter Estimation
What Inversion Can and Cannot Test

pages.text: Model Inversion and Fundamentals Recovery Model inversion is the procedure by which a quantitative spatial or trade model is "run backwards": its equilibrium conditions are solved from observed endogenous variables — wages, employment, trade shares, commuting flows, land rents, and population — to recover the unobserved exogenous fundamentals — productivity, amenities, and sometimes trade or commuting costs or match-quality parameters — that rationalise the data as an equilibrium of the model. When the inversion is exact and unique, it converts an untestable assignment of fundamentals into a deterministic mapping from data plus parameters to fundamentals. This recovered set of fundamentals is the essential input for structural estimation of the model's parameters and for counterfactual analysis that conditions on the observed initial equilibrium. The technique is the epistemological twin of exact-hat algebra: inversion makes fundamentals observable, while hat algebra makes them unnecessary for counterfactuals. The Identification Problem Every quantitative spatial model in this literature starts from a decomposition problem: observed outcomes are equilibrium responses to unobserved locational characteristics, and those characteristics are themselves a mix of exogenous fundamentals and endogenous externalities. ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density states the challenge directly: high land prices and concentrated activity are consistent with strong agglomeration forces, but equally with shared amenities or common natural advantages. redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial frames the issue at the level of the model class: quantitative spatial models are typically exactly identified, with a one-to-one mapping from the observed endogenous variables (employment and wages) to the exogenous primitives (productivity and amenities), so a model can always be constructed that rationalises any observed spatial distribution. redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare adds the labour-market dimension: with heterogeneous worker preferences, each location faces an upward-sloping supply of population, expected utility is equalised across locations while real incomes differ, and the mapping from location characteristics to populations and wages remains one-to-one. allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography formalises the ambiguity in continuous space, where overall productivity and amenities each combine a fundamental component with endogenous spillovers that depend on the surrounding density of activity; the same observed schedules can be generated by many such decompositions. The identification problem therefore has two halves: recovering fundamentals given parameters, and separating the two using independent variation. As redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial notes, observed wages and populations cannot by themselves identify the structural parameters, because any change in a parameter can be offset by a change in the recovered fundamentals. The Inversion Theorem: Exact Recovery of Fundamentals The core theoretical result is that, given parameters and data on the endogenous variables, the unobserved fundamentals are uniquely determined up to a normalization. redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial demonstrates the theorem for a canonical new economic geography model: inverting the model uses its equilibrium equations to solve for the quality-adjusted land supplies $\{H_n\}$ and productivities $\{A_n\}$ from observed populations $\{L_n\}$ and wages $\{w_n\}$ — the reverse of equilibrium, which determines $\{L_n, w_n\}$ from $\{A_n, H_n\}$. redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare proves the analogous proposition for a Ricardian model with heterogeneous preferences: given parameters, a parameterisation of bilateral trade costs, and data on populations, wages, and land supplies, there exist unique values of amenities $\{B_n\}$ and productivities $\{A_n\}$ consistent with the data, up to a choice of units; the proof is recursive — income-equals-expenditure and trade shares give productivities, land market clearing gives rents, the price index gives prices, and residential choice probabilities give amenities. allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography establishes the continuous-space version: for any continuous population and wage schedules there exists a unique (to-scale) pair of productivity and amenity functions that make those schedules a regular spatial equilibrium. monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting states the applied version for a model with both trade and commuting: given observed data on wages, employment by workplace, commuting flows, and land area, and a parameterisation of trade and commuting costs, the model recovers unique values of the unobserved productivity and amenities that exactly rationalise the data as an equilibrium. The inversion therefore supplies a deterministic mapping from data plus parameters to fundamentals, and the same arguments apply whether the researcher observes trade costs and infers trade shares or observes bilateral trade shares and recovers the costs. Conditions for Uniqueness and Invertibility Inversion inherits its properties from equilibrium uniqueness, because a model with multiple equilibria could in principle rationalise the same data with different fundamentals. allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography provides the sharpest statement for continuous space: writing the dispersion-and-agglomeration exponents as $\gamma_1 \equiv 1 - \alpha(\sigma-1) - \beta\sigma$ and $\gamma_2 \equiv 1 + \alpha\sigma + (\sigma-1)\beta$, a regular equilibrium exists only when $\gamma_1 \neq 0$; when $\gamma_1 > 0$ all equilibria are regular; and the equilibrium is unique when $\gamma_2/\gamma_1 \in [-1, 1]$, in which case it can be computed by a simple iterative procedure. When $\gamma_1 < 0$, no equilibrium is point-wise locally stable. redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial shows that in its discrete new economic geography example the same logic reduces to $\sigma(1-\alpha) > 1$, which guarantees $\gamma_2/\gamma_1 \in (0,1)$ and that dispersion forces dominate agglomeration forces, so the inversion recovering $\{A_n, H_n\}$ has a unique solution. redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare obtains the corresponding condition $\sigma(1-\tilde{\alpha}) > 1$ with worker heterogeneity, which specialises to Helpman's condition $\sigma(1-\alpha) > 1$ in the no-heterogeneity limit. The role of regular equilibria matters for the empirical strategy: ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density notes that once agglomeration forces are present multiple equilibria are possible, but the mapping from data and parameters to structural residuals remains unique regardless, because the equilibrium conditions contain enough information to solve for the residuals even when the model is not globally concave. Current assessment (2026-07): The regularity condition appears under different notation — $\gamma_1 > 0$ in Allen–Arkolakis and $\sigma(1-\alpha) > 1$ in the Redding–Rossi-Hansberg survey — but it is the same economic object: dispersion forces (inelastic land, commuting costs) must dominate agglomeration forces for the inversion to be well-defined and the counterfactual determinate. Empirical Implementation Applied implementations differ in which fundamentals are recovered and from which data. monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting inverts a trade-and-commuting model for US counties: using the equality between income and expenditure, county trade deficits $D_i$ allocated from the Commodity Flow Survey, observed wages, employment, average residential income, and residents, the model yields a system of $N$ equations in $N$ unobserved county productivities, $$w_i L_i - \sum{n \in N} \frac{L_i \left(d{ni} w_i / A_i\right)^{1-\sigma}}{\sum{k \in N} L_k \left(d{nk} w_k / A_k\right)^{1-\sigma}} \left[\bar{v}n R_n + D_n\right] = 0,$$ which is solved for a unique vector of productivities; the commuting model is then inverted to recover the "ease of commuting" $\mathcal{B}{ni} \equiv B{ni}\kappa{ni}^{-\varepsilon}$ for every pair, with the distance coefficient estimated at $-4.43$ against $-1.29$ for goods trade and the Fréchet heterogeneity parameter at $\varepsilon = 3.30$. ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density performs the block-level analogue for Berlin, recovering adjusted overall productivity, amenities, and density of development from floor prices, wages, residence employment, and commuting market access, without taking a stand on the relative importance of externalities versus fundamentals; the commuting semi-elasticity is estimated at $\nu = \varepsilon\kappa = 0.07$ and the Fréchet parameter at $\varepsilon = 6.83$. redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial provides a worked illustration of the same procedure on a $30 \times 30$ grid, in which adding population data for a region would immediately yield estimates of its productivity. tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure shows that the commuting market access terms of an urban model can themselves be recovered uniquely (to scale) from residential populations, employment, commute costs $d{ij} = \exp(\kappa t{ij})$, and the commuting elasticity. All three need the levels of endogenous variables — heavier data than exact-hat-algebra counterfactuals, which require only initial-equilibrium values. Inversion as Input to Parameter Estimation Because inversion recovers fundamentals conditional on parameters, it is naturally embedded in a two-step estimation strategy: invert to obtain structural residuals, then estimate parameters from moment conditions in those residuals. ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density is the canonical implementation. Given parameters, adjusted production and residential fundamentals are closed-form functions of observed data and parameters — the structural residuals — and the paper estimates the agglomeration and commuting parameters by efficient GMM on moment conditions that impose that changes in these residuals are uncorrelated with the exogenous change in the surrounding concentration of activity induced by Berlin's division and reunification. The central estimates are an elasticity of productivity with respect to workplace employment density of about 0.07 and an elasticity of amenities with respect to residence density of about 0.15, both highly localised. redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial describes the same division of labour abstractly: recovered fundamentals let the observed variation in the data be decomposed within the model into the contributions of each fundamental, and additional data not used in the quantification, or exogenous shocks, provide the overidentification checks that identify parameters. monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting estimates the commuting and trade elasticities from gravity equations first and then recovers fundamentals, while tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure estimates spillover parameters by GMM from model-inferred productivities and amenities, with TransMilenio providing the exogenous shock to commuting market access that identifies the residential supply elasticity and the productivity and amenity spillovers. Recovering Match-Quality and Network Fundamentals The inversion logic extends beyond productivity and amenities to the match and network objects that microfound spatial choice. tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure models each worker's productivity with each potential employer as a draw from a location-specific Fréchet distribution $F(\varepsilon_j) = \exp(-\tilde{T}g \varepsilon_j^{-\theta_g})$, where $\theta_g$ controls the dispersion of match productivities and $\tilde{T}g$ their level; recovering these match-productivity fundamentals (with $\theta_H = 2.44 < \theta_L = 4$ for high- and low-skill workers, and $T_g$ calibrated to the college wage premium) is the same operation as recovering productivity in a trade model, and the structural residual in the reduced form reflects changing exogenous location fundamentals — productivities, amenities, and floorspace supplies. ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density recovers commuting market access, a network object that summarises access to jobs, from the labour market clearing condition before productivity and amenities are solved. monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting treats the ease of commuting as the network fundamental recovered from observed commuting flows, and redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial shows that if bilateral trade shares rather than trade costs are observed, then trade costs can also be recovered alongside productivities and land supplies. These recovered network objects are themselves the subject of dedicated measurement (see commuter-market-access). What Inversion Can and Cannot Test The defining epistemic caveat is that an inverted model's ability to explain the data is not a test of the model. redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial is explicit: because the model is exactly identified, the unobserved fundamentals are free parameters that can be adjusted to ensure the model exactly matches the data, so the model's fit cannot be used as evidence in its favour — the recovered fundamentals account for the variation in the data but do not explain it. Inversion tests only whether some fundamentals can rationalise the observed outcomes, not whether the model's mechanisms are correct. Breaking the circularity requires independent variation. ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density provides the cleanest example: a model with exogenous productivity and amenities, inverted to fit pre-war Berlin, is used to predict the counterfactual treatment effects of division; because those predicted effects are substantially smaller than the actual ones, the exogenous-fundamentals model is rejected, and the exogenous variation of the Berlin Wall validates the estimated agglomeration mechanisms. allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography and redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare make the same point formally: without overidentification checks or natural experiments, the same data can be rationalised by many parameterisations, and different models imply different recovered fundamentals even when they fit identically. Across the corpus, inversion alone never validates a model: validation comes from out-of-sample predictions or natural experiments, of which the Berlin Wall is the cleanest. The relationship to the other tools of the toolkit follows directly. Inversion recovers the unobserved fundamentals that make the data an equilibrium; exact-hat-algebra then cancels those fundamentals in counterfactual computation, so they need never be solved; and the sufficient-statistics-in-spatial-models of the welfare literature summarise counterfactual welfare without any reference to the fundamentals at all. The three are complementary answers to the same identification problem: make the unobservables observable, render them irrelevant, or summarise the outcome that does not depend on them. Open Questions The static, single-sector setting in which inversion is best understood does not yet cover the frontier of the literature. redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial identifies the open cases: models with firm entry, physical capital, or dynamics break the one-to-one mapping, and the curse of dimensionality grows with the number of locations, so that exact inversion becomes computationally demanding. kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial develops a dynamic spatial model in which the steady state is unique under a spectral-radius condition and the transition path can be characterised analytically, but the inversion of such dynamic models — recovering fundamentals that rationalise an observed transition — is considerably harder than the static case. desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development embeds the same dynamics through innovation and technology diffusion. Identification of parameters is also fragile when the GMM objective is not globally concave: ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density shows by grid search and Monte Carlo that its particular objective is well behaved, but notes this is a property to be verified case by case rather than assumed. Current assessment (2026-07): Exact inversion is fully worked out for static gravity-class models; the frontier is inversion under dynamics (Kleinman–Liu–Redding), endogenous capital, and many-location settings where the mapping is no longer one-to-one or globally concave. Beyond the Static Formula: Factor Mobility
Envelope-Theorem Sufficient Statistics in Urban Settings
Structural Assumptions and the Limits of the Shortcut
pages.excerpt: A sufficient statistic in quantitative spatial economics is a low-dimensional observable, or combination of observables, that fully summarises a counterfactual's welfare or treatment effect, so that computing the full general-equilibrium re-solution is unnecessary. The canonical…
pages.text: Sufficient Statistics in Spatial Models A sufficient statistic in quantitative spatial economics is a low-dimensional observable, or combination of observables, that fully summarises a counterfactual's welfare or treatment effect, so that computing the full general-equilibrium re-solution is unnecessary. The canonical example is the home-trade-share formula: in the Eaton–Kortum class of trade models the welfare gain from a trade-cost change is $\hat{W} = \hat{\pi}{nn}^{-1/\theta}$, a function only of the change in the domestic expenditure share and the trade elasticity. Redding (2016) extends the logic to models with labour mobility, where the sufficient statistic becomes the change in domestic trade shares plus the reallocation of population across locations. Tsivanidis (2026) shows that an envelope-theorem sufficient statistic — the first-order value-of-travel-time-savings measure — approximates the full general-equilibrium welfare effect of a transit investment. This page covers what makes a statistic sufficient, when the shortcut is exact, and when it misleads. What Makes a Statistic Sufficient The shortcut works because of a separation between the object of interest and the mechanism that produces it. In the quantitative spatial class of models reviewed by redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial, the welfare effect of a policy that changes trade costs can be expressed solely in terms of empirically observable sufficient statistics, even though the full equilibrium involves the entire vector of wages, populations, trade shares, and price indices across all locations. The sufficient statistics are functions of the initial equilibrium, so they can be measured without solving the counterfactual. eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade supplies the microfoundation: a Fréchet distribution of technology with shape parameter $\theta$ generates a gravity equation for bilateral trade and a price index that depends on the domestic technology and trade share, which is what makes the domestic share a sufficient statistic for welfare. redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare shows that the same property survives the introduction of labour mobility, at the cost of adding a second statistic for population reallocation. The role of the initial equilibrium is the same as in exact-hat-algebra — counterfactual outcomes are computed from observed initial values plus an assumed change in primitives, and the sufficient statistic is the collapsed version of that computation for the welfare object. Not every outcome admits a sufficient statistic; in general it is aggregate welfare, not the distribution of economic activity, that can be summarised by a low-dimensional object, and caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta shows that in multi-sector economies even welfare requires the sector-level breakdown rather than a single number. The Canonical Sufficient Statistic: Home-Trade-Share Welfare In the Eaton–Kortum model, country $n$'s expenditure share on its own goods is $\pi{nn} = T_n c_n^{-\theta} / \Phi_n$ with $\Phi_n = \sum_i T_i (c_i d{ni})^{-\theta}$, and the exact price index is $P_n = \gamma \Phi_n^{-1/\theta}$, so the welfare gain from any trade-cost change that leaves technology unchanged is the ratio of counterfactual to initial domestic expenditure shares raised to the power of the inverse trade elasticity, $$\hat{W}n = \hat{\pi}{nn}^{-1/\theta}.$$ The same formula holds across the class of models identified by the literature: Armington differentiation by origin, Eaton–Kortum Ricardian competition, and Melitz with a Pareto productivity distribution all deliver it, because they share the gravity structure and the constant trade elasticity (eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Applied work operationalises the formula directly, as tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china do for Chinese internal and international trade liberalisation, where the welfare consequences of measured cost changes are evaluated through exactly such trade-share statistics. caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta emphasises what happens outside that class: in a multi-sector model with input–output linkages, a single aggregate elasticity is insufficient, and welfare must be computed from sector-level domestic shares and sector-specific trade elasticities, with the change in welfare decomposed into terms-of-trade and volume-of-trade effects. The formula is therefore not universal — it is conditional on the gravity class and on the elasticity being the correct structural object for the model at hand. Current assessment (2026-07): The home-trade-share formula is the most-used welfare number in this corpus — it underlies the headline gains reported in the trade and migration synthesis pages — and its validity everywhere hinges on the model being inside the gravity class with a single trade elasticity. Beyond the Static Formula: Factor Mobility When labour is mobile across locations, the pure domestic-share formula fails because population reallocation itself carries welfare consequences through the price of the immobile factor, land. redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare derives the factor-mobility generalisation: with heterogeneous worker preferences, expected utility conditional on living in a location is equalised across locations while real incomes differ, and the common welfare gain between an autarky equilibrium ($A$) and a trade equilibrium ($T$) is $$\frac{\bar{U}n^T}{\bar{U}n^A} = \left(\frac{1}{\pi{nn}^T}\right)^{\frac{\alpha}{\theta}} \left(\frac{L_n^A}{L_n^T}\right)^{\frac{1}{\epsilon} + (1-\alpha)},$$ where $\pi{nn}^T$ is the open-economy domestic trade share, $L_n^A$ and $L_n^T$ are populations in the closed and open economies, $\theta$ the trade elasticity, $\epsilon$ the labour-supply elasticity, and $\alpha$ the consumption share. The domestic trade share and the population reallocation are together sufficient statistics for welfare; measuring welfare from the domestic share alone, without controlling for the population change, produces errors of the same order of magnitude as the true welfare gains. The redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial survey writes the same result for its new economic geography example as $\hat{\bar{V}} = (\pi{nn}^0/\pi{nn}^1)^{\alpha/(\sigma-1)}(\lambda_n^0/\lambda_n^1)^{(\sigma(1-\alpha)-1)/(\sigma-1)}$, a direct analogue of the international-trade result, with the population term added because land is an immobile factor. Applied work shows the magnitude: tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china finds that reducing China's migration costs so that one-third of workers migrate across provinces raises real GDP per worker by 12.8% and welfare by 45.6%, numbers computable because the model's welfare change is summarised by migration shares and real-income changes. monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting documents the commuting dimension of the same logic. Envelope-Theorem Sufficient Statistics in Urban Settings In urban models the sufficient-statistics logic takes an envelope-theorem form. tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure shows, first, that the change in the entire distribution of economic activity across a city in response to a transit improvement depends only on the change in two commuting-market-access terms and a structural residual of exogenous location fundamentals — the reduced-form elasticities of outcomes to commuting market access, together with the commuting elasticity and the change in commute costs, are sufficient statistics for the relative changes in activity. Second, Proposition 2 applies the envelope theorem: when the equilibrium is efficient, the first-order welfare impact of a change in infrastructure is precisely the value of travel time savings, the standard partial-equilibrium measure. This result builds directly on the commuting-gravity structure that ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density and monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting established, and that redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial surveys as a central building block of quantitative urban models. In Bogotá, the first-order travel-time-savings approach delivers a welfare gain of 1.25%, whereas the full sufficient-statistics implementation yields 2.39%; the travel-time measure thus accounts for only about 52% of the total gain, and of the gap between the two, roughly three-quarters is attributable to amenity and productivity externalities and one-quarter to approximation error. When the full multi-group model is estimated, average welfare effects of 1.93%–2.41% bracket the 2.39% sufficient-statistics number, so the aggregate shortcut performs well for total welfare. Across the corpus, aggregate sufficient statistics are accurate for total welfare but systematically silent on who wins and who loses — the distributional layer always requires re-solving the full model. Aggregate Versus Local Effects The same shortcut rarely works for local or distributional objects. redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare shows that at the regional level, using each region's domestic trade share without controlling for its population change produces discrepancies from the true welfare gain of roughly the same magnitude as the gain itself, whereas aggregating to the national level and using the country-level domestic share gives a much better approximation, because both the true common gain and the measured country-level gain are weighted averages of region characteristics. redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial makes the general point that the welfare statistic summarises the common change in utility while the reallocation of activity across locations — the object of most policy interest for individual places — is not summarised by any single scalar. monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting documents the empirical counterpart for local employment elasticities: the general-equilibrium elasticity of employment with respect to a local productivity shock varies from about 0.5 to 2.5 across US counties, so a single average elasticity, or a sufficient statistic derived from it, is misleading when applied to any individual county, and the heterogeneity is not captured by standard controls. tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure is explicit that its sufficient-statistics approach speaks to aggregate effects and is silent on the distribution of impacts across worker groups, which is why the full model must be estimated for distributional questions. A researcher who needs the welfare of a particular group, or the reallocation of population and wages across locations, must re-solve rather than use the scalar shortcut. Structural Assumptions and the Limits of the Shortcut What the sufficient statistic hides is exactly the structure that generates it. The number $\hat{\pi}{nn}^{-1/\theta}$ is a function of the assumed trade elasticity, and different elasticity values — or different models — imply different welfare numbers from the same trade-share change. caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta is the canonical caution: once sectors have different elasticities, a single statistic is not merely imprecise but conceptually wrong, and the welfare calculation requires the full set of sectoral trade elasticities, which are rejected as equal by the data. eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade shows that $\theta$ governs the strength of comparative advantage, so the welfare number inherits the uncertainty in $\theta$; the elasticity is estimated, not given. The applied literature consequently treats the sufficient-statistic magnitude as conditional: tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china reports welfare gains that depend on estimated migration and trade costs and on the Fréchet parameter, and redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial notes that the same trade-share change delivers different welfare effects in constant- versus increasing-returns models once population is mobile. The practical risk is mistaking the sufficient statistic for a structural elasticity or a policy lever — the statistic summarises welfare under the assumed model but is not itself a parameter that can be moved. Current assessment (2026-07): The persistent pitfall in applied work is to treat a sufficient statistic as if it were a structural or policy elasticity; the correct reading is that the statistic is a function of the model's elasticity and inherits all of its identifying assumptions. Dynamic Sufficient Statistics The static logic generalises to dynamic settings, at the cost of additional state variables. kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial develops a dynamic spatial model with forward-looking migration and capital accumulation in which the welfare consequences of a shock are the present value of utility along the transition path, not a static comparison of steady states; the model preserves a form of exact-hat computation for counterfactuals and characterises the transition path analytically by spectral methods, so that dynamic welfare can be expressed in terms of the initial distribution and the change in fundamentals rather than a full simulation. desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development similarly evaluates welfare as discounted lifetime utility $\sum_t \beta^t u_t^i$, with a balanced-growth path in which welfare and real consumption grow at a common rate that depends on the spatial distribution of employment. redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare supplies the bridge from the static result, since its sufficient statistic is derived from an initial-equilibrium condition that dynamic models inherit period by period. redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial situates these dynamic extensions as the natural generalisation of the static toolkit, where the sufficient statistic is no longer a single number but the distribution of discounted welfare responses. Open Questions Several boundaries of the sufficient-statistics method remain open. The known results cover the gravity class with CES demand and a single immobile factor; extensions to firm entry, capital, and non-CES demand do not in general admit the same low-dimensional summary, as the multi-sector results of caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta and the dynamic models of kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial and desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development illustrate. Whether a statistic is robust across model classes is a separate question: tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure shows that the relative counterfactual impacts are invariant across a family of urban models that share a gravity equation for commuting, but the level of aggregate welfare depends on structural parameters that must be calibrated. Finally, the interface between sufficient statistics and estimation is unresolved — the statistic is only as good as the elasticity that enters it, so the gains from the shortcut in computation are paid back in sensitivity to estimated parameters. pages.title: The Economics of Density: Evidence From the Berlin Wall
pages.excerpt: Paper claim — A quantitative model of internal city structure with agglomeration and dispersion forces over thousands of heterogeneous blocks, structurally estimated using Berlin's division and reunification, recovers substantial and highly localized production externalities…
pages.text: The Economics of Density: Evidence From the Berlin Wall (2015) Paper claim — A quantitative model of internal city structure with agglomeration and dispersion forces over thousands of heterogeneous blocks, structurally estimated using Berlin's division and reunification, recovers substantial and highly localized production externalities (productivity–density elasticity ≈ 0.07) and residential externalities (amenity–density elasticity ≈ 0.15) that together account for the observed reorganization of economic activity within West Berlin. Raw markdown: ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density Research Question How strong are the agglomeration and dispersion forces that shape the internal structure of cities, and can they be separated from variation in exogenous locational fundamentals (natural advantages for production, residential amenities)? The central identification challenge is that high land prices and dense economic activity in neighboring locations are equally consistent with strong agglomeration spillovers and with shared fundamentals; the paper asks whether an exogenous shock to the surrounding concentration of activity can disentangle the two. Model / Experimental Design A quantitative general-equilibrium model of a single city embedded in a wider economy, comprising a large number of discrete, arbitrarily heterogeneous blocks (i = 1, …, S). Workers. Perfectly mobile within the city and the wider economy (reservation utility Ū). Cobb–Douglas preferences over a tradable final good and residential floor space (expenditure share on floor space 1 − β = 0.25). Each worker draws an idiosyncratic utility shock for every residence–workplace pair from an independent Fréchet distribution (shape parameter ε), following McFadden (1974) and Eaton and Kortum (2002); iceberg commuting cost d_ij = e^{κτ_ij} rises with travel time τ_ij in minutes. The Fréchet structure yields residential and workplace choice probabilities and a gravity equation for commuting flows. Firms. Perfect competition, constant returns; Cobb–Douglas production in labor and commercial floor space (floor-space cost share 1 − α = 0.20). Zero-profit and profit-maximization conditions link productivity, wages, and commercial floor prices. Land market. No-arbitrage allocation of floor space between commercial and residential use (with a tax-equivalent land-use wedge ξ_i); competitive construction sector combining land and capital (land cost share in construction 1 − μ = 0.25); observed floor price is the max of commercial and residential price. Agglomeration forces.
