pages.text: Migration Barriers and Spatial Inequality Spatial inequality — the dispersion of real incomes, productivity, and welfare across locations within a country — is shaped by the interaction between migration barriers (hukou restrictions, moving costs, information frictions) and the underlying spatial distribution of productivity, amenities, and firm-level distortions. While migration barriers preserve spatial income differences by preventing labor from moving to high-productivity locations, their removal does not unambiguously reduce spatial inequality: when workers migrate to already-productive regions, the resulting agglomeration economies can widen the gap between winning and losing regions even as they raise national welfare. In China these forces are compounded by the state's own spatial instruments — rationed construction-land quotas, cross-regional capital allocation, and fiscal transfers — which are themselves drivers of regional gaps. The literature now spans migration frictions, firm-level misallocation, land-supply tilt, capital-flow distortions, and skill-heterogeneous human-capital allocation, together producing a fundamental tension between aggregate efficiency and spatial equity. Measuring Spatial Inequality in China China exhibits among the highest levels of spatial income inequality of any major economy. The ratio of real GDP per worker between the top five and bottom five provinces was approximately 4:1 in 2000 (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china), and the cross-province dispersion of nominal GDP per worker substantially exceeded that across U.S. states. Within provinces, the average ratio of real GDP per worker in non-agriculture relative to agriculture was also around 4:1, reflecting both productivity differentials and the barriers that prevented workers from moving out of agriculture. The large within-sector income gaps across provinces — even after controlling for rural-urban price differences — pointed to significant frictions in both goods and labor markets as the fundamental drivers of persistent spatial inequality (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china; ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). The sectoral divide is thus as large as the geographic one, and the two interact: the same barriers that keep workers in poor provinces also keep them in agriculture, so decompositions of China's spatial inequality must separate frictions to moving across locations from frictions to moving across sectors. Migration Barriers as Determinants of Spatial Inequality The hukou (household registration) system is the largest and most consequential migration barrier in modern China. Each citizen is assigned a hukou in a specific location and category, and changing either requires government approval; since the 1980s the prohibition on moving has been relaxed but replaced by restricted access to public services, higher costs for healthcare and children's education, and limited employment rights for migrants without local hukou (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china; wu-you-2025-urbanization). Tombe and Zhu (2019) estimate that the average cost of moving from rural to urban areas within a province in 2000 was equivalent to shrinking one's real income by a factor of nearly three; between-province moves were an order of magnitude more costly. In their decomposition, migration contributed roughly one-tenth to aggregate labor productivity growth between 2000 and 2005, with about five-sixths of these gains coming from the reallocation of labor from agriculture to non-agriculture rather than from equalization across locations — so the largest gains from liberalization come from moving workers out of agriculture, not from narrowing inter-regional gaps. Wu and You (2025) estimate that the overall hukou system created an average GDP loss of 13.6% and a welfare loss of 4.7% over 2000–2020, and show that it is generally welfare-reducing to restrict the size of any city through migration barriers. These aggregate results, however, mask important distributional consequences. Firm-Level Frictions and the Spatial Distribution of Distortions Spatial inequality in China is not only a story of migration barriers keeping workers away from productive regions. Firm-level frictions — output and labor wedges that distort firm decisions within each location — are themselves spatially distributed in a way that amplifies income disparities. Li, Ma, and Tang (2024) estimate that friction dispersion is systematically higher in poorer prefectures: the median standard deviation of output frictions is 0.086–0.084 in the richest coastal regions but 0.108 inland, and the correlation between frictions and productivity is substantially positive in poor regions (0.242) but near zero on the coasts. These spatial patterns explain approximately 13% of the observed cross-prefecture variation in per-capita GDP. The spatial distribution of frictions also reinforces migration flows: because the most distorted locations are also the poorest, the friction gradient and the income gradient point in the same direction, so migration toward less-distorted regions and friction reduction in distorted regions operate on the same spatial fault lines. Crucially, policies that reduce this dispersion reduce spatial inequality — the opposite of what migration liberalization does — because poorer prefectures, starting from higher dispersion, benefit disproportionately from uniform reductions (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). The Migration-Misallocation Interaction The most striking finding in this literature is that migration and firm-level misallocation interact in opposing ways for aggregate welfare versus spatial equity. Li, Ma, and Tang (2024) show that reducing the dispersion of firm-level frictions by 0.01 raises aggregate welfare by 3.19% and reduces the Gini coefficient of real wages by 0.30 percentage points. When the same 3.19% welfare gain is achieved through migration liberalization instead, the Gini coefficient increases by 0.002, because migrants move to richer, less-distorted prefectures and the resulting population concentration amplifies productivity advantages. Without migration, the same friction reduction yields a larger welfare gain (3.37% vs. 3.19%) since workers cannot escape distorted regions, but the reduction in spatial inequality is smaller (Gini declines 0.25 vs. 0.30). Migration is thus a safety valve for aggregate welfare but an amplifier of spatial disparities (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). Cross-pattern observation: The opposing effects of migration liberalization and misallocation reduction on spatial inequality are robust across multiple model specifications in Li, Ma, and Tang (2024), including alternative congestion, migration, and substitution elasticities, and the qualitative pattern has been corroborated in dynamic QSE frameworks (kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial). The Agglomeration Channel The reason migration to productive regions worsens spatial inequality lies partly in agglomeration economies. Ma and Tang (2020) show that destination cities benefit from migrant inflows because endogenous firm entry expands the variety of available goods and lowers prices, dominating congestion: over 2000–2005 the 40 cities that received net population inflows experienced a 4.7% increase in real income and a 4.0% increase in welfare after congestion disutility. However, Wu and You (2025) reveal a critical tension: most large Chinese cities have surpassed their locally optimal sizes but remain below their nationally optimal sizes. When migration barriers are removed, the inflow of workers — especially low-skilled workers, disproportionately affected by hukou restrictions — depresses native welfare in the most productive cities through crowding in publicly-provided private goods, rising housing prices, and dilution of land-rent income shares. Agglomeration thus creates a virtuous cycle for receiving cities and a vicious cycle for sending regions, widening spatial inequality even as it raises national output. The Land-Supply-Tilt Channel Spatial inequality is also manufactured by the state's allocation of a second immobile factor: land. Since 2003, centrally rationed construction-land quotas have tilted toward central and western provinces: the eastern share of national land supply fell from 65% in 2003 to roughly one-third by 2017, while the western share rose to about 40% by 2014 (zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation). This narrowed aggregate regional GDP gaps — the eastern GDP share fell from a 59.5% peak to 54.5% by 2019 — but rationed land precisely where productivity and migrant inflows were highest, contributing to coastal house-price growth (110% versus 80% in central/western provinces over 2002–2012 in the model's calibration). Zhao and Chen (2021) quantify the trade-off. A GDP-maximizing land allocation would give more land to the eastern provinces, raising GDP by 5.26% and welfare by 4.58% while suppressing Beijing and Shanghai house prices, but it would widen the per-capita income gap by 8.24%. A gap-minimizing allocation would shrink the gap by 2.50% yet raise GDP by only 1.61%. The actual 2013–2017 allocation sat between these poles (GDP +2.31%, welfare +2.57%, per-capita gap −0.73%, house-price divergence +1.23%) — a balance between efficiency and equity. Land rationing and hukou rationing are two halves of the same problem: allocating land east without relaxing migration widens per-capita gaps (+8.24%), while relaxing migration without loosening land supply raises house-price divergence (+26.22%). Jointly reallocating land and population eastward achieves both goals — welfare +47.13%, per-capita gap −13.50% (zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation). Cross-pattern observation: Across the corpus, the state's spatial instruments — land quotas, capital allocation, and fiscal transfers — are themselves drivers of spatial inequality, not just correctives for it: Zhao–Chen show the land tilt trades aggregate efficiency for regional equity, Zhao–Wang–Dai–Chen show state-directed capital flows compress efficiency in return for narrowing regional totals, and Zhou–Gong show fiscal equalization buys equity only at a measured efficiency cost. The Cross-Regional Capital-Flow Channel A third state-driven channel operates through capital. Zhao, Wang, Dai, and Chen (2025) document, from firm registration data, that China's capital flows run against unit capital returns: the highest-return southeast coast is in net capital outflow, while lower-return central and western regions receive a disproportionate share of new investment. Two interacting distortions explain the reversal. Cross-regional investment distortions — local-government tax incentives, cheap land, and subsidies offered to attract external capital — drive a wedge between the effective and the observed return. Product-market segmentation operates like tariff-jumping in international trade: to avoid high internal trade barriers, firms build plants directly in protected local markets, so capital follows protected markets rather than high returns. In a quantitative spatial general-equilibrium model, the two factors contribute roughly equal shares — 45.5% to investment distortions, 44.3% to trade barriers, 10.2% to their interaction — and ignoring the interaction understates the gains from domestic trade opening by about 20% (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). No single-market reform suffices: lowering either distortion alone mitigates but does not reverse the against-returns pattern — only simultaneous liberalization of both markets makes returns and flows positively correlated. The spatial-inequality consequences cut both ways: state-directed capital toward lagging regions narrows regional total-output gaps but depresses aggregate efficiency, while market integration raises efficiency but compresses the resources of underdeveloped regions, widening per-capita gaps unless labor co-moves toward productive regions (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions; zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). This is the capital-market counterpart to the within-prefecture wedge story. Human-Capital Spatial Allocation The fourth channel concerns who moves, not just how many. Liu, Wang, and Chen (2024) build a quantitative spatial model with heterogeneous skills, cross-skill productivity spillovers, and public-service congestion, and ask whether China's spatial distribution of human capital is efficient. It is not: the Pareto-efficient allocation distributes high-skill workers more evenly across regions than the current distribution — high-skill workers should move toward initially smaller cities and low-skill workers toward initially larger ones — and optimizing this allocation raises social welfare. The gains operate through cross-skill spillovers: ignoring the productivity and public-service spillovers between skill groups drastically shrinks the measured gain from reallocation (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation). Two fiscal instruments can decentralize the efficient allocation. A transfer system redistributing from high-skill workers in high-wage cities to low-skill workers in low-wage cities moves the economy onto the Pareto frontier; a local property tax financing public services acts as a partial substitute, shrinking the required transfers while preserving the welfare gain. Hukou mobility frictions cut the achievable welfare gain by around 2.4 percentage points, echoing the finding that migration barriers distort not only the level of labor but also its skill composition (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation). Because high-skill workers are the most mobile and the most complementary to agglomeration, this channel connects directly to the migration-misallocation and agglomeration results (wu-you-2025-urbanization; li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). Counterfactual Policy Analysis Full hukou liberalization would raise national GDP by an average of 13.6% and welfare by 4.7% over 2000–2020; tier-1 cities would absorb 87.6% more population, tier-3 cities would lose 9.1%, natives in tier-1 cities would lose 10–17% in welfare, and migrants would gain 5–8%. The gains are front-loaded — GDP rises 23.3% in 2000 but only 4.3% by 2020 (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Misallocation reduction (SOE reform, financial deepening) raises aggregate welfare and reduces spatial inequality simultaneously, benefiting poorer prefectures most (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). Targeted liberalization with complements — notably raising the price elasticity of urban land supply, the largest single reliever of the local-national tension — faces the constraint that developable land in the most productive sites is scarce, with the built-up share of tier-1 cities' developable land rising from 25.7% to 44.1% under a doubling of the land-supply elasticity (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Land and fiscal instruments. Jointly reallocating land quotas and relaxing migration into the coastal provinces raises welfare by roughly 47% while cutting the per-capita gap by about 13.5% (zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation). Equalizing per-capita productive expenditure raises output by 1.505% and welfare by 1.555%; equalizing social-security expenditure raises welfare by 2.693% at a small output cost (−0.625%), with social-security equalization the more efficient inequality-reducing instrument (zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization). Land-ownership reform that lets migrants retain land rights regardless of residence raises welfare by nearly 12% (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Transport and digital infrastructure. Internal trade cost reductions produce larger gains than external ones (11.4% vs. 2.9% in the Tombe-Zhu framework), and network infrastructure can narrow the digital divide between regions (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china; liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). Current wiki assessment (2026-07): No single policy simultaneously maximizes aggregate welfare and minimizes spatial inequality in China. Migration liberalization delivers large aggregate gains but worsens spatial inequality; misallocation reduction improves both but addresses a different margin. The land, capital-flow, and human-capital channels add instruments — land-quota reallocation, unified-market reform, property-tax and transfer design — that, combined with migration liberalization and compensatory fiscal transfers, form the emerging policy consensus for managing the efficiency-equity trade-off. Cross-Country Perspective on Spatial Inequality and Migration China's spatial inequality is large by international standards. Tombe and Zhu (2019) estimate that lowering migration costs to a one-third inter-provincial migrant share (comparable to the U.S.) would raise real GDP by 12.8% and welfare by 45.6%. Institutional differences in land markets play a key role: because collective rural land ownership gives migrants no land-based benefit upon moving, land reform that preserves land rights regardless of residence yields a welfare gain of nearly 12%. Dynamic considerations also matter: Kleinman, Liu, and Redding (2023) estimate an average half-life of around 20 years for income convergence driven by capital-migration dynamics, and adding migration to macro models slows convergence because workers move toward initially productive regions rather than toward regions where their marginal product is highest in the long run (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). At the global scale the gains are far larger. Desmet, Nagy, and Rossi-Hansberg (2018), in a dynamic spatial growth model of the world at $1^{\circ}\times1^{\circ}$ resolution, find that fully liberalizing migration would raise world welfare by roughly 306% (and output by about 126%) in present discounted value, with 70.3% of the world's population moving across countries at impact; under current frictions the world takes around 400 years to reach its balanced-growth path (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). Current wiki assessment (2026-07): Chinese estimates of the welfare gain from domestic migration liberalization (Tombe–Zhu 45.6%; Wu–You 4.7%) sit far below the Desmet–Nagy–Rossi-Hansberg global free-migration upper bound of roughly 306%. Part of the gap reflects scope — the global exercise includes international migration, where barriers are far higher than domestic hukou costs — but the magnitude also indicates that China's internal barriers remain economically first-order, and that the efficiency-equity tension documented for China is one instance of a general spatial-development problem. Frontier: QSE Policy Translation for China The synthesis of firm-level frictions, migration barriers, and agglomeration economies carries direct implications for China's "common prosperity" agenda. First, policy packages that combine multiple instruments are essential: pairing hukou reform with SOE reform and financial deepening in lagging regions can achieve the welfare gains of migration liberalization while offsetting its distributional costs (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation), and the land-plus-hukou and unified-market-plus-labor packages dominate any single instrument (zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation; zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). Second, fiscal compensation mechanisms need calibration: the welfare losses of tier-1 natives (10–17%) require compensation, and fiscal-equalization results identify productive-expenditure equalization for output and social-security equalization for welfare and inequality, with conditional transfers tied to migrant inflows as a targeted complement (zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization; wu-you-2025-urbanization). Third, land reform deserves a central place: loosening land quotas in productive cities, linking new construction-land quotas to migrant inflows, and shifting local-official assessment from aggregate to per-capita targets directly attacks the land-rationing channel (zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation). Fourth, unified national market reform — reducing cross-regional investment distortions and local trade protection, with consumption-tax reform to align local incentives — addresses the against-returns capital flows (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). Finally, digital infrastructure and data-market integration offer novel channels for reducing spatial inequality without physical relocation (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure; lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market). Current wiki assessment (2026-07): the degree to which digital infrastructure and data-market integration have reduced spatial inequality in practice is still being evaluated, and whether improved connectivity promotes out-migration from lagging regions or attracts investment remains context-dependent. The calibration of a full package that moves land, capital, people, and fiscal transfers simultaneously remains an open frontier. pages.text: Network infrastructure — broadband internet, mobile communication networks, and data centers — is the digital-era equivalent of transport infrastructure, reducing the costs of transmitting information across space and thereby lowering the search, matching, and information frictions that segment regional markets. When regions differ in their digital connectivity, welfare gains depend not only on average improvement but crucially on how much the gap between leading and lagging regions narrows: the same total investment yields substantially larger gains when it reduces inequality than when it deepens already-advantaged areas. Recent quantitative estimates indicate that China's network infrastructure expansion between 2012 and 2019 raised aggregate welfare by approximately 10.30 percent, a magnitude comparable to the estimated effects of major institutional reforms such as hukou liberalization or large-scale road construction, and allowing for interregional labor mobility raises these gains further to 11.09 percent. These welfare improvements operate through two distinct channels: a direct reduction in the iceberg trade costs faced by tradable-goods sectors, and a general-equilibrium spillover through input-output linkages that raises productivity in non-tradable sectors as well. The rapid narrowing of the digital divide — measured by a fall in the Gini coefficient of base station density from approximately 0.70 to 0.39 over the same period — is not merely an equity achievement but a quantitatively important efficiency mechanism driving the aggregate gains. Network Infrastructure as a Trade Cost-Reducing Technology Trade costs comprise not only physical transport and tariff barriers but also the costs of searching for trading partners, verifying product quality, and coordinating supply chains across space. Network infrastructure primarily addresses this last category by lowering the cost of acquiring information about distant suppliers and buyers, reducing what can be called the "non-transport frictions" in interregional trade (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). The effect is nonlinear: in regions where network penetration is low, the marginal impact of additional infrastructure on trade costs is large; as connectivity approaches saturation, the marginal benefit diminishes. This carries a critical implication — investment allocated to narrowing the gap between connected and unconnected regions generates a higher aggregate return than the same investment concentrated in already-connected areas, because the marginal welfare gain per unit of infrastructure is decreasing in the initial stock of connectivity (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). Across the empirical literature, the pattern that digital connectivity reduces trade costs more sharply in remote regions has proven robust. The trade-creating effect of the internet is consistently largest for pairs involving a developing or remote region, and smallest between already-connected advanced economies. The Quantitative Spatial Equilibrium Framework with Network Infrastructure The welfare effects of network infrastructure cannot be captured by partial-equilibrium analysis alone, because trade cost reductions ripple through price indices, factor markets, and input-output linkages. The model embeds network infrastructure into a multi-region, multi-sector QSE framework covering 269 Chinese cities, three tradable sectors (agriculture, mining, manufacturing) and three non-tradable sectors (construction, retail, financial services), linked through a city-level input-output structure calibrated to the China Carbon Accounting Database. Consumers maximize Cobb-Douglas utility over sectoral composites; intermediate goods are produced under constant returns with labor and composite intermediates, subject to Fréchet-distributed productivity draws (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china; allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography). The theoretical innovation is the incorporation of network infrastructure into the trade cost equation. The iceberg cost from region \(i\) to region \(n\) in sector \(j\) takes the form \(\tau{ni}^j = \kappa{ni}^j / \exp(\beta_i int_i)\), where \(\kappa{ni}^j\) is the geographic component and \(int_i\) is the base station density in the exporting region. The parameter \(\beta_i\) differs between regions above and below the mean connectivity level: \(\beta_1 = 0.03\) for leading regions and \(\beta_2 = 0.11\) for lagging regions, implying a unit increase in connectivity reduces trade costs nearly four times as much from a lagging region. These parameters are estimated through a gravity regression instrumenting infrastructure with "Broadband China" pilot status and distance to the "eight-vertical-eight-horizontal" fiber-optic backbone nodes. First-stage F-statistics range from 86 to 175 across specifications (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). Digital Divide Narrowing as a Welfare Mechanism Between 2012 and 2019, the spatial distribution of network infrastructure in China underwent a dramatic equalization. The Gini coefficient of base station density across Chinese cities fell from approximately 0.70 to 0.39, reflecting the rapid build-out of mobile networks in the central and western regions that had previously lagged far behind the coast (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). This convergence was not a natural byproduct of market forces alone — it was actively shaped by the "Broadband China" strategy (announced 2013), subsequent "Digital China" and "Network Power" initiatives, and specific large-scale projects such as the Guizhou Big Data Center, which transformed a previously landlocked province into a national data-processing hub. The welfare significance of this narrowing lies in the nonlinearity documented above. Because lagging regions have a higher marginal return to connectivity, catch-up from the low-infrastructure tail generates disproportionately large welfare gains. A counterfactual that optimally reallocates new base stations to maximize a Foster welfare function — balancing average connectivity against equality — finds that welfare gains could have been raised from 10.30 percent to approximately 15.1 percent under a more equal distribution. Notably, an allocation that maximizes only average connectivity or only minimizes the Gini coefficient both yield lower welfare than the balanced optimum, confirming that the digital divide channel is not merely an equity concern but an efficiency mechanism (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). Cross-pattern observation: The finding that infrastructure has higher marginal returns in lagging regions parallels a robust result in the transport literature. Studies of China's highway network — including ma-tang-2020-geography-trade — find that road improvements in interior provinces generated larger trade cost reductions per kilometer than comparable coastal investments. This pattern appears general: the marginal benefit of reducing a spatial friction is decreasing in the initial level of access. Decomposing the Welfare Estimates The headline result from the structural estimation — a 10.30 percent aggregate welfare gain from 2012 to 2019 — is stable across a battery of robustness checks: alternative trade elasticities (ranging from 2 to 8), changes in the base year (2012 versus 2007), controls for concurrent tariff reductions, and variations in the estimated infrastructure parameters (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). When the model is extended to allow for interregional labor mobility — rather than assuming a fixed population in each region — the welfare gain rises to 11.09 percent, because workers reallocate toward the regions where trade cost reductions have raised labor demand, amplifying the productivity response. A decomposition of the welfare gains reveals a striking regional pattern. At the national level, roughly 53 percent operates through input-output linkages — as trade costs fall, regions expand imports of intermediate inputs, lowering production costs across supply chains — and 47 percent through the direct trade-share channel. In the eastern coastal region, input-output linkages account for nearly 60 percent of the gain, reflecting dense production networks. In the western region, the direct trade-share channel dominates at over 63 percent, because western economies rely more heavily on importing manufactured goods from the east than on supplying intermediates to complex supply chains (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). Sectoral heterogeneity is equally pronounced. Tradable sectors with high non-transport frictions — petroleum processing, chemicals, and non-metallic mineral products — experience the largest welfare gains. Some tradable sectors, including textiles and transport equipment, record small negative effects because improved connectivity allows production to concentrate in advantaged locations. Among non-tradable sectors, wholesale and retail trade benefit most, reflecting the role of e-commerce in expanding search scope. Current assessment (2026-07): The 10.30 percent estimate captures general-equilibrium effects through trade costs and input-output linkages but does not incorporate dynamic effects on firm innovation, technology adoption, or new service varieties. If these channels were included, the estimate should be interpreted as a lower bound on the total contribution of digital connectivity during this period. The Data Market Complementarity Network infrastructure provides the physical backbone without which the modern data economy cannot function at scale. Lin, Liu, and Zhou (2026) develop a QSE model with a data production sector to study the construction of a nationally integrated data market. Their counterfactual simulations show that unifying fragmented regional data markets — where "data islands" and "data chimneys" segment access across provincial boundaries — would generate additional welfare gains beyond those captured by the infrastructure channel alone, because unification enables the non-rival data factor to achieve its full scale economy. In the integrated data market, an intermediary collects raw data from consumers in all regions, processes it into workable data (primarily in western regions following the "East Data, West Computing" logic, where cooling and electricity costs are lower), and sells it to firms in both the east and the west. The simulated sales price of data falls by approximately 41 percent in the east and 36 percent in the west relative to the segmented baseline, driven by two mechanisms: a resource allocation effect (processing shifts to lower-cost western locations) and a scale economy effect unique to non-rival factors (the same dataset sold to many firms). Firms increase data input, and aggregate GDP rises by about 12.3 percent, with eastern welfare increasing by approximately 6.5 percent and western welfare by 3.5 percent (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market). The complementarity between network infrastructure and data market integration is bidirectional. Infrastructure provides the physical backbone, but its value is magnified by institutional data market integration: without common standards and data property rights frameworks, even the best physical network cannot eliminate the market segmentation that prevents data from achieving scale economies. Infrastructure investment and data market reform are strategic complements — the marginal return to each is increasing in the level of the other. Historical Parallel: Transport Infrastructure Then, Digital Now The endogeneity between infrastructure and spatial economic change has a clear historical precedent. Trew (2020) models the evolution of the transport sector in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century England and Wales alongside the growth of trade and output, using registration-district data on occupational structure across 1710–1881. Transport infrastructure was not a top-down public investment but largely driven by local private enterprise — turnpike trusts, canal companies, and railway firms — that responded to local demand. As industrial hotspots emerged in the North and Midlands, demand for transportation improvements grew to move output over increasing distances; those improvements then fed back into the location and scale of production, accelerating the industrial takeoff. Trew's counterfactual analysis yields two findings relevant to contemporary China. First, the spatial distribution of infrastructure matters as much as its timing: a uniform investment program delivers far less growth acceleration than one concentrated where local demand has emerged. Second, exogenously imposed transport improvements can, under certain conditions, delay growth by interfering with agglomeration dynamics. The Liu-Zhang-Cai results echo this: concentrating network infrastructure on the coastal manufacturing belt would have maximized short-run output growth, but the welfare-optimal allocation is more spatially balanced because the digital divide channel generates larger welfare gains per unit of investment in lagging regions (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure; trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure). Regional Heterogeneity and Remaining Policy Scope The welfare gains from network infrastructure are distributed unevenly. By 2019, eastern regions gained approximately 10–12 percent, western regions 9–11 percent, and central regions 7–9 percent. The central region's smaller gain reflects a composition effect: its initial infrastructure was moderate, so it benefited less from catch-up than the west, and its production networks are less integrated than the east's. The reallocation counterfactual raises the national gain from 10.30 percent to 15.11 percent, with the central region experiencing the largest improvement (from approximately 8 percent to 15.6 percent), confirming substantial room for optimization (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). Wu and You (2025) provide a complementary perspective through the lens of the hukou system, the world's largest internal migration restriction. Their calibrated spatial equilibrium model estimates that the hukou system reduced GDP by 13.6 percent and welfare by 4.7 percent between 2000 and 2020. This connects to network infrastructure in two ways. First, infrastructure and labor mobility are partial substitutes: better digital connectivity in interior regions enables remote access to public services (telemedicine, online education, remote government administration), reducing the marginal benefit of migrating to a coastal city and thereby lowering the effective hukou wedge. Second, because large Chinese cities have already surpassed their locally optimal sizes, further hukou liberalization could worsen congestion; network infrastructure partly relaxes this constraint by making public services partially delocalizable (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Current assessment (2026-07): Whether further digital infrastructure investment in lagging regions can substantially reduce spatial inequality depends on the strength of offsetting agglomeration forces. If connectivity primarily enables interior regions to export goods more cheaply, it narrows spatial disparities. If it primarily enables coastal firms to manage remote operations more efficiently, it could reinforce the coastal core's dominance. The Liu-Zhang-Cai results suggest the former effect dominates in China's current stage, but this balance could shift as the economy matures. Frontier: QSE Policy Translation for China The integration of network infrastructure and data market reforms has direct implications for three policy domains central to China's "Digital China" and "common prosperity" agendas. The first concerns digital infrastructure as a substitute for physical mobility. The post-COVID acceleration of telecommuting, e-commerce, and remote service delivery suggests that network quality in interior regions can reduce the need to migrate to coastal cities, lowering congestion in megacities while improving welfare in sending regions. Wu and You (2025) show that the hukou wedge is economically large, with the market valuation of an urban hukou in a tier-2 city estimated at 90,000–126,000 RMB in 2017. If high-quality digital connectivity makes education and healthcare partially remotely accessible, this wedge shrinks, and the welfare cost of maintaining migration barriers rises accordingly. A quantitative extension of the Liu-Zhang-Cai framework that endogenizes the substitutability between digital access and physical presence for public-service consumption would allow policymakers to calibrate the optimal sequencing of infrastructure investment and hukou reform. The second policy pathway concerns the complementarity between infrastructure, data markets, and labor reform as a coordinated package. Lin, Liu, and Zhou (2026) identify a multiplier effect: a unified data market amplifies the growth impact of any given productivity or trade-cost shock. Combined with the finding that network infrastructure's welfare effect rises from 10.30 to 11.09 percent under labor mobility (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure), this implies that the three reforms should be pursued as a sequenced package: better networks raise the return to data market integration, data market integration raises the demand for networks, and labor mobility amplifies both. The third policy pathway concerns the resilience function of digital infrastructure. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated that regions with robust network connectivity sustained smaller output losses during mobility restrictions, because firms could shift to remote operation. Network infrastructure thus serves as insurance against asymmetric shocks — a function not captured in steady-state welfare estimates. Embedding stochastic disruptions into a dynamic QSE framework (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china) would allow a quantitative assessment of the optimal level of network investment when resilience is valued alongside steady-state efficiency. This direction is particularly relevant as China's "Digital China" strategy enters its implementation phase, with projected investment in 5G networks, data centers, and the "East Data, West Computing" architecture expected to exceed several trillion yuan over the coming decade (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure; lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market; wu-you-2025-urbanization). pages.text: Overview This wiki synthesises a single-paradigm literature built on quantitative spatial and trade general-equilibrium (QSE) models. Its twenty-six papers all descend from one toolkit — Eaton and Kortum's (2002) Ricardian model with Fréchet-distributed productivity and the structural gravity equation it generates — extended over two decades into a general theory of where economic activity locates, how that location responds to costs and policies, and how much aggregate welfare and inequality are shaped by space. The corpus divides into two bodies: a general apparatus (quantitative trade with input-output linkages, spatial equilibrium with costly goods trade and mobile factors, agglomeration and the internal structure of cities, transport infrastructure, and dynamic spatial growth with structural transformation) and a large applied sub-literature that ports that apparatus onto China's institutions — the hukou registration system, centrally allocated land quotas, fiscal expenditure equalization, the unified national market, and the energy-to-carbon dual-control transition. This page maps the corpus along five axes, each developed in dedicated pages, lays out the tensions between the threads, and describes the literature's frontier: policy translation of quantitative spatial equilibrium to Chinese institutions. The quantitative trade / spatial-equilibrium backbone The corpus's foundation is Eaton and Kortum's (2002) Ricardian model, in which each location draws productivity for each good from a Fréchet distribution with location parameter $T_i$ (absolute advantage) and dispersion parameter $\theta$ (comparative advantage). Trade follows a structural gravity equation in which the share of importer $n$'s spending from source $i$ is $\pi{ni} = T_i(c_i d{ni})^{-\theta}/\Phi_n$, where $d{ni}$ are iceberg trade costs and $\Phi_n$ summarizes world technology and barriers. The dispersion parameter doubles as the trade elasticity, estimated at a central value of 8.28 with bounds from 3.60 (wage data) to 12.86 (price data), and it scales the welfare gains from trade: a country's real income is a function of its domestic expenditure share, making the "home share" a sufficient statistic for gains (eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Two extensions turn this single-sector trade model into the quantitative spatial equilibrium toolkit. Caliendo and Parro (2015) add many sectors, sector-specific trade elasticities, and input-output linkages, solving the model in relative changes ("exact-hat algebra") from base-year data alone. Because sectoral input-bundle costs depend on the price indices of input-supplying sectors, trade-cost changes propagate through the production network; welfare effects are on average 71% lower in a one-sector model than in the full model, and sectoral elasticities range from 0.37 to 51.08 (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta). The trade framework was then fused with labor mobility across many asymmetric locations. Allen and Arkolakis (2014) characterize the equilibrium of a continuous-space economy with costly trade and mobile labor as a system of integral equations, with existence and uniqueness governed by a balance condition on agglomeration and dispersion forces, and show the model can be inverted to recover unobserved productivities and amenities from observed wages and populations (allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography). Redding and Rossi-Hansberg's (2017) survey codifies the resulting menu of building blocks — preferences, production technology, and frictions on the movement of goods, ideas, and people — and the properties that make the framework tractable: gravity equations for all bilateral flows, exact inversion, and exact-hat counterfactuals from initial-equilibrium data alone (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Redding (2016) supplies the refinement that matters for the rest of the corpus: with labor mobile, welfare gains from a trade-cost change depend jointly on changes in domestic trade shares and in population, because the price of the immobile factor (land) adjusts and locations with better access must pay higher real incomes to attract heterogeneous-taste workers. The same model can be built on constant-returns or increasing-returns microfoundations, which predict identically when labor is immobile but diverge once workers can relocate (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). Cross-paper pattern (2026-07): The entire corpus — international trade, within-country trade, commuting, migration, and internal city structure — rests on a single Fréchet/gravity structure. The three microfoundations (Armington CES, Eaton–Kortum Fréchet, Melitz firm heterogeneity) deliver the same aggregate gravity equation and are isomorphic for many predictions, differing mainly in the structural interpretation of the elasticity and in predictions that involve firm entry (eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial; ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). Agglomeration, density, and internal city structure A second thread asks what happens within the distribution of locations: why economic activity concentrates into cities and dense blocks. The organizing quantities are agglomeration forces (productivity and amenity externalities from surrounding density) and dispersion forces (inelastic land, commuting costs, congestion, and idiosyncratic taste heterogeneity). The canonical evidence comes from the quantitative urban model estimated on Berlin's division and reunification by Ahlfeldt, Redding, Sturm, and Wolf (2015), which yields a gravity equation for commuting flows and structural estimates of the elasticity of productivity with respect to workplace-employment density of about 0.07 and of amenities with respect to resident density of about 0.15, both highly localized in space (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Tsivanidis' (2026) study of Bogotá's TransMilenio bus rapid transit extends the model to a developing-city setting with multiple skill groups and transit modes, estimating productivity spillovers and constructing residence and firm commuting market access (RCMA/FCMA) as the objects through which transport shocks reallocate activity within a city (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Across cities, commuting is the margin that ties labor markets together: commuting flows obey a gravity equation far more distance-sensitive than goods trade (a distance elasticity around −4.4 for commuting versus −1.3 for goods), and the openness of a county's commuting market determines how local employment responds to labor-demand shocks (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). The balance of agglomeration and dispersion forces also determines whether spatial equilibria are unique, whether agglomeration self-reinforces into multiple equilibria, and how large a city should be; in China, Wu and You (2025) find that most large cities are already too large from a local perspective but too small from a national one, so that the hukou system both corrects and distorts city size at once (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Density is also a growth force: Desmet and Rossi-Hansberg's (2014) spatial development model makes innovation a scale effect of density, so agglomeration and technology interact dynamically (desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development). Transport infrastructure and welfare The most policy-relevant application of the QSE toolkit is the welfare evaluation of transport infrastructure, and the corpus now spans every scale of the question. The unifying result is that market access is the causal channel: a transport improvement raises access to goods, jobs, and workers, shifting prices, wages, employment, and land values, and the general-equilibrium gains are systematically larger than the direct time-savings benefit. Removing the U.S. Interstate Highway System would lower welfare by 1.1–1.4% in Allen and Arkolakis' model (allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography); a transport improvement in Redding's (2016) synthetic grid economy raises common welfare by roughly 9% while reallocating up to about 60% of population, so reduced-form infrastructure regressions cannot separate reallocation from creation of activity (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare); and for Bogotá's TransMilenio, the standard value-of-travel-time-savings measure captures only about 52% of the full general-equilibrium welfare gain (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). The same logic holds through different channels: reducing commuting costs raises US welfare by about 3.3% for the median observed reduction (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting); removing the automobile from Berlin would cut city employment by about 14%, showing how transport interacts with agglomeration (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density); and China's network-infrastructure build-out — the digital analogue of roads — lowered inter-regional trade costs by roughly 3% by 2019 and raised aggregate welfare by about 10%, with about half the gain routed through input-output linkages (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). Historically, infrastructure is itself endogenous: Trew's models of the First Industrial Revolution show that the timing and spatial distribution of transport investment determine whether it accelerates or delays takeoff, and that lower transport costs can slow innovation by diluting agglomeration (trew-2014-spatial-takeoff; trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure). The welfare and incidence results across these settings are developed in transport-infrastructure-and-urban-welfare. Structural transformation, technology diffusion, and regional convergence A fourth thread connects spatial equilibrium to growth and development. Structural change is inherently spatial: sectoral reallocation operates across regions with heterogeneous specialization, so the same aggregate shift produces regional winners and losers. Eckert and Peters (2022) show that during the first US structural transformation (1880–1920, when the agricultural employment share fell from 50% to 25%) wages rose fastest in the most agricultural regions — the opposite of the standard "exposure" intuition — because technology diffusion let lagging rural regions catch up; their estimated catch-up parameters imply that without diffusion, rural America would have fallen further behind and industrialization would have been slower (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change). Desmet and Rossi-Hansberg (2014) document the modern mirror image: the take-off of services productivity in the mid-1990s, the spatial concentration of services, and the rise in land-rent dispersion (desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development). At the global scale, Desmet, Nagy, and Rossi-Hansberg (2018) embed Fréchet trade, innovation, and migration frictions in a $1^\circ\times1^\circ$ dynamic spatial growth model, finding a transition to the balanced-growth path lasting roughly 400 years and a reversal in the density-income correlation from about −0.41 to +0.65: today's dense poor regions become tomorrow's dense rich regions. Fully liberalizing migration would raise welfare by about 306% (amenity-adjusted real GDP) and output by 126% in present-discounted value, with 70% of the world population moving across countries at impact (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). Within countries, convergence has been slowing: Kleinman, Liu, and Redding (2023) show that the correlation between income growth and initial income across US states fell from negative to roughly zero between 1963 and 2017, with average convergence half-lives of about 20 years, driven by the interaction of capital accumulation and migration frictions (kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial). China converges even more slowly once migration enters the dynamic QSE framework, with GDP-convergence half-lives exceeding 30 years and population distribution — not capital — determining the long-run spatial structure (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). The spatial-takeoff literature rounds out the thread: the initial concentration of manufacturing productivity was necessary for England's industrial takeoff, and energy costs shaped where innovation first occurred (trew-2014-spatial-takeoff). Chinese applications: hukou, land, fiscal, and environmental policy A large applied sub-literature ports the QSE toolkit onto China's institutions and asks how much of the country's growth and inequality is attributable to spatial frictions. Tombe and Zhu's (2019) canonical model of internal and international trade with migration finds that reductions in internal trade and migration costs account for about 28% of China's aggregate labor-productivity growth between 2000 and 2005, versus about 8% from reductions in international trade costs — an internal-frictions-dominant result that reframes the "export-led growth" narrative (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Subsequent papers each isolate a specific institutional margin. Wu and You (2025) model the hukou system as a fiscal wedge between natives and migrants, estimating that removing all internal migration restrictions would raise average GDP by 13.6% and welfare by 4.7%, while the largest cities are locally too large but nationally too small (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Zhao and Chen (2021) analyze the central allocation of new urban land quotas, which tilted toward the interior after 2003, documenting an efficiency-equity tension: allocating land to the efficient coast maximizes GDP but widens regional income gaps, and the actual allocation sits between the extremes (zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation). Zhou and Gong (2024) find that equalizing productive fiscal expenditure raises output and welfare together (output +1.5%, welfare +1.6%), while equalizing social-security spending raises welfare more (about +2.7%) at a small output cost (−0.6%) (zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization). Other papers examine capital, people, and the environment. Zhao, Wang, Dai, and Chen (2025) model cross-regional investment distortions under local-government incentives alongside product-market segmentation, finding the two contribute roughly equally (about 45% and 44%) to the "capital flowing against returns" pattern and that single-market reform alone cannot reverse it (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). Liu, Wang, and Chen (2024) show that with cross-skill productivity and public-service spillovers, redistributing from high-skill, high-wage cities to low-skill, low-wage cities reaches the Pareto frontier, and that a property tax partially substitutes for spatial transfers (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation). Li, Ma, and Tang (2024) estimate that reducing within-prefecture misallocation and liberalizing migration achieve similar aggregate welfare gains but have opposite effects on spatial inequality (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation), while Ma and Tang (2020) find, in a Melitz model with firm entry, that destination cities benefit from migrant inflows — the opposite of the Tombe–Zhu result without an extensive margin (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). On the environmental margin, Luo and Luo (2025) build a quantitative spatial general-equilibrium model with trade, migration, and carbon constraints, finding that command-style carbon control produces a welfare loss (−0.114%) roughly two and a half times that of a carbon market (−0.046%), with carbon leakage exceeding 20% of the domestic reduction under every national instrument (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). Where the underlying Chinese raw texts are MinerU-VLM conversions, a few headline magnitudes carry OCR-uncertainty flags on the individual pages. Cross-paper pattern (2026-07): Across the hukou, land-quota, fiscal-equalization, and carbon-policy papers, the same efficiency-equity tension recurs: removing a spatial friction raises aggregate output and welfare, while the equalizing reform that narrows regional gaps usually trades away some efficiency — and the optimal policy is a combination (land reform with hukou reform, market integration with labor co-location, carbon pricing with revenue redistribution) rather than any single instrument (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china; zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation; zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization; zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions; luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). Tensions across the threads Read together, the threads pull in different directions. The most visible disagreement is over the magnitude of the gains from removing migration frictions: Tombe and Zhu's counterfactual of lowering migration costs to US-comparable levels implies welfare gains of roughly 46%, whereas Wu and You's hukou-as-fiscal-wedge model implies a welfare gain of only 4.7% from removing all internal migration restrictions. The gap reflects substance, not arbitrariness — different counterfactuals (US-mobility costs versus zero hukou wedge), different treatment of agglomeration and city-size externalities, and different welfare concepts. A second tension concerns reallocation versus welfare: population reallocations can be an order of magnitude larger than common welfare gains, so evaluations keyed to where activity moves can misstate who actually benefits (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). A third concerns the welfare effects of migration on destination cities: without an extensive margin, Tombe and Zhu find migrants depress destination real wages, while Ma and Tang, with endogenous firm entry, find all destination cities benefit — the sign of the local effect turns on whether firm entry is modeled (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china; ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). Finally, the constant-versus-increasing-returns distinction, innocuous when labor is immobile, changes counterfactual predictions for population and wages once workers can relocate (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). These are scope conditions rather than contradictions, and the wiki's debate pages, notably government-and-urbanization and the migration-welfare mechanism pages, keep them explicit. Current assessment (2026-07): The mobility-gains magnitude disagreement is real and unresolved. The 46%-versus-4.7% spread reflects model differences (agglomeration and city-size externalities, the intensive margin of the hukou wedge) more than measurement error; the wiki's current best reading is that the aggregate gains from migration reform are large but smaller than the earliest QSE estimates, and that distributional consequences for destination-city natives are the binding political constraint (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china; wu-you-2025-urbanization; ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). Policy translation: quantitative spatial equilibrium adapted to Chinese institutions The frontier of this corpus is its self-identifying sub-literature: a set of papers that take the QSE toolkit — Fréchet mobility, model inversion, exact-hat counterfactuals — and point it at China-specific institutions rather than at the abstract space of the theory papers. The recurring template is the same across every paper. The model nests a Chinese policy wedge inside the standard spatial structure: the hukou system enters as a migration cost or a fiscal wedge in Tombe–Zhu and Wu–You (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china; wu-you-2025-urbanization); centrally allocated construction-land quotas enter as a spatial supply shifter in Zhao–Chen (zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation); local-government investment and trade-protection incentives enter as wedges on capital and goods flows in Zhao–Wang–Dai–Chen (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions); fiscal expenditure and the property tax enter as spatially differentiated public goods and taxes in Zhou–Gong and Liu–Wang–Chen (zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization; liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation); and the energy-to-carbon dual-control constraint enters as a compliance cost on energy use in Luo–Luo (luo-luo-2025-carbon-control-spatial-transmission). The dynamic-QSE survey of Zhao, Chen, and Fu (2022) explicitly frames the "new development pattern" and the unified national market as the agenda to which this toolkit is being applied (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). The shared method explains why this thread is a frontier rather than a collection of case studies. Because each paper solves for general equilibrium, the policy conclusions are statements about spatial allocation: hukou reform is worth more when land quotas move with people; fiscal equalization can raise output and welfare simultaneously only when it corrects misallocation rather than merely redistributing; market integration must pair capital-market and product-market reform or it fails to reverse capital flowing against returns; carbon pricing beats command control because the latter melts carbon revenue into deadweight loss. The same toolkit also carries the literature forward into new factor markets — data, modeled as a non-rival factor whose market segmentation leaves large gains on the table in a unified data market (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market). Current assessment (2026-07): The Chinese-applied sub-literature is the corpus's most active frontier and its weakest-evidence zone at the same time: it is where the strongest policy claims are made (hukou and land reform raising GDP by double digits; market integration reversing capital misallocation) but where the underlying raw texts are the least clean (OCR conversions), the corpora are single-country, and the identification of structural elasticities is thinnest. The wiki treats these magnitudes as model-conditional point estimates rather than established facts. Open questions Dynamic multi-sector models. Caliendo–Parro style input-output amplification has not yet been fully combined with forward-looking capital accumulation and innovation; the corpus currently separates static multi-sector trade from dynamic single-sector growth (caliendo-parro-2015-trade-welfare-nafta; kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial). Services diffusion. Whether technology diffuses as readily in services as in agriculture and manufacturing is untested; Eckert and Peters conjecture weaker services diffusion could amplify regional inequality (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change). Identification of elasticities. The trade, commuting, and migration elasticities are the single most important inputs to every counterfactual, yet they are estimated from cross-sections or a few natural experiments, and the calibration of Chinese applications reuses a small set of values (θ = 4, migration elasticity around 1.5) across papers (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china; eaton-kortum-2002-technology-geography-trade). Political economy. The fiscal and hukou papers show that local governments have incentives to distort spatial allocation, but who pays for reform and how it becomes incentive-compatible is only beginning to be modeled (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). External validity. City-level results from Berlin and Bogotá, and historical results from England, are each identified from one setting; whether they transfer to other cities and eras is open (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density; tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure; trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure).
