pages.excerpt: Spatial public finance is the study of how government tax and expenditure policy reshapes the spatial distribution of economic activity through general-equilibrium rather than direct-incidence channels. In a quantitative spatial equilibrium, a fiscal instrument applied in one…
pages.text: Spatial public finance is the study of how government tax and expenditure policy reshapes the spatial distribution of economic activity through general-equilibrium rather than direct-incidence channels. In a quantitative spatial equilibrium, a fiscal instrument applied in one region does not stay there: it alters local wages, prices, migration flows, and trade shares, which feed back onto output and welfare everywhere through factor mobility and goods-market linkages. The Chinese sub-literature ports this toolkit onto the country's defining fiscal institutions — regionally targeted expenditure equalization, centrally rationed construction-land quotas, the hukou household-registration system, and the tax-and-transfer architecture between central and local government — and arrives at two headline results. First, removing spatial misallocation can raise national output and welfare simultaneously: equalizing per-capita productive expenditure raises output by roughly 1.5 percent and welfare by a comparable margin. Second, the efficiency–equity trade-off reappears precisely when fiscal instruments are used for pure redistribution: equalizing social-security spending delivers a larger welfare gain at a small output cost, while land and migration reforms that maximize efficiency widen regional income gaps unless paired with complementary population policies. Fiscal policy in spatial equilibrium: the conceptual frame In the quantitative spatial equilibrium paradigm, locations are not independent observations: they are systematically linked through costly goods trade, commuting, and migration, so a policy in one region shifts the balance of agglomeration and dispersion forces everywhere (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). A tax, transfer, or public-expenditure program acts as a wedge on locational choice — it changes the real income a household can attain in each region, and hence the migration margin, and it changes unit production costs, and hence trade shares. The structural approach makes counterfactuals tractable by inverting the model to recover unobserved regional productivity and amenity from observed data, then solving for the equilibrium response to a policy change; reduced-form estimates of the same policy are exposed to the Lucas critique because the spatial linkages that transmit the shock are held fixed (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Two distinct normative problems run through the Chinese applications. The first is misallocation removal: when labor is trapped in low-productivity regions by frictions, reallocating factors toward more productive places raises aggregate output and welfare together (zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization; li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). The second is redistribution: when the goal is to narrow regional income gaps, fiscal instruments deliberately pull factors toward lower-productivity regions, which can lower aggregate output even as they raise average welfare and reduce inequality (zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization). The central contribution of this literature is to show that the same instrument can sit on either side of that line, and that general-equilibrium effects — not the direct transfer itself — determine which outcome dominates (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation; zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation). Expenditure equalization: productive versus social-security spending Zhou and Gong's quantitative spatial model of regional expenditure equalization draws the cleanest distinction between the two faces of fiscal policy. The model nests heterogeneous residential preferences and interregional migration with two expenditure types: productive expenditure, which raises local total factor productivity, and social-security expenditure, which raises the public good available to residents (zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization). Holding total public spending fixed, equalizing per-capita productive expenditure raises aggregate output by 1.505 percent and resident welfare by 1.555 percent: reallocating public inputs toward lower-productivity regions removes a misallocation whose efficiency cost exceeds any loss from relocating labor. Equalizing social-security expenditure instead raises welfare by 2.693 percent while reducing output by 0.625 percent — the spending pulls labor toward regions with lower wages and productivity, improving average welfare at a real efficiency cost. Both policies reduce measured welfare inequality, but social-security equalization is the more effective instrument for that purpose: the Gini coefficient of welfare falls by 2.469 percent under social-security equalization against 0.990 percent under productive-expenditure equalization. The distinction is not knife-edge. As the degree of equalization rises continuously, the output gain from productive-expenditure equalization first rises and then falls, peaking at roughly 82 percent equalization, while welfare keeps improving monotonically; for social-security expenditure, every step toward equalization raises welfare and lowers output further (zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization). A selective-subsidy variant — adding new spending to low-expenditure regions rather than cutting high-expenditure regions — produces larger gains on both margins (output +3.467 percent and welfare +2.263 percent for productive spending; welfare +4.896 percent for social-security spending), because high-spending regions are never harmed. Cross-paper pattern: Across zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization and li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation, the removal of spatial misallocation raises output and welfare together; the trade-off between the two only re-emerges when policy is aimed at pure redistribution. Instruments operating on factor allocation (productive spending, friction dispersion) dominate on both margins, whereas instruments operating on locational amenities (social-security spending, migration liberalization) trade efficiency against equity. Human capital, cross-skill spillovers, and the property tax Fiscal instruments also shape the spatial allocation of types of labor. Liu, Wang, and Chen build a quantitative spatial model with two skill groups whose productivity and public-service consumption spill over across skill types, and ask what fiscal policy implements the constrained Pareto-efficient allocation of human capital (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation). Two spillover forces are key: positive productivity spillovers from agglomeration, which favor concentrating high-skill workers in large cities, and public-service spillovers, where low-skill population exerts congestion partly offset by high-skill residents. Because the market fails to internalize these externalities, China's observed human-capital distribution sits inside the Pareto frontier, and reallocating workers across cities can raise both groups' welfare; when cross-type spillovers are shut down, the same reallocation buys almost nothing, indicating that skill complementarity is the operative mechanism. The implementing policy is a spatial transfer program: reaching the Pareto-efficient frontier requires redistributing from high-skill workers in high-wage cities to low-skill workers in low-wage cities, and the optimal equilibrium is more spatially balanced than the status quo — high-skill workers move toward initially smaller cities and low-skill workers toward larger ones (liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation). A property tax that finances local public services partially substitutes for these transfers: when a regionally differentiated property tax is introduced, the required transfers shrink, and the welfare gain from optimal reallocation is if anything larger than in the no-tax baseline, because the tax ties local revenue to service provision. Hukou-related migration frictions blunt the policy: using measured city-level settlement-threshold indices, the welfare gain from optimal reallocation falls by roughly 2.4 percent under the hukou friction — the same institutional wedge that wu-you-2025-urbanization and zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization identify as the principal barrier to factor mobility. Land allocation, transfers, and the central-local fiscal structure A second fiscal channel operates on the supply side: the central government's rationing of construction-land quotas, which since 2003 has tilted new urban land toward central and western provinces and compressed it in the east (zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation). Zhao and Chen calibrate a quantitative spatial model with residential and industrial land, interprovincial migration, and domestic and international trade, and evaluate the actual 2013–2017 allocation against counterfactual targets. The actual westward tilt raised GDP by 2.31 percent and total welfare by 2.57 percent while narrowing the interregional income gap by 0.73 percent — but it also widened regional housing-price divergence by 1.23 percent, since fast-growing eastern cities received less land. The pure efficiency target, maximization of GDP, allocates more land to eastern provinces: it raises GDP by 5.26 percent and suppresses eastern house prices (price divergence falls by 8.53 percent) but at the cost of widening the income gap by 8.24 percent. Minimizing the income gap raises GDP only 1.61 percent. The real-world allocation sits between these poles, and the paper reads it as a deliberate balance of efficiency against equity. The deeper finding is that land allocation alone cannot escape the efficiency–equity trade-off, because the income gap is fundamentally a migration problem. When land policy is combined with hukou reform that lowers migration costs into eastern provinces — moving people and land in the same direction — both objectives improve simultaneously: the combined policy raises welfare by roughly 47 percent and narrows the income gap by 13.5 percent, though destination-province house prices rise. The same logic underlies the paper's trade result: lowering domestic interprovincial trade costs delivers far larger gains than lowering international trade costs, consistent with the dominant role of internal over external frictions in tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china. Local government incentives and market integration Where land and expenditure policies are decided, local-government objectives intrude, and the resulting distortions are a fiscal phenomenon in their own right. Zhao, Wang, Dai, and Chen document that capital in China flows against the rate of return — more capital is allocated to regions with lower unit capital returns — and decompose this "capital flows against returns" pattern into two sources (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). Using a quantitative spatial model with micro-founded cross-regional investment decisions and product-market segmentation, they find that removing cross-regional investment distortions accounts for 45.489 percent of the improvement in capital allocation, trade barriers for 44.321 percent, and the interaction reinforcement between the two markets for the remaining 10.19 percent. Ignoring the product–capital market interaction understates the gains from domestic trade opening by roughly 20 percent. Strikingly, reforming either market alone does not reverse the misallocation: capital still flows toward low-return regions because firms jump trade barriers by investing in the protected market (tariff-jumping); only simultaneous integration of both markets makes capital flow toward high-return regions. The root cause is local-government behavior. Under an objective that values both local output and fiscal revenue, cutting the capital tax rate to attract investment raises local-government utility up to a point and then lowers it (the inverted-U of investment competition), and the observed economy sits on the rising segment — so governments keep distorting. Trade protection, in contrast, is monotonically costly to local government utility once trade opens, because with production-based taxation the local government loses revenue when its market is penetrated. The incentive-compatibility fix is fiscal: moving the consumption tax from the production site to the consumption site converts the local government's response to trade opening from monotone decline into a U-shape that rewards open, consumption-friendly environments (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). Cross-paper pattern: Across zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions and zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation, local-government objectives that reward aggregate local output or fiscal revenue distort spatial allocation — through investment attraction, trade protection, and land-leasing — and the correction is not to forbid local discretion but to change the fiscal incentive (per-capita evaluation, consumption-tax reform). The theme also runs through li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation, where spatially dispersed firm-level frictions in poorer regions are partly policy-created. The hukou system as a fiscal wedge The hukou system is the most studied fiscal institution in the Chinese spatial literature, and its modern treatment is as a resource transfer between natives and migrants rather than a pure iceberg cost on mobility. Wu and You model hukou as a fiscal wedge — migrants pay more for local public services and receive a smaller share of local land income than natives — and estimate that removing all hukou restrictions from 2000 onward would have raised GDP by 13.6 percent and welfare by 4.7 percent on average across 2000–2020, with the GDP effect large early (23.3 percent in 2000) and fading as migration adjusts (wu-you-2025-urbanization). The welfare gain is far smaller than the GDP gain because migrants moving to high-wage cities face higher housing costs. Because the system transfers resources, its distributional logic differs from an iceberg friction: natives in the most desirable cities lose welfare when restrictions are relaxed, and their representative resident — who shares in local land rents — is already worse off under existing sizes, implying that China's largest cities are too large locally but too small nationally. The magnitudes are sensitive to how the wedge is modeled. Tombe and Zhu's quantitative analysis of China's trade and migration frictions calibrates a migration elasticity of $\kappa = 1.5$ and a trade elasticity of $\theta = 4$ and finds that lowering migration costs to US inter-state mobility levels would raise welfare by roughly 46 percent (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Their framework captures a second, land-based fiscal wedge: because land is collectively owned and migrants forfeit claims to land income when they leave their registration, the effective cost of migration in 2000 averaged a factor of about 5.3 — a migration utility cost of 2.8 combined with a land-income loss of 1.9 — making the land–hukou interaction quantitatively central. Combining land reallocation with lower migration costs raises welfare by roughly 47 percent in zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation, and the hukou friction measurably shrinks the welfare gains from optimal reallocation in liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation. Current assessment (2026-07): The magnitude of the aggregate welfare gains from hukou reform is genuinely contested in this corpus — roughly 4.7 percent (Wu–You, fiscal-wedge model), 46 percent (Tombe–Zhu, iceberg-cost plus land-forfeiture model at US mobility levels), and about 47 percent when land reform is bundled with migration liberalization (Zhao–Chen). The spread is not noise: it tracks whether hukou is modeled as a transfer (smaller gain, larger distributional conflict) or as a pure mobility cost (larger gain). The directional conclusion — removing the wedge raises aggregate welfare — is unanimous; the size is not. Place-based versus people-based policy A sharp contrast emerges when the same aggregate welfare gain is achieved by two very different instruments. Li, Ma, and Tang structurally estimate firm-level output and labor frictions across Chinese prefectures and show that reducing the dispersion of these frictions by 0.01 raises aggregate welfare by 3.19 percent (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). Because poorer regions carry higher friction dispersion, the same uniform reduction benefits them disproportionately, draws population toward smaller and poorer prefectures, and lowers the Gini coefficient of real wages by about 0.26 percent — a place-based improvement that reduces spatial inequality. Liberalizing migration barriers to deliver the same 3.19 percent welfare gain achieves the opposite on distribution: migrants move to richer, less-distorted prefectures, agglomeration amplifies the productivity advantage of large cities, and spatial inequality rises. Migration also changes the incidence of the frictions themselves — with migration shut down, the same friction-dispersion cut yields a larger aggregate gain (3.37 percent), because people can no longer escape the most distorted prefectures, and a smaller inequality improvement. This welfare-equivalence-with-opposite-incidence result is the analytical core of the place-based-versus-people-based debate in the Chinese context. It echoes wu-you-2025-urbanization, where the welfare gain from removing hukou restrictions coexists with losses to natives in destination cities, and it frames the policy-design lesson drawn across the corpus: an efficiency-oriented spatial policy generally needs a complementary people-based or place-based transfer to keep regional inequality in check (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation; zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions). It also explains why zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization finds social-security equalization to be the more effective inequality instrument: it operates directly on the locational utility of poorer regions rather than on the factor allocation margin. Policy translation: Chinese spatial fiscal institutions Read together, the five Chinese-application papers constitute a program of "policy translation" — porting the quantitative spatial toolkit onto the institutions through which Chinese fiscal policy operates. Four translations stand out. First, the unified national market (全国统一大市场) agenda: zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions and zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation both find that integration gains are large but conditional — capital and product markets must be reformed together, and land and population must move in the same direction — converting an abstract slogan into a set of complementarity conditions. Second, land-quota trading: zhao-chen-2021-interregional-land-allocation argues for flexible, cross-provincial tradable construction-land quotas tied to migrant inflows, so that land follows population. Third, hukou liberalization tied to fiscal equalization: the welfare losses from the hukou wedge (wu-you-2025-urbanization; tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china) are largest where local public services are most unequal, so equalizing per-capita fiscal expenditure — the policy zhou-gong-2024-public-expenditure-equalization quantifies — is the fiscal counterpart of migration reform. Fourth, property-tax design: liu-wang-chen-2024-human-capital-spatial-allocation shows a local property tax financing public services can substitute for central transfers and help implement the optimal allocation of human capital. A fifth translation concerns how policy is evaluated. zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china argues that the final determinant of economic structure is population distribution rather than capital accumulation, and that aggregate convergence hides divergence in regional output levels — a warning against evaluating spatial policy on aggregate totals. The fiscal papers operationalize this by reporting income gaps, Gini coefficients, and welfare inequality alongside GDP, and the recurring pattern is that per-capita and welfare measures can move opposite to aggregate measures (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions; li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). Current assessment (2026-07): The five-paper consensus on the unified national market is that its core content is fiscal-institutional: equalize per-capita productive and social expenditure, let land quotas trade and follow population, replace hukou-rationed access with equalized services, align local-government incentives through consumption-tax and per-capita-evaluation reform, and treat property tax as a service-financing instrument. No single instrument does all the work; the recurring failure mode is a single-market or single-instrument reform that ignores complementarities. The frontier beyond these static results is dynamic and political-economic. The dynamic framework of zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china shows that convergence with migration is slow and non-monotonic, so steady-state comparisons may mislead policy; capital dynamics, intertemporal fiscal choice, and the migration–savings interaction all remain open. Politically, the local-government incentive results (zhao-wang-dai-chen-2025-cross-regional-investment-distortions) point to deeper reform of intergovernmental fiscal relations — expenditure assignment, revenue sharing, and official evaluation — that static models only proxy. External validity is also limited: magnitudes are calibrated to Chinese data of the 2000s and 2010s, and the OCR-degraded tables in the raw markdowns mean several point estimates should be read with caution rather than as precise benchmarks. pages.excerpt: Lead Structural transformation — the secular reallocation of employment out of agriculture toward manufacturing and then services that accompanies economic growth — is, in a spatial economy, never purely an aggregate phenomenon. Because regions enter the process with…
pages.text: Structural Transformation and Regional Convergence Lead Structural transformation — the secular reallocation of employment out of agriculture toward manufacturing and then services that accompanies economic growth — is, in a spatial economy, never purely an aggregate phenomenon. Because regions enter the process with heterogeneous sectoral specialization, the same aggregate shift lands differently across space: regions specialized in a contracting sector are disproportionately exposed to its decline, while regions that already host expanding industries benefit disproportionately from their growth. This page integrates a body of evidence spanning the first US structural transformation of 1880–1920, the postwar US services transition, the global development path, and contemporary China around a central claim: whether sectoral reallocation raises or lowers regional inequality is governed less by the reallocation itself than by the spatial forces — technology diffusion, trade, and migration — that accompany it. In the theory reviewed here, structural change is inherently urban-biased, yet in the data the initially most agricultural US regions grew fastest in wages precisely when the agricultural share was halving. The resolution of that puzzle turns on productivity catch-up through technology diffusion — a mechanism that, carried into services, global development, and the Chinese economy, determines how much of the gains from growth spread to lagging regions. Structural Change Is Inherently Spatial The starting point of the modern treatment is that sectoral reallocation operates across regions whose pre-existing specialization differs. In a static quantitative spatial framework, location-specific wages, employment, and sectoral composition are jointly determined by productivity, amenities, trade costs, and land endowments, so that the same aggregate shock has heterogeneous regional incidence (redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Superimposing structural change on such an economy generates a Bartik-like exposure logic: regions specialized in the sector that is shrinking are the ones most exposed to its decline, even when every region faces the same aggregate productivity path. Eckert and Peters formalize this logic in a two-sector model of the United States and show that a region's agricultural employment share is a sufficient statistic for its exposure to the agricultural decline: the wage elasticity with respect to agricultural revenue productivity falls monotonically with the local agricultural share, while the industrialization elasticity is U-shaped, largest at intermediate specialization (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change). Because standard macroeconomic models of structural change abstract from geography, they remain silent on who gains and loses regionally; the theories reviewed here instead treat aggregate growth, sectoral reallocation, and regional development as simultaneously determined equilibrium objects (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change; desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development; desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development). The spatial content is not incidental. In the 1880 United States, one-fifth of workers lived in commuting zones that were 80 percent agricultural while another fifth lived in zones that were only 10 percent agricultural, and wages in the industrialized zones were nearly twice as high — initial conditions that, combined with differential exposure, determine which regions feel the subsequent structural shift most acutely (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change). The Urban Bias of Sectoral Reallocation — and What Reversed It Given the exposure structure, the sign of the spatial response is determined analytically. Eckert and Peters show that if sectoral productivity grows uniformly across space, trade is free, and population growth is spatially balanced, then a falling aggregate agricultural share necessarily produces urban-biased wage growth: rural regions are more exposed to the relatively slow-growing sector, so the same productivity growth translates into lower wage growth where agriculture looms large (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change). This inherent urban bias does not require faster physical productivity growth in manufacturing than in agriculture — it can arise even when agricultural physical productivity grows faster, because revenue productivity is shaped by relative prices and by the falling expenditure share of food under non-homothetic preferences. The first US structural transformation contradicts this prediction sharply. Between 1880 and 1920 the agricultural employment share fell from 50 to 25 percent, yet wages in the initially most agricultural commuting zones grew 1.5 to 2 percentage points per year faster than in urban areas, and the standard deviation of log wages across commuting zones fell from 0.41 to 0.22 (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change). The model's analytical decomposition attributes local wage growth and industrialization to two margins — the incidence of sectoral shocks and the region's exposure to them — and implies that the reversal must have come from spatially uneven productivity growth tilted toward rural areas. The same conclusion emerges from the historical takeoff literature, where the spatial concentration of activity is itself a precondition for industrialization: Trew's calibrated model of the English Industrial Revolution finds that manufacturing takeoff occurs in the North (location 305, Lancashire) only because a geographically small region of high productivity there reaches the scale required to overcome the fixed costs of energy-intensive innovation; when the manufacturing productivity distribution is flattened, takeoff happens immediately and everywhere, and when only the London productivity peak is retained, no industrial takeoff occurs within 150 periods (trew-2014-spatial-takeoff). Geography, in short, determines not just who benefits from structural change but whether structural change takes off at all. Technology Diffusion and the "Benefit of Backwardness" Across the models in this corpus, technology diffusion is the spatial force that can offset — and even reverse — the urban bias. In Eckert and Peters' framework, regions adopt technologies from each other, and the resulting law of motion for local productivity embeds a catch-up parameter per sector: adoption costs depend on a region's lagged own productivity and a distance-weighted aggregate of other regions' productivity, so that when the catch-up parameters are positive, lagging regions grow faster — a "benefit of backwardness" that produces convergence in spatial productivity levels (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change). Estimating the model on 495 commuting zones between 1880 and 1920 delivers $\lambda_A = 0.73$ in agriculture and $\lambda_M = 0.28$ in manufacturing, implying that backward regions experienced faster productivity growth in both sectors. The empirical counterpart is the data's rural wage premium: wages in the initially most agricultural regions grew 1.5 to 2 percentage points per year faster than in urban areas, and the model's decomposition attributes nearly 2 percentage points of that annual rural wage growth to agricultural TFP growth alone. The quantitative importance of this diffusion is established by a counterfactual that shuts down cross-region technology adoption while re-estimating aggregate productivity growth so that the time-series facts are unchanged. This "no catch-up" calibration still matches aggregate structural change, but its spatial predictions reverse: wage growth becomes about 0.5 percentage points per year faster in cities, rural industrialization slows sharply, and the coefficient on initial agricultural specialization in the wage-growth regression flips sign (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change). The same logic operates at global scale in the dynamic model of Desmet, Nagy, and Rossi-Hansberg, where the degree of spatial diffusion enters the technology-accumulation equation and acts as a dispersion force: without any diffusion, no balanced growth path with a non-degenerate distribution of employment exists, and weaker diffusion lowers the incentive to concentrate and innovate (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development; desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development). Trew's endogenous-infrastructure model embeds the same mechanism in the historical takeoff, where the spatial distribution of transport improvements determines whether lagging industrial regions catch up (trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure). Cross-paper pattern: Across the historical and global models in this collection — Eckert–Peters' catch-up parameters, Desmet–Nagy–Rossi-Hansberg's diffusion frontier, and Trew's infrastructure-mediated diffusion — technology diffusion consistently appears as the spatial force that offsets the inherent urban bias of structural change and delivers rural and lagging-region convergence. When diffusion is weak, the Bartik-exposure logic dominates and regional inequality rises; when it is strong, catch-up growth can overturn the bias entirely. Structural Transformation and the Take-Off of Services Structural transformation does not end with agriculture. In the Desmet–Rossi-Hansberg framework, non-homothetic preferences with an elasticity of substitution below one imply that, as manufacturing productivity grows faster than services, the relative price of manufactured goods falls and employment shifts toward the sector with the rising relative price — services (desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development). Because this reallocation enlarges the scale of service-producing locations, it endogenously accelerates service-sector innovation: the calibrated model generates a service productivity take-off around the mid-1990s in the United States, accompanied by increasing spatial concentration of services and rising dispersion of land rents across metropolitan areas. This mechanism reverses the Baumol cost-disease prediction of stagnating services — rather than the low-productivity sector dragging down aggregate growth, structural transformation makes services concentrated enough for innovation to take off endogenously. The historical models embed an analogous channel through agricultural subsistence. Stone–Geary preferences with a subsistence agricultural requirement mean that productivity gains in agriculture release labor into manufacturing, powering the earliest stages of industrialization (trew-2014-spatial-takeoff; trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure). Eckert and Peters use a richer non-homothetic class — the Price-Independent Generalized Linear (PIGL) preferences of Boppart — in which the agricultural expenditure share declines with real income and asymptotes to a positive floor; the income-elasticity channel operates alongside sectoral productivity growth in driving the sectoral reallocation (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change). Across these specifications the same force is at work: the shift out of a maturing sector is driven by income effects, and its spatial footprint is shaped by where the expanding sector can agglomerate enough to innovate. Regional Convergence: Beta-Convergence and Its Slowdown Where diffusion is strong, structural change and growth should produce convergence in regional incomes; where it is weak, divergence. The most direct evidence on the pace of regional convergence comes from the United States. Kleinman, Liu, and Redding measure the correlation between ten-year-ahead income growth and initial income per capita across US states and document a secular decline in this convergence coefficient across 1963–2017 — from −0.0257 in 1963–1980 to −0.0148 in 1980–2000 and to +0.0076 (statistically indistinguishable from zero) in 2000–2017 (kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial). Their dynamic spatial model, in which forward-looking capital accumulation by immobile landlords interacts with migration, yields average convergence half-lives of about 20 years and a maximum around 80 years; the spectral decomposition shows that the decline in convergence is largely explained by initial conditions — the inherited gap of capital and labor from steady state — rather than by the pattern of subsequent fundamental shocks, because the empirical productivity and amenity shocks load on eigencomponents with relatively fast convergence while the steady-state gaps load on slow-moving ones (kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial). The dynamic quantitative spatial equilibrium survey applies the same half-life concept to China and finds that introducing interregional migration dramatically slows convergence: GDP and capital half-lives exceed thirty years and tend to rise over time, in contrast to the roughly decade-scale half-lives of a no-migration new-classical benchmark, because population and capital dynamics interact and slow each other's adjustment (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). Population, not capital, ultimately determines the long-run spatial structure: capital adjusts to the distribution of people, so regional outcomes hinge on where workers can move. Current assessment (2026-07): The evidence on the US convergence slowdown points to initial conditions — the inherited gap of capital and labor from steady state — as the dominant explanation, with subsequent productivity and amenity shocks playing a secondary, faster-converging role (kleinman-liu-redding-2023-dynamic-spatial; zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). For China, the same toolkit suggests that migration frictions slow convergence so much that steady-state analysis is a poor guide to the transition path. Global Development Paths and the Density–Income Reversal At the global scale, the interaction between diffusion, structural change, and migration frictions produces a striking prediction about which regions will be rich in the long run. Desmet, Nagy, and Rossi-Hansberg solve a dynamic spatial growth model on a $1^\circ \times 1^\circ$ grid (about 65,000 cells), in which firms invest in local innovation, technology diffuses across space, and migration is subject to origin- and destination-specific frictions (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). With current migration restrictions unchanged, the transition to the balanced growth path takes about 400 years, and the correlation between GDP per capita and population density — currently about −0.41 — rises to +0.65: today's dense-but-poor regions (much of sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and East Asia) become tomorrow's dense-and-rich regions, a productivity reversal in which North America and Europe fall behind in relative population and productivity terms. Migration policy reshapes which regions benefit. With full liberalization, about 70 percent of the world's population would move across countries at impact, Europe and the eastern United States remain strong, and the present-discounted gains are large — output up 125.8 percent and welfare up 305.9 percent (desmet-nagy-rossi-hansberg-2018-geography-development). The mechanism behind the reversal is exactly the diffusion-plus-density logic of this page: dense locations invest more in innovation, and when migration frictions trap people in dense low-productivity regions, those regions converge to the frontier; freer migration instead lets people move to already-productive, high-amenity places, aligning the future high-density regions with current high-income ones. Contemporary Relevance: The Services Transition, China, and Open Questions Whether the second great sectoral transition — manufacturing to services — raises or lowers regional inequality remains the central open question, and the corpus's answer is conditional on diffusion. Eckert and Peters conjecture that today's shift toward services may be amplifying regional inequality precisely because technology appears to diffuse more slowly in the service sector than it did in agriculture and manufacturing; this is a conjecture about parameter values, not a direct test, and no paper in this collection estimates a services catch-up parameter (eckert-peters-2022-spatial-structural-change). The Chinese evidence is indirect but suggestive. Zhao, Chen, and Fu's application of the dynamic toolkit finds that population distribution, not capital accumulation, ultimately determines the long-run spatial structure of the Chinese economy — capital adjusts to population in the long run, so regional outcomes hinge on where people can move — and that per-capita incomes converge across provinces only partially, because idiosyncratic locational preferences prevent absolute convergence (zhao-chen-fu-2022-dynamic-qse-china). Wu and You calibrate a system-of-cities model to China and show that most large cities have already surpassed their locally optimal size while remaining below their nationally optimal size, so migration restrictions that restrain city growth tend to reduce aggregate welfare even where they correct local overexpansion (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Li, Ma, and Tang quantify a complementary margin: firm-level frictions are more dispersed in poorer prefectures, and reducing that dispersion raises aggregate welfare while lowering spatial inequality, whereas migration liberalization with unchanged frictions raises welfare but worsens spatial inequality because people move toward already-large, less-distorted cities (li-ma-tang-2024-migration-misallocation). Current assessment (2026-07): Whether the manufacturing-to-services transition is amplifying regional inequality is conjectural in this corpus. Eckert and Peters flag weaker diffusion in services as the likely culprit, but no direct estimate of a services catch-up parameter exists here. The Chinese applications are consistent with the diffusion mechanism — spatial inequality falls when lagging regions can catch up — but none of them isolates the services channel, and the historical results' external validity for contemporary service economies remains untested. pages.title: Trade and Migration Cost Reductions in China
headings: Frontier: QSE Policy Translation for China
pages.excerpt: Between 2000 and 2007, China experienced simultaneous reductions in internal trade costs — driven by the dismantling of inter-provincial trade barriers, state-owned enterprise reforms, and transport infrastructure expansion — and in migration costs, following the relaxation of…
pages.text: Between 2000 and 2007, China experienced simultaneous reductions in internal trade costs — driven by the dismantling of inter-provincial trade barriers, state-owned enterprise reforms, and transport infrastructure expansion — and in migration costs, following the relaxation of the hukou household registration system. These cost declines fueled the largest internal migration in human history and a rapid increase in inter-provincial trade. Using an Eaton-Kortum quantitative spatial equilibrium model with endogenous migration, Tombe and Zhu (2019) find that the combined reduction in internal trade and migration costs accounts for roughly 28 percent of China's aggregate labor productivity growth between 2000 and 2005, while external trade cost reductions associated with WTO accession account for only 8 percent. This finding fundamentally challenges the "export-led growth" narrative for China and redirects attention to the productivity gains from internal market integration and labor mobility. Subsequent work using a Melitz-based framework (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade) reaches complementary results for aggregate welfare but reveals sharply different predictions for the local distribution of migration's benefits, a tension with direct implications for hukou reform policy. Background: Internal Barriers in 2000 At the turn of the century, China's internal economic integration was severely constrained by overlapping frictions in goods and labor markets. Inter-provincial trade costs were substantial: the trade-weighted average cost of shipping goods between Chinese provinces was comparable to or exceeded the cost of shipping goods between China and many foreign trading partners (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Home shares of provincial expenditure — the fraction of spending allocated to locally produced goods — exceeded 80 percent in most interior provinces, reflecting a combination of local protectionist policies, underdeveloped transport infrastructure, and the legacy of planned-economy fragmentation. On the labor side, the hukou system imposed the dominant barrier. Each Chinese citizen was assigned an agricultural or non-agricultural registration tied to a specific administrative unit. Changing either the category or location of one's hukou required government approval, which was extremely difficult to obtain. Workers who migrated without changing their hukou faced restricted access to local public services, higher costs for healthcare and children's education, and — prior to the 2003 administrative reforms — the risk of arrest and deportation (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). As a consequence, despite a 4:1 ratio in real GDP per worker between the top and bottom five provinces, only 4.2 percent of total employment consisted of inter-provincial migrants in 2000. Within-province rural-to-urban migration was more common, at 14.3 percent of employment, but still modest relative to the agricultural productivity gap, which averaged roughly 4:1 within provinces as well. Cross-paper pattern: The coexistence of high internal trade barriers and severe migration restrictions in China around 2000 reflects a dual-friction structure common to many large developing economies, but the institutional form — a household registration system governing social service access combined with local government market protection — is specific to China's transitional institutional environment (wu-you-2025-urbanization). Quantitative Framework: Eaton-Kortum with Migration The core decomposition results rely on a two-sector, multi-region general equilibrium model that extends the Eaton and Kortum (2002) framework to include internal trade, international trade, and worker migration (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). The model features N Chinese provinces plus a rest-of-world region, each with agricultural and non-agricultural sectors. Productivity in each location-sector follows a Fréchet distribution with dispersion parameter $\theta = 4$, governing the elasticity of trade flows to trade costs. Goods trade is subject to iceberg costs $\tau{ni}^j$, which are estimated from observed trade shares using the Head-Ries index. Worker mobility is the key extension. Workers differ in idiosyncratic location-sector preferences, drawn from a Fréchet distribution with dispersion parameter $\kappa = 1.5$, estimated from bilateral migration flows. Migration costs $\mu{ni}^{jk}$ are modeled as flow costs — recurring utility penalties rather than one-time fixed costs — reflecting the institutional reality of the hukou system, where migrants must permanently forgo access to local public services. The collective ownership of land creates an additional barrier: workers who leave their hukou location lose claims to land income, captured by a "rebate rate" $\delta{nn}^{jj}$ that raises the effective cost of migration. This institutional realism is essential for matching the observed migration patterns, particularly the predominance of young, temporary migrants. Estimated Cost Declines (2000–2007) Both trade and migration costs fell substantially over the first half of the 2000s. Internal trade costs declined by 10–15 percent on average between 2002 and 2007, while external trade costs fell by nearly 10 percent in non-agriculture and roughly 25 percent in agriculture (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). The internal cost declines reflected a combination of deliberate policy reforms — including a 2001 State Council directive prohibiting local market protections, SOE reforms that reduced local governments' incentives for protectionism, and major investments in highway infrastructure — though the model does not separately identify the contribution of each factor. Migration costs declined even more dramatically. By 2005, average migration costs fell to 82 percent of their 2000 level, with between-province migration costs dropping to 61 percent of their initial level. In levels, the average cost of moving from rural to urban within a province in 2000 was equivalent to shrinking one's real income by a factor of nearly 3, while between-province agriculture-to-non-agriculture moves carried costs averaging 25 times income — an order of magnitude higher (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). The decline was driven by the 2003 national administrative reform that streamlined temporary residence permits, targeted hukou reforms in Beijing, Shanghai, Zhejiang, Jiangsu, and Shandong, and the expansion of the highway network that reduced the effective distance cost of moving. Decomposition Results: Internal versus External The headline quantitative result of Tombe and Zhu (2019) is that reductions in internal trade and migration costs together account for roughly 28 percent of China's aggregate labor productivity growth between 2000 and 2005 (15.8 percentage points out of 57.1 percent total growth), while external trade cost reductions account for only 8 percent (4.5 percentage points). This result is robust across all possible orders of introducing the cost changes into the counterfactual decomposition, with small standard deviations across permutations. The disproportionate importance of internal relative to external trade cost reductions stems from a simple structural fact: most Chinese provinces trade substantially more with other Chinese provinces than with foreign countries. In 2002, the average province's spending share on goods from other Chinese provinces was roughly 10–20 percent, compared to 2–14 percent on foreign imports, and the increase in internal trade shares over the period was nearly seven times larger than the increase in external trade shares (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Because the direct welfare effect of a trade cost reduction is proportional to the initial volume of trade, the larger base of internal trade delivers larger gains from a comparable proportional cost reduction. This mechanism is reinforced by input-output linkages: intermediate inputs magnify the gains from trade cost reductions, and when the model shuts down intermediate inputs, the contribution of internal trade cost reductions falls from 11.2 percent to 3.1 percent of GDP per worker. Current assessment (2026-07): The dominance of internal over external trade cost reductions in explaining China's growth during the WTO accession period has been broadly accepted in the QSE literature and is consistent with similar findings for other large economies (Caliendo, Parro, and Tsyvinski 2017). The result has shifted policy attention toward internal market integration as a growth strategy. Gains from Migration Reallocation The estimated reduction in migration costs generates substantial reallocation of labor from agriculture to non-agriculture and from interior to coastal provinces. In response to the measured cost declines, the stock of within-province migrants increased by roughly 15 percent and between-province migrants by roughly 82 percent (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). The national share of labor in agriculture declined by 3 percentage points. Approximately 90 percent of the aggregate productivity gains from migration come from agriculture-to-non-agriculture reallocation, reflecting the large and persistent sectoral productivity gap. Aggregate labor productivity rises by 4.8 percent and aggregate welfare by 11.1 percent from the migration cost reductions alone. The larger welfare gain reflects the direct utility benefit of lower migration costs for migrants themselves, in addition to the productivity gain from reallocation. Importantly, these gains are substantially smaller than the 10.8 percent productivity gain implied by a back-of-the-envelope calculation that ignores diminishing returns. Land as a fixed factor dampens the productivity gain from 4.8 to 5.3 percent when removed, and regional comparative advantage further reduces it to 6.5 percent when goods are assumed to be perfect substitutes. The full model's lower estimate highlights the importance of general equilibrium forces in migration analysis. Remaining Scope for Reform Despite the substantial declines, internal trade and migration costs in China remain high relative to developed-economy benchmarks, implying large potential gains from further reform. Lowering China's average internal trade costs to the levels measured in Canada would generate welfare gains of roughly 12.5 percent in real GDP and 16.3 percent in aggregate welfare (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Reducing migration costs to levels consistent with US inter-state mobility rates — where roughly one-third of workers live outside their state of birth — would increase real GDP per worker by 12.8 percent and welfare by a dramatic 45.6 percent, as the direct welfare effect of lower migration costs compounds the productivity gain. Land reform offers a third channel. Under China's collective land ownership system, migrants forfeit the returns to land in their home registration area. Allowing workers to retain land income regardless of residence — equivalent to private land ownership with a functioning rental market — would increase the stock of migrants dramatically: within-province migrants nearly double and between-province migrants rise by 38 percent (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). The welfare gain from land reform alone is nearly 12 percent, though real GDP per worker falls by 2.4 percent as workers move disproportionately from high-GDP urban areas to lower-GDP rural areas, revealing an important distinction between welfare and measured output effects. Current assessment (2026-07): The estimated potential gains from further hukou reform in Tombe and Zhu (2019) are consistent with the broader range estimated in the optimal city size literature, including Wu and You (2025), who find that most large Chinese cities are above their locally optimal population but below the nationally optimal level. Modeling Contrast: Eaton-Kortum versus Melitz The Tombe and Zhu (2019) framework builds on the Eaton-Kortum model, which assumes perfect competition, constant returns to scale, and — crucially — no firm entry and exit margin. This modeling choice has important implications for the predicted local welfare effects of migration. In the Eaton-Kortum structure, inflows of workers depress local nominal wages through increased labor supply, and because there is no endogenous increase in the number of firms or product varieties, the wage reduction translates directly into lower local real income. The aggregate gains from migration in this framework come entirely from the reallocation of labor across space and sectors, not from local variety or scale effects. Ma and Tang (2020) develop an alternative framework based on the Melitz (2003) model, featuring monopolistic competition, heterogeneous firms, fixed entry costs, and endogenous firm entry and exit. In this structure, migration inflows have two countervailing local effects. On the one hand, they depress nominal wages and increase congestion, as in the Eaton-Kortum framework. On the other hand, they expand local market size, induce entry of new firms, increase product variety, and lower the ideal price index. The net local welfare effect is theoretically ambiguous. In the quantitative application to 279 Chinese prefecture-level cities, Ma and Tang (2020) find that the variety channel dominates: all 40 cities receiving net population inflows experience higher real wages and welfare, with an average real income gain of 4.7 percent and welfare gain of 4.0 percent. When they shut down the firm entry margin — thereby replicating the Eaton-Kortum structure within their model — the local impacts of migration turn negative, confirming that the modeling choice is the decisive factor. Cross-paper pattern: The Eaton-Kortum versus Melitz contrast is one of the most consequential modeling choices in the applied QSE literature for China, as it reverses the sign of migration's local welfare effect and therefore inverts the policy implications for hukou liberalization. Resolving this tension is an active frontier. Frontier: QSE Policy Translation for China The Tombe-Zhu framework has been extended and refined along several dimensions that deepen its relevance for Chinese policy design. Li, Ma, and Tang (2024) introduce firm-level output and labor frictions into a multi-region Melitz framework with migration, showing that within-prefecture misallocation of resources across firms interacts meaningfully with migration flows. They find that reducing the dispersion of firm-level frictions increases aggregate welfare by 3.19 percent (for a 0.01 reduction in standard deviations), and crucially, that migration alleviates the aggregate impact of these micro-frictions — people leave heavily distorted regions for less distorted ones — but worsens spatial inequality. This extension demonstrates that the gains from migration liberalization and the gains from reducing within-region misallocation are substitutes for aggregate welfare but have opposite effects on spatial equity. The post-2005 expansion of digital infrastructure has further reduced internal trade costs through channels not captured in the 2000–2005 period studied by Tombe and Zhu. The construction of fiber-optic networks and the development of data markets create new mechanisms for spatial integration — data as a non-rival factor can reduce coordination costs across regions and enable new forms of inter-provincial trade in services (lin-liu-zhou-2026-data-market). Network infrastructure improvements continue to lower the effective distance between Chinese cities, complementing the earlier wave of highway expansion (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). These developments suggest that the internal trade cost reductions documented for 2000–2007 may have continued, with implications for the ongoing policy push toward a "unified domestic market." Current assessment (2026-07): The QSE framework for China has matured from a single-model decomposition exercise into a family of extended models incorporating firm heterogeneity, dynamic migration, infrastructure network effects, and non-rival data factors. The challenge for policy translation is to determine which modeling assumptions best capture the specific mechanism targeted by a given reform — Eaton-Kortum for aggregate reallocation effects, Melitz for local welfare and variety effects, and Li-Ma-Tang for firm-level distortion interactions. pages.title: Transport Infrastructure and Urban Welfare
headings: Market Access as the Causal Channel
Digital and Network Infrastructure as Trade-Cost Reducers
pages.excerpt: Transport infrastructure is the single most policy-relevant application of the quantitative spatial equilibrium (QSE) toolkit, and the corpus assembled here spans every scale of the question: the U.S. Interstate Highway System in a continuous-space model, a transport improvement…
pages.text: Transport Infrastructure and Urban Welfare Transport infrastructure is the single most policy-relevant application of the quantitative spatial equilibrium (QSE) toolkit, and the corpus assembled here spans every scale of the question: the U.S. Interstate Highway System in a continuous-space model, a transport improvement in a synthetic grid economy with mobile labor, Bogotá's TransMilenio bus rapid transit within a single city, the removal of the automobile from Berlin, commuting-cost reductions across U.S. counties, endogenous infrastructure in the First Industrial Revolution, and China's network and digital infrastructure. The unifying answer is threefold. First, the causal channel through which transport investment raises welfare is market access — the general-equilibrium reorganization of where people live, where firms produce, and what goods trade where — rather than the direct saving of travel time. Second, standard cost-benefit measures built on time savings or direct transport-cost reductions capture only part of the welfare gain, because the rest arrives through reallocation, agglomeration, and trade linkages that those measures miss. Third, the gains are heterogeneous: they depend on the characteristics and centrality of the locations connected, on who can substitute away from costly commutes, and on whether the activity that appears in one place is created or merely moved from another. Market Access as the Causal Channel The mechanism common to every scale is market access. A transport improvement lowers the cost of reaching jobs, workers, and suppliers, and in general equilibrium this shifts the price index, wages, employment, and land prices across space — effects that accrue even to locations not directly on the new infrastructure. The canonical statement comes from allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography, whose continuous-space model of the U.S. economy estimates trade costs from the actual transportation network and computes the counterfactual removal of the Interstate Highway System. The price index rises most in the Rocky Mountains — the most remote region — while California and the Eastern Seaboard, with better alternative modes and closer production, lose least; population redistributes accordingly. Welfare depends on the change in the share of expenditure on locally produced goods, a sufficient statistic for a location's accessibility to the rest of the economy. Within cities, Tsivanidis operationalizes market access as commuter market access, decomposed into a residential component (RCMA, residents' access to jobs) and a firm component (FCMA, firms' access to workers). TransMilenio increased access to jobs most in Bogotá's outskirts and firms' access to workers most in the center; the model predicts — and the data confirm — that changes in these two access terms, together with reduced-form elasticities of population, employment, and floorspace prices to them, are sufficient statistics for the change in the entire distribution of activity across the city (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). At the county scale, monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting shows commuting openness is itself a margin of infrastructure policy: reductions in the ease of commuting between counties — the empirical counterpart of road and transit investment — raise aggregate welfare by around 3.3% for the median observed improvement, large relative to the gains from opening the closed economy to international trade. Across the corpus the framing is the same: infrastructure is not a local treatment but a change in the access of every location to every other, and the welfare object is the general-equilibrium response to that change (allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography; tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure; redding-rossi-hansberg-2017-quantitative-spatial). Time Savings vs. General Equilibrium The benchmark against which all of these results are measured is the value of travel time saved (VTTS): the standard practice multiplies the reduction in travel time by the value of time and sums it up. The corpus shows this first-order measure is systematically incomplete. Tsivanidis provides the sharpest statement: an application of the envelope theorem to the social planner's problem in an efficient economy shows that the elasticity of welfare to a transit change is exactly proportional to a weighted average of time savings, so in an efficient equilibrium with an infinitesimal shock the VTTS is the correct first-order welfare effect. In Bogotá, however, the VTTS delivers a welfare gain of 1.25% against 2.39% for the full general-equilibrium model — the VTTS captures only about 52% of the total, with roughly one quarter of the gap approximation error from the finite shock and three quarters due to amenity and productivity externalities; Tsivanidis rejects the hypothesis that the VTTS accounts for the whole gain (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). The Interstate-Highway counterfactual points the same way: the welfare loss from removing the system (1.1–1.4%) comes substantially from general-equilibrium price-index and reallocation effects rather than from direct time savings alone (allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography). Across Tsivanidis, Redding, and Allen–Arkolakis, general-equilibrium and indirect effects are roughly half or more of measured infrastructure welfare, so a cost-benefit analysis that values only time savings understates the returns to transport investment (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure; redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare; allen-arkolakis-2014-trade-topography). Reallocation vs. Creation of Activity A second, related distinction separates the movement of existing activity across space from the creation of new activity, and reduced-form infrastructure regressions — comparing locations directly treated by a new road or railroad to untreated locations — cannot tell the two apart. In Redding's grid economy, the transport improvement raises the common level of expected utility by around 9% while population reallocations range up to roughly 60% — reallocations are large relative to welfare, echoing Fogel's point that large-scale reallocation need not imply welfare gains of the same magnitude. Because expected utility is equalized across locations, the welfare effect on treated locations is shared with the economy as a whole, and the true welfare treatment effect is zero: the reduced-form effects the model generates — positive for population, wages, land rents, and even for an "immobile welfare" measure computed under the false assumption of immobile labor — mask this, and an analyst using that measure would estimate a treatment effect of 0.2179, an order of magnitude larger than the truth (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare). This is the general-equilibrium-treatment-effect critique of infrastructure evaluation. Treated locations gain population and wages partly at the expense of untreated locations and partly through genuine gains in access; only a structural model that separates the market-access channel from the reallocation channel can distinguish creation from movement. Tsivanidis makes the same point within a city, where the general-equilibrium adjustment of commuting and land and labor markets is the mechanism through which transit gains are realized, not a nuisance to be differenced out (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Current assessment (2026-07): Reduced-form infrastructure regressions cannot separate reallocation from creation. When welfare — rather than local population or output — is the object, a structural model with mobile factors and market access is required; the QSE results imply the ratio of reallocation to net welfare creation can be as large as six or seven to one (redding-2016-goods-trade-factor-mobility-welfare; tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Infrastructure, Density, and Agglomeration Feedbacks Transport investment interacts with agglomeration, and the interaction runs in both directions: infrastructure that raises access to dense centers can strengthen agglomeration economies, but lower transport costs can also weaken the density that generates agglomeration, with dynamic consequences that are often counterintuitive. The Berlin evidence makes the density channel concrete. Ahlfeldt, Redding, Sturm, and Wolf estimate a quantitative urban model on the natural experiment of Berlin's division and reunification, in which the loss and restoration of access to the pre-war central business district shifted land prices, workplace, and residence employment exactly as the model predicts. Their out-of-sample counterfactual removes the automobile: if travel times were those of public transport alone, total city employment and output would fall by around 14% and 12%, with floor prices declining by 20% and locations becoming less specialized. The commuting technology itself — the infrastructure that lets people live apart from where they work — is what allows cities to realize the productivity of their densest locations (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). TransMilenio shows the same feedbacks within a developing city, raising productivity in newly accessible employment locations and reshaping amenities through changes in neighborhood composition — the externalities behind most of the VTTS gap (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). But the relationship between lower transport costs and agglomeration is not monotonic. Desmet and Rossi-Hansberg show that although increases in transport costs lead to the standard static losses familiar from trade models, they also generate dynamic gains by producing denser areas that, together with a scale effect in innovation, imply faster growth (desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development). Trew finds the same tension in the First Industrial Revolution: higher transport costs encourage the spatial concentration that lets firms reach the scale required to overcome the fixed costs of innovation, so a reduction in transport costs can actually delay the industrial takeoff (trew-2014-spatial-takeoff). Cross-paper pattern (2026-07): A transport-cost/agglomeration tension runs through the growth models. In Desmet–Rossi-Hansberg and Trew, lower transport costs weaken density and slow the innovation density supports, so static welfare gains can be partially offset by slower dynamic growth. In the static urban models of Ahlfeldt et al. and Tsivanidis, by contrast, density feedbacks amplify the static gains. The sign depends on whether the density channel operates through static productivity spillovers (amplifying) or scale-dependent innovation (potentially dampening) (desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development; trew-2014-spatial-takeoff; ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Distributional and Incidence Effects Who captures the gains from transport infrastructure is as important as their total size, and the corpus shows that the incidence is not what simple intuition suggests. In Bogotá, the poor rely most heavily on public transit — before TransMilenio, low-educated workers were about 23% more likely than the rich to use buses rather than cars, and buses were 36% slower. Yet the full model shows that welfare inequality actually rises by a mild 0.59% because of the BRT. Two forces favor the high-skilled. First, incidence depends on the ability to substitute away from costly commutes: high-skilled workers have more inelastic demand for particular home and work locations (a lower commuting elasticity), so they bear more of the costs of long commutes and benefit more when those commutes are shortened. Second, the large shift in the supply of low-skilled labor across the city lowers low-skilled wages. These forces offset the direct benefit the poor receive from using the system more (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). The pattern generalizes. Monte, Redding, and Rossi-Hansberg show that the elasticity of local employment to a labor-demand shock varies from around 0.5 to 2.5 across U.S. counties and commuting zones, well explained by commuting openness — so the incidence of any infrastructure or productivity change depends on the pre-existing structure of commuting linkages, not just on who is treated (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting). In Berlin, the auto-removal counterfactual shows floor prices fall substantially more in remote locations with poor public transport than in central ones, so the welfare cost of losing the automobile is borne disproportionately by the least accessible residents (ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). The within-city versus across-city distinction also shapes incidence. Wu and You find, in a system of cities calibrated to China, that most large cities have surpassed their locally optimal sizes even though they are too small from the national perspective; relaxing internal migration restrictions would raise migrant and aggregate welfare but lower the average welfare of natives in the most desirable cities through crowding and higher housing costs (wu-you-2025-urbanization). This local-versus-national tension is the distributional heart of the infrastructure question, and it is why land-value capture is attractive as a financing and incidence instrument: Tsivanidis estimates that a well-targeted scheme selling development rights near stations would have increased the welfare gains of TransMilenio by around 36% while covering 19–64% of its capital costs (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Endogenous Infrastructure and Path Dependence Infrastructure is not only an exogenous shock; it is also an endogenous outcome, and the corpus shows that the spatial pattern of infrastructure investment — not just its total amount — determines its growth effects. Trew develops a model of the First Industrial Revolution in which transport infrastructure is built endogenously by infrastructure companies that lease land and collect rents from the firms that use the improved transport. The counterfactuals are striking: bringing the spatially heterogeneous infrastructure improvements forward by 50 years accelerates the industrial takeoff from 1782.7 to 1777.6, while bringing the same improvements forward uniformly — spreading each period's investment evenly across all locations — delays takeoff to 1787.3, with growth never reaching 1.5% in the simulated period. The mechanism is the tension identified above: localized infrastructure releases transport labor into manufacturing and agriculture, making firms large enough to amortize the fixed costs of innovation, while uniform improvements lower transport costs everywhere and mute the gains from releasing labor out of transport services (trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure). The path dependence is historical as well as spatial. In Trew's earlier work on the spatial takeoff, the location of the industrial revolution depends on initial manufacturing productivity and energy costs — Newcastle's cheap coal cannot overcome its distance from London and low initial productivity, so the North of England remains the cradle of industrialization across all transport-policy counterfactuals (trew-2014-spatial-takeoff). Infrastructure, once built, is persistent, and the locations it connects inherit an advantage that later policy can reinforce or fail to reverse. Current wiki assessment: The endogenous-infrastructure result — that localized, targeted infrastructure investment can accelerate growth while uniform investment may not — is the strongest policy message of the historical papers, and it resonates with the modern market-access evidence: what matters is not the miles built but the access to dense markets they create (trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure). Digital and Network Infrastructure as Trade-Cost Reducers The Chinese extension treats digital and network infrastructure as the modern analogue of roads and rails: an investment that lowers the cost of transacting across regions. Liu, Zhang, and Cai build a multi-industry QSE model with input-output linkages and measure the welfare effect of China's network-infrastructure build-out. They estimate that network infrastructure caused a cumulative decline in inter-regional trade costs of about 3.19% and raised aggregate welfare by roughly 10.3% over 2012–2019 — robust to the trade elasticity, base year, and tariff assumptions, and rising to 11.09% when interregional labor mobility is allowed. The gain decomposes into a direct trade-cost channel and an input-output channel: network infrastructure both lowers the cost of moving goods, benefiting tradable industries, and strengthens input-output linkages that spill over to non-tradable industries (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure). The mechanism is the same as for physical infrastructure — reduced trade costs raise market access — but the welfare magnitude matches or exceeds that of major institutional reforms. Tombe and Zhu estimate that reductions in China's internal trade and migration costs between 2000 and 2005 account for a large share of aggregate labor productivity growth, with internal reforms more important than external trade liberalization; moving internal trade costs to Canadian levels would raise aggregate welfare by 16.3% (real GDP up 12.5%), while lowering migration costs to U.S. mobility levels would raise welfare by 45.6% (tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Ma and Tang similarly show that inter-city migration amplifies the welfare gains from trade through endogenous firm entry, with migrant inflows raising destination-city welfare by about 4% despite congestion (ma-tang-2020-geography-trade). Network investment thereby joins these institutional reforms on the same footing. Current assessment (2026-07): China's network infrastructure delivers welfare gains (~10.3%) comparable to those from major institutional reforms such as hukou relaxation and road construction, and operates through the same market-access and input-output channels the transport literature identifies. Narrowing the digital divide is welfare-enhancing for efficiency as well as equity, because it is the reduction in trade costs — which requires balanced rather than lopsided network coverage — that drives the aggregate gain (liu-zhang-cai-2026-network-infrastructure; tombe-zhu-2019-trade-migration-china). Open Questions Several questions remain open across the corpus. First, measuring the full general-equilibrium welfare gains requires taking congestion, housing supply, and land-value capture seriously: Tsivanidis shows congestion slightly raises the measured welfare gain of transit, while the failure of housing supply to respond is precisely why land-value capture would have added a third to the gains (tsivanidis-2026-urban-transit-infrastructure). Second, external validity across city types is uncertain — parameters estimated in Bogotá or Berlin may not transfer to cities with different transport networks, housing markets, or income distributions (monte-redding-rossi-hansberg-2018-commuting; ahlfeldt-redding-sturm-wolf-2015-economics-density). Third, dynamic welfare remains largely unmeasured: the static models capture the equilibrium response to infrastructure but not the long-run growth effects, which can amplify or offset the static gains depending on whether density strengthens or weakens innovation (desmet-rossi-hansberg-2014-spatial-development; trew-2020-endogenous-infrastructure). Fourth, the political economy of who pays for and captures infrastructure gains — the local-versus-national tension in Wu and You, the natives-versus-migrants incidence in Tsivanidis, the fiscal-equalization trade-offs in the Chinese applications — is the least understood dimension (wu-you-2025-urbanization).
